Proposal for Ripasudil (Y-39983; Selleckchem S8443)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Ripasudil, also known by its research designation Y-39983 and commercially available as Selleckchem S8443, is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor developed originally as a Rho‐associated coiled‐coil containing protein kinase (ROCK) inhibitor. It belongs to a class of therapeutics that act in an ATP‐competitive manner to inhibit the activity of ROCK isoforms, enzymes that are critical regulators of actomyosin contractility and cell adhesion. Ripasudil was synthesized following the structural optimization of earlier compounds such as fasudil and Y-27632, with the aim of increasing both potency and ocular tolerability. Its chemical origins are linked to the rational design strategies that sought to improve enzyme inhibitory selectivity and to enhance the pharmacokinetic profile for local ocular application. Members of the ROCK inhibitor class have seen prior use in settings that require modulation of actin cytoskeleton dynamics, such as the treatment of glaucoma via enhanced aqueous humor outflow, and have also been explored in contexts involving wound healing and anti-fibrotic effects in various ocular tissues (Chatzimichail et al., 2025; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, ripasudil has been approved in Japan for the treatment of glaucoma and ocular hypertension, where it is delivered topically in the form of eye drops, demonstrating a well-established safety profile and a low incidence of systemic adverse effects. In preclinical models, it has demonstrated efficacy by increasing ocular blood flow, modifying trabecular meshwork cell contractility, and reducing intraocular pressure, thereby serving as a stepping stone and proof-of-concept for the utility of ROCK inhibitors in ocular disorders. Beyond its approved use in glaucoma, investigations of ROCK inhibitors—including ripasudil—have extended into experimental applications in corneal endothelial regeneration and have been evaluated in combination with anti-VEGF therapies for diabetic macular edema. Although direct clinical evidence specifically for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is not available, multiple lines of preclinical research have shown that the ROCK inhibitor class modulates pathways which are believed to underlie the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Notably, the mechanistic studies have identified the role of ROCK signaling in cytoskeletal reorganization, matrix contractility, and fibrosis, all of which are processes particularly relevant to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) barrier dysfunction seen in dry AMD (Singh & Singh, 2023; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Moreover, the ocular pharmacokinetic profile of ripasudil—demonstrated by rabbit intravitreal studies showing a half-life of approximately 14 hours and negligible systemic exposure—is supportive of repurposing this candidate for posterior segment indications, including dry AMD (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, ripasudil exerts its therapeutic activity by competitively inhibiting the ATP-binding site of ROCK isoforms, thereby preventing the phosphorylation of downstream effectors such as myosin light-chain (MLC), myosin-binding subunit of MLC phosphatase (MYPT1), and LIM kinase. These phosphorylation events normally lead to enhanced actomyosin contractility, stress-fiber formation, focal adhesion assembly, and ultimately contribute to a contractile, stiffened cell phenotype. In the context of the retinal pigment epithelium, this contractility is thought to be exacerbated under conditions of oxidative stress, contributing to disassembly or mislocalization of tight junction proteins such as zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin, which are essential for maintaining transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and barrier integrity. By inhibiting ROCK, ripasudil reduces actomyosin-driven contraction and stress-fiber formation, thereby promoting cortical F-actin remodeling and facilitating the proper membrane relocalization of tight-junction proteins. The specificity of ripasudil has been demonstrated by its greater than 100-fold selectivity against other kinases such as protein kinase C (PKC) and myotonic dystrophy kinase-related Cdc42-binding kinase (MRCK), highlighting the mechanistic precision by which it modulates ROCK-dependent signaling cascades (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Additionally, while several studies indicate that the ROCK inhibitor class generally targets both ROCK1 and ROCK2 isoforms, quantitative biochemical data have shown that ripasudil exhibits potent enzyme inhibitory activity with IC₅₀s in the low nanomolar range (with values reported around 51 nM for ROCK1 and 19 nM for ROCK2 in some studies, though the candidate hypothesis posits values of approximately 29 nM for ROCK1 and 68 nM for ROCK2). This inhibitory profile is particularly relevant because emerging research indicates that ROCK2, in particular, is upregulated in the pathological conditions of dry AMD and plays a key role in mediating cytoskeletal changes that disrupt RPE tight junction integrity (Adams & Papillon, 2020; Cheng et al., 2025). The inhibition of ROCK thereby is expected to have a dual benefit of cytoprotection and restoration of cell junction architecture, ultimately leading to improved barrier function (Ghenciu et al., 2025; Singh & Singh, 2023).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing ripasudil for dry AMD is that by blocking ROCK activity in oxidatively stressed retinal pigment epithelium cells, the compound will lead to a reduction in actomyosin contractility, thereby alleviating the formation of pathological stress fibers that otherwise disrupt the organization of tight junction complexes. Under normal physiological conditions, tight junction proteins such as ZO-1 and occludin are localized at the plasma membrane in a continuous, belt-like manner that is essential to maintain TEER and restrict paracellular permeability. However, in dry AMD, oxidative damage, inflammation, and mechanical stress lead to cytoskeletal reorganization and a discontinuous distribution of these critical proteins, resulting in impaired barrier function and contributing to the pathogenesis of the disease. Preclinical studies, particularly those employing ARPE-19 cell models subjected to toxic insults such as paraquat or sodium iodate (NaIO₃), have demonstrated that ROCK inhibitors can dose-dependently restore TEER (with reported improvements up to 70%) and re-establish the membrane continuity of ZO-1, suggesting that these agents can “rescue” the RPE barrier phenotype under injurious conditions (Singh & Singh, 2023; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). It is expected that ripasudil, with its potent ROCK-inhibitory activity and favorable ocular pharmacokinetics (including intravitreal retention times supportive of sustained action), will similarly promote the cortical redistribution of F-actin, leading to the re-localization of junctional molecules back to the cell membrane. This mechanistic restoration should result in improved transepithelial electrical resistance and a concomitant reduction in paracellular permeability, effectively reinforcing the RPE barrier—a central therapeutic target in dry AMD. Moreover, the activation of protective cellular pathways through ROCK inhibition may also confer additional anti-apoptotic and anti-inflammatory effects, further contributing to the survival and functional integrity of the RPE under chronic oxidative stress (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating ripasudil as a candidate for repurposing in dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths become apparent. First, its established clinical use for glaucoma means that its safety, tolerability, and ocular pharmacokinetic properties are well characterized—attributes that significantly lower the translational barrier for its application in other ocular diseases. The intravitreal pharmacokinetic data, with a half-life of approximately 14 hours in rabbit models and negligible systemic exposure, suggest that therapeutic concentrations capable of modulating ROCK activity in the retina can be achieved with acceptable dosing regimens (Yamaguchi et al., 2016). Second, the mechanistic rationale is compelling: ROCK signaling is intimately involved in mediating actomyosin contractility, stress-fiber formation, and subsequent disruption of tight junction architecture in epithelial cells. Given that ROCK2 in particular is implicated in the pathological processes observed in the RPE in dry AMD, the ability of ripasudil to inhibit this pathway could translate into measurable improvements in barrier function, as indicated by preclinical assays demonstrating TEER restoration and the re-localization of ZO-1 in ARPE-19 cells (Singh & Singh, 2023; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Third, the compound exhibits a favorable selectivity profile, with negligible off-target activity against other kinases such as PKC and MRCK, which minimizes the risk of unintended effects in non-target tissues. This specificity is critical when repurposing drugs for chronic conditions such as dry AMD, where long-term ocular safety is paramount (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Despite these strengths, there are notable weaknesses and gaps that must be addressed before ripasudil can be confidently advanced as a therapeutic for dry AMD. A primary limitation is the paucity of direct experimental evidence in RPE models of dry AMD. While the hypothesis is supported by data from related in vitro systems (e.g., ARPE-19 cells subjected to oxidative stress), robust in vivo studies in animal models that recapitulate the full spectrum of dry AMD pathophysiology are still needed. In particular, data demonstrating that ripasudil can restore tight junction integrity and improve TEER in the context of chronic, progressive RPE dysfunction remain limited (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Furthermore, although the compound’s ROCK inhibitory activity is well documented, the available literature does not consistently detail the isoform-specific effects in RPE cells; given that ROCK1 and ROCK2 may play distinct roles in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, clarifying the relative contributions of each isoform is essential. The candidate hypothesis posits specific IC₅₀ values for ROCK1 and ROCK2, yet discrepancies exist across reported studies regarding the precise inhibitory concentrations, which indicates that further biochemical characterization is warranted (Adams & Papillon, 2020; Cheng et al., 2025). Another consideration is the potential for adverse effects when repurposing a drug originally optimized for anterior-segment diseases for posterior-segment applications. Although the ocular safety profile of ripasudil in glaucoma is well established, the long-term impact of ROCK inhibition on RPE cell biology in an aged population—especially in the context of dry AMD—remains uncertain. Off-target cytoskeletal effects in other retinal cell types, possible modulation of inflammatory responses, and the risk of inadvertently triggering compensatory signaling pathways are all factors that must be carefully evaluated in preclinical studies (Iancu et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2025). Lastly, while the pharmacokinetic data support retinal exposure after intravitreal or possibly topical administration, optimizing the delivery method to ensure sustained and localized drug levels in the RPE without causing ocular surface toxicity (such as conjunctival hyperemia or corneal epithelial disturbances) will be critical. Innovative delivery systems, such as sustained-release intravitreal implants or depot formulations, may offer solutions but require further development (Yamaguchi et al., 2016; Singh & Singh, 2023).

In conclusion, the repurposing of ripasudil for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration is supported by a strong mechanistic rationale and a favorable safety profile derived from its established use in glaucoma. The compound’s capacity to inhibit ROCK-mediated actomyosin contraction and promote cortical F-actin remodeling positions it as a promising agent for restoring RPE barrier function—one of the key pathological features of dry AMD. However, the current literature reveals significant gaps in direct evidence regarding its effects on RPE tight junction proteins, TEER restoration, and the isoform-specific roles of ROCK in the RPE under oxidative stress. To advance ripasudil as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, additional preclinical investigations—ideally incorporating robust animal models of dry AMD and detailed biochemical analyses of ROCK isoform activity in RPE cells—are required. Additionally, optimizations in drug delivery methodology to achieve sustained posterior-segment exposure while minimizing adverse ocular events will be imperative. Overall, ripasudil presents a compelling candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, with its strengths in mechanistic specificity, favorable ocular pharmacokinetics, and established clinical safety underscoring its potential. Nonetheless, the outlined weaknesses and knowledge gaps necessitate a rigorous program of targeted research to validate its efficacy in restoring RPE barrier integrity and to ensure its long-term safety in the intended patient population (Chatzimichail et al., 2025; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Singh & Singh, 2023; Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Adams & Papillon, 2020; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Proposal for SAR407899 (Selleckchem S2921)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SAR407899 (Selleckchem S2921) is a small-molecule ATP-competitive inhibitor of Rho-associated coiled-coil containing kinases (ROCKs) that targets both ROCK1 and ROCK2, placing it within the widely studied class of dual ROCK1/2 inhibitors used as chemical tools and therapeutic candidates across vascular, fibrotic, and ocular indications driven by actomyosin contractility and cytoskeletal dysregulation (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). The ATP-binding pockets of ROCK1 and ROCK2 are highly conserved, which has historically favored development of dual-isoform inhibitors (e.g., fasudil, Y-27632, ripasudil, netarsudil) rather than isoform-selective agents; SAR407899 is listed among this majority class of dual-acting molecules in contemporary reviews of rho-kinase modulators for retinal disease (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Multiple dual ROCK inhibitors have been clinically applied: fasudil is approved systemically for cerebral vasospasm and has been evaluated intravitreally for retinal disease, while ripasudil and netarsudil are approved as topical ophthalmic solutions for glaucoma/ocular hypertension, establishing the translational precedent and safety framework for the class in ocular tissues (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Leong et al., 2025). At a mechanistic level, all members of this class block ROCK catalytic activity by binding to the ATP site, thereby reducing phosphorylation of canonical substrates such as MYPT1 (the myosin phosphatase target subunit) and myosin regulatory light chain (MLC), and decreasing downstream actomyosin tension, stress fibers, and focal adhesion assembly that collectively drive barrier breakdown, contraction, and fibrosis (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Leong et al., 2025). While “soft drug” and kinase-selectivity strategies have been advanced to improve tissue targeting and reduce off-target activity, the broad conclusion from medicinal chemistry and pharmacology reviews is that most clinical-grade ROCK inhibitors remain dual-isoform ATP-competitive agents with some potential for off-target kinase interactions at higher exposures—an interpretive caveat for both efficacy and safety (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Liu et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Direct preclinical or clinical reports on SAR407899 in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) or age-related macular degeneration (AMD) were not identified in the provided literature set; the compound is listed among “double-acting ROCK inhibitor molecules” considered for retinal vascular disease, but no SAR407899-specific ocular pharmacokinetic, penetration, or efficacy data are supplied in the excerpts (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). In contrast, there is substantial class-level evidence that dual ROCK1/2 inhibition is active in posterior segment disease biology relevant to dry AMD pathogenesis and sequelae (barrier failure, low-grade inflammation, extracellular matrix remodeling), and that ROCK pathway blockade by other chemotypes can beneficially modulate RPE/retinal fibrosis and endothelial barrier endpoints across models (Nourinia et al., 2018; Zandi et al., 2025). For endothelial barrier function, ripasudil preserved ZO-1 localization and reversed VEGF-induced TEER loss in human retinal microvascular endothelial cells (HRMECs), and suppressed retinal p-MYPT1 in a murine retinal vein occlusion model, demonstrating target engagement and barrier preservation by ROCK inhibition in retina (albeit on the vascular rather than RPE side of the BRB) (Hida et al., 2018). For RPE morphology and barrier integrity in vivo, intravitreally applied fasudil reversed Rho pathway–driven cytoskeletal abnormalities (apical constriction and stress fibers) and improved RPE barrier integrity in disease-relevant paradigms, establishing that pan-ROCK antagonism can correct RPE junctional dysfunction at the tissue level (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). In fibrotic endpoints applicable to geographic atrophy progression and subretinal scarring, both pan-ROCK (fasudil) and ROCK2-selective (belumosudil) inhibitors reduced canonical fibrosis drivers (TGF-β1, fibronectin, vimentin, α-SMA) and ROCK pathway activity (p-MYPT1) in choroid–RPE complex and retina in vivo, with concomitant preservation of retinal morphology and decreased fibrosis volume in a mouse CNV-associated fibrosis model (Zandi et al., 2025). Additional dual ROCK inhibitors (AMA0428) suppressed angiogenesis, inflammation, and fibrosis in a mouse CNV model more broadly than VEGFR2 blockade alone, underscoring the ability of ROCK pathway inhibition to simultaneously normalize vessels, reduce leakage, and block matrix deposition—features highly relevant to AMD (Hollanders et al., 2015; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Clinically, small trials combining intravitreal fasudil with bevacizumab in refractory diabetic macular edema (DME) showed short-term improvements in visual acuity and central macular thickness versus anti-VEGF alone, consistent with anti-permeability and vasoregulatory actions of ROCK inhibitors in human retina; while not dry AMD, these studies provide translational class experience for retinal application and intravitreal dosing (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Nourinia et al., 2018). Taken together, the literature supports class-level efficacy signals in pathways relevant to dry AMD (barrier/tight junctions, fibrosis/TGF-β–driven contraction, vascular normalization/inflammation), but it provides no SAR407899-specific RPE or dry AMD results, PK, or ocular penetration data in the provided excerpts (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
ROCK1 and ROCK2 are serine/threonine kinases activated by RhoA-GTP that increase cellular contractility and cytoskeletal tension by two concerted mechanisms: (1) direct phosphorylation of myosin regulatory light chain (MLC), and (2) phosphorylation of MYPT1, the regulatory subunit of myosin phosphatase, which inhibits phosphatase activity and sustains high p-MLC; ROCK also signals via LIM kinases to inactivate cofilin, stabilizing actin stress fibers and focal adhesions—all of which favor junctional opening and motile/contractile phenotypes (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Leong et al., 2025). In retinal and RPE-relevant systems, this signaling axis links directly to barrier dysregulation, fibrosis, and inflammation: high glucose and VEGF increase ROCK activity and p-MLC in retinal microvascular endothelium, augmenting adhesion molecule expression (ICAM-1), leukocyte adhesion, and hyperpermeability; conversely, ROCK inhibitors reduce ICAM-1, leukostasis, endothelial damage, and vascular leakage in diabetic retina models, consistent with reduced actomyosin tension and barrier preservation (Nourinia et al., 2018). Direct demonstration of ROCK pathway inhibition in vivo includes suppression of retinal p-MYPT1 by ripasudil in a murine retinal vein occlusion model and preservation of ZO-1 and TEER in VEGF-challenged HRMECs, indicating that ROCK blockade stabilizes tight-junction complexes and restores barrier function under stress (Hida et al., 2018). In RPE, Rho/ROCK activation produces cytoskeletal remodeling (apical constriction and stress fiber formation) leading to intercellular junction opening—and intravitreally delivered fasudil reversed these morphological abnormalities and improved RPE barrier integrity, linking ROCK activity to the outer BRB in vivo (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Fibrotic contraction in vitreoretinal disease is mechanistically tied to ROCK: TGF-β–activated contractility proceeds via ROCK-dependent MLC phosphorylation, and ROCK inhibitors suppress TGF-β–induced collagen gel contraction by RPE, reduce proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) progression in rabbits, and decrease subretinal fibrosis after CNV, while lowering p-MYPT1 in choroid–RPE complex (Nourinia et al., 2018; Zandi et al., 2025). Inflammation intersects ROCK signaling via NF-κB and other pathways: ROCK activity upregulates inflammatory mediators (e.g., NF-κB targets, MCP-1/CCL2, iNOS), and ROCK inhibitors reduce inflammatory cell infiltration and cytokine production in ocular models, further supporting secondary barrier stabilization and anti-fibrotic effects (Singh & Singh, 2023; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). In AMD-relevant immunity, ROCK2-selective signaling is linked to age-related macrophage polarization toward proangiogenic M2 (MaDAMs) in human AMD eyes; ROCK2-selective inhibition improved macrophage phenotype and reduced CNV in models, whereas pan-ROCK fasudil did not share all of these benefits in the immune compartment, suggesting non-redundant isoform roles in the aging choroid–retina milieu (Nourinia et al., 2018; Yamaguchi et al., 2017). These combined data establish a coherent molecular mechanism whereby dual ROCK1/2 inhibition should reduce p-MYPT1/p-MLC, relax actomyosin tension, stabilize junctional complexes (occludin/ZO-1), oppose TGF-β–driven fibrotic conversion, and blunt inflammatory cascades that exacerbate outer BRB failure in dry AMD; however, whether dual versus ROCK2-selective inhibition optimally tunes the immune/fibrotic axis in AMD remains an open question raised by macrophage-focused studies (Nourinia et al., 2018; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed in vitro assay—complement-activated RPE monolayers exposed to IL-1β with readouts of TEER, FITC-dextran permeability, and occludin/ZO-1 transcription and membrane localization—the class mechanism predicts that a potent dual ROCK1/2 inhibitor such as SAR407899 should reduce ROCK pathway activation (↓p-MYPT1, ↓p-MLC), relax cortical actomyosin and stress fibers, and thereby re-stabilize tight junction architecture and function, yielding increased TEER, reduced paracellular flux, and normalized junctional protein localization (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Leong et al., 2025). Supportive precedent for barrier rescue by ROCK inhibition includes restoration of endothelial tight junction integrity and TEER in VEGF-challenged HRMECs by ripasudil and suppression of retinal p-MYPT1 in vivo, establishing that ROCK blockade reverses injury-induced barrier dysfunction and engages the canonical substrate axis in retina (Hida et al., 2018). In RPE, in vivo fasudil reversed Rho-pathway–induced cytoskeletal remodeling and improved barrier integrity, implying that ROCK inhibition can directly stabilize the outer BRB at the epithelial level, although quantitative TEER and occludin/ZO-1 readouts in RPE cultures are not provided in the excerpts and should be generated in the proposed assay (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Inflammatory cytokines can feed into ROCK pathway activation and barrier loss, and the Rho/ROCK axis is intertwined with NF-κB–dependent cytokine expression; therefore, ROCK inhibition in the IL-1β paradigm is mechanistically plausible for barrier rescue even though IL-1β-specific RPE TEER data are not available in the provided sources (Singh & Singh, 2023; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). Given the contribution of ROCK to TGF-β–driven epithelial–mesenchymal transition and gel contraction by RPE, a dual inhibitor is also expected to suppress fibrotic gene expression trajectories in longer assays (α-SMA, collagen/fibronectin) while relieving junctional stress that promotes delamination and barrier failure, which aligns with the anti-fibrotic outcomes seen in subretinal fibrosis models after fasudil or ROCK2-selective inhibition (Nourinia et al., 2018; Zandi et al., 2025). Of note, ROCK2-targeted approaches may provide added benefit on age-related macrophage polarization and fibrosis in AMD models, but dual inhibition has demonstrated broad anti-contractile and anti-permeability effects across ocular compartments; head-to-head comparison of dual versus ROCK2-selective inhibition under IL-1β/complement challenge would be informative (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Nourinia et al., 2018). Finally, delivery modality will strongly influence the magnitude and duration of barrier rescue: topical dosing of some ROCK inhibitors can reach the posterior segment in rabbits but shows variable retinal pharmacodynamics between agents, and intravitreal routes with sustained-release formulations have been explored for fasudil to address short intraocular half-life—implications that apply to any repurposed ROCK inhibitor considered for RPE-centric therapy (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
Strengths  
- Target validity and mechanistic convergence: ROCK1/2 are central regulators of cytoskeletal tension and tight-junction stability via the MYPT1/MLC and LIMK/cofilin axes, providing a direct mechanistic handle on epithelial barrier integrity and fibrotic conversion relevant to outer BRB failure and atrophic remodeling in dry AMD (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Leong et al., 2025). The same axis is mechanistically operative in retinal vascular endothelium where barrier protection by ROCK inhibition has been demonstrated quantitatively (TEER, ZO-1), strengthening the translational rationale for barrier rescue across the BRB (Hida et al., 2018).  
- RPE-relevant in vivo effect: Intravitreal fasudil reversed RPE cytoskeletal abnormalities and improved epithelial barrier integrity in vivo, demonstrating that the class mechanism extends to outer BRB pathology and is not restricted to vascular endothelial cells (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).  
- Anti-fibrotic efficacy in choroid–RPE complex: Both dual and ROCK2-selective inhibitors reduced fibrotic markers and p-MYPT1 in murine subretinal fibrosis models after CNV, with histologic preservation of retinal architecture and reduced fibrosis volume, supporting the concept that ROCK blockade can oppose late-stage fibrotic drivers of vision loss that are inadequately addressed by anti-VEGF monotherapy (Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Broader AMD-relevant biology: ROCK inhibition reduces angiogenesis, inflammation, and fibrosis in CNV models (e.g., AMA0428), normalizes pathological vessels, and modulates age-related macrophage polarization—processes integral to AMD pathogenesis in both neovascular and atrophic trajectories (Hollanders et al., 2015; Nourinia et al., 2018).  
- Translational feasibility: Multiple ROCK inhibitors have been successfully delivered to the eye topically and intravitreally with acceptable safety, including demonstration that topical ripasudil can reach retina/choroid in rabbits and that intravitreal fasudil combinations are feasible in small human DME studies—experience that de-risks ocular delivery strategies for the class (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Weaknesses and Gaps  
- Absence of SAR407899-specific ocular data in RPE/AMD: The provided literature contains no quantitative potency/selectivity corroboration, ocular penetration, retinal tissue levels, or preclinical efficacy for SAR407899 in RPE barrier models, IL-1β paradigms, or AMD models; thus, key assertions in the working hypothesis (e.g., occludin/ZO-1 transcriptional rescue in RPE, primary human RPE TER recovery, ocular PK levels, ERG improvements in NaIO3) are not supported here and cannot be validated from the excerpts (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021). This represents the primary evidence gap and limits compound-specific confidence versus class-level rationale (Yamaguchi et al., 2017).  
- Isoform selectivity considerations: Several AMD-relevant studies point to ROCK2-specific biology in macrophage polarization and possibly fibrosis, with selective ROCK2 inhibition conferring benefits not fully reproduced by pan-ROCK inhibitors in the aged immune compartment; whether dual inhibition is advantageous or dilutes ROCK2-targeted immune modulation in dry AMD remains unresolved (Yamaguchi et al., 2017; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).  
- Incomplete RPE barrier readouts: Although class-level rescue of endothelial TEER/ZO-1 and RPE morphological barrier integrity have been shown, the excerpts lack direct RPE TEER, permeability, or occludin/ZO-1 imaging/quantification under inflammatory (IL-1β) challenge, necessitating foundational in vitro work before prioritizing SAR407899 for in vivo dry AMD studies (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Hida et al., 2018).  
- Delivery and exposure constraints: Reviews emphasize short intraocular half-lives and the need for repeated dosing or sustained-release formulations for posterior-segment efficacy; topical penetration to retina/choroid varies across molecules (e.g., ripasudil reaches the posterior segment in rabbits whereas topical fasudil did not at matched dosing), underscoring the necessity of SAR407899-specific ocular PK and exposure–response characterization to inform route and formulation (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).  
- Off-target liabilities and dose selection: ATP-competitive ROCK inhibitors can exhibit off-target kinase inhibition at higher concentrations, raising interpretive and safety issues that must be managed through careful dose–exposure selection and orthogonal on-target biomarkers such as p-MYPT1 in ocular tissues (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Liu et al., 2018).

Programmatic Implications and Recommended Next Steps  
On the strength of the mechanistic and preclinical class data, dual ROCK1/2 inhibition remains a credible strategy to stabilize RPE junctions and suppress fibrotic conversion in dry AMD; however, SAR407899 must earn its place in this mechanism by producing compound-specific evidence on RPE barrier endpoints and ocular exposure (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Zandi et al., 2025). A staged validation package is recommended:  
- In vitro RPE barrier assays: Quantify TEER, FITC-dextran flux, and occludin/ZO-1 localization in primary human RPE or iPSC-RPE monolayers under IL-1β and complement co-challenge ± SAR407899; include p-MYPT1 and p-MLC immunoblotting or phospho-ELISA to verify on-target modulation; adopt assay conditions paralleling endothelial TEER paradigms where ROCK inhibition preserved ZO-1 and TEER (Hida et al., 2018; Kaneko et al., 2016).  
- Isoform pharmacology: Use siRNA or selective pharmacologic comparators (e.g., belumosudil for ROCK2) to benchmark dual versus ROCK2-selective effects on RPE barrier rescue and inflammatory readouts, informed by the macrophage polarization literature in AMD (Nourinia et al., 2018; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).  
- Ocular PK and delivery: Establish intraocular distribution and time–concentration profiles for SAR407899 in relevant species after topical and intravitreal routes; given literature on short half-life and variable posterior penetration, consider sustained-release intravitreal formulations analogous to those explored for fasudil if topical exposure proves inadequate (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).  
- In vivo efficacy: Progress to subretinal fibrosis or oxidative injury models that interrogate outer BRB integrity and fibrotic remodeling (e.g., CNV-associated fibrosis with extended fibrotic endpoints) to test whether SAR407899 reproduces the anti-fibrotic and barrier-preserving signals seen with fasudil/belumosudil, incorporating p-MYPT1 as a pharmacodynamic biomarker (Zandi et al., 2025).  
- Combinatorial positioning: Given evidence that ROCK inhibition complements anti-VEGF therapy by reducing inflammation and fibrosis and may normalize pathological angiogenesis without abrogating physiological revascularization, consider combination designs if SAR407899 shows single-agent barrier/fibrosis activity (Hollanders et al., 2015; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Bottom line: Repurposing SAR407899 for dry AMD is mechanistically well-justified at the class level, but the absence of SAR407899-specific ocular and RPE data in the provided literature requires a focused preclinical package to substantiate the specific claims in the hypothesis and to determine whether dual inhibition delivers the desired balance of epithelial barrier rescue and anti-fibrotic efficacy relative to ROCK2-selective alternatives (Nourinia et al., 2018; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

I cannot answer specific claims in the hypothesis regarding SAR407899’s kinase selectivity (>200-fold), ocular penetration to retina (~0.3 µM), full TER recovery in primary human RPE, or functional rescue in NaIO3 models (+28% ERG b-wave), because the provided context contains no SAR407899-specific biochemical, PK, or preclinical efficacy data supporting those statements (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Proposal for Omaveloxolone (RTA-408; Tocris 5030)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Omaveloxolone (RTA-408; also known as CDDO-DFPA; N-(2-Cyano-3,12-dioxo-28-noroleana-1,9(11)-dien-17-yl)-2,2-difluoropropanamide) is a semisynthetic oleanane triterpenoid created by lead optimization of the natural product oleanolic acid, a plant-derived pentacyclic triterpene produced via the mevalonate pathway (squalene → 2,3-oxidosqualene → β-amyrin → erythrodiol → oleanolic acid) and abundantly available from Oleaceae (e.g., olive) and other botanical sources (over 1,600 species; Nakagami, 2016; Masullo et al., 2017; Pollier & Goossens, 2012). The oleanane scaffold was iteratively diversified by Sporn, Gribble, Honda and collaborators to introduce enone and cyanoenone Michael acceptors on rings A and C, yielding the CDDO class (2-cyano-3,12-dioxo-oleana-1,9(11)-dien-28-oic acid and derivatives) as extraordinarily potent anti-inflammatory and Nrf2-inducing agents; C-28 esters/amides and further A/C-ring modifications produced multiple clinical candidates including CDDO-Me (bardoxolone methyl, RTA-402) and RTA-408 (omaveloxolone) (Honda et al., 2000; Pollier & Goossens, 2012; Cheng et al., 2021). RTA-408 specifically is a C17-modified difluoro-propanamide on an oleanane core and belongs to the second generation of synthetic triterpenoids designed to preserve high Nrf2 potency while controlling electrophilicity and pharmacokinetics (Nakagami, 2016; Cuadrado et al., 2019).

At the pharmacological class level, synthetic oleanane triterpenoids are electrophilic “antioxidant inflammation modulators” that activate the KEAP1–NRF2–ARE pathway through covalent (but often reversible) Michael addition to redox-sensitive cysteines on KEAP1, particularly Cys151 on the BTB domain, thereby stabilizing Nrf2 and inducing a coordinated cytoprotective gene program; they concurrently suppress inducible pro-inflammatory mediators (e.g., iNOS, COX-2) with dose-dependent bifunctionality (cytoprotection at low concentrations; pro-oxidant/apoptotic signaling at higher exposure) (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Liby et al., 2007). This scaffold has been extensively explored as a drug platform across oncology, nephrology, cardiopulmonary, inflammatory, and neurological indications, with bardoxolone methyl and omaveloxolone translating to clinical studies and, for omaveloxolone, regulatory approval in Friedreich’s ataxia (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Zahir et al., 2025). Within ophthalmology, oleanane triterpenoids and close congeners (dh404, CDDO-TFEA, CDDO-EA, CDDO-Me) have shown robust Nrf2-mediated protection in retinal models, and RTA-408 itself has been advanced into ocular clinical trials evaluating postoperative ocular pain/inflammation and corneal endothelial cell loss after cataract surgery, positioning this mechanism squarely within ocular translational scope (Cheng et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History  
The oleanane triterpenoid class has a two-decade translational history that began with demonstrations that cyano-enone–bearing derivatives are sub-nanomolar inducers of the Nrf2 transcriptome and suppressors of inflammatory enzymes in vitro and in vivo, a property mapped by SAR to the presence/placement of A-ring 1-en-3-one and C-ring 9(11)-en-12-one Michael acceptors (Honda et al., 2000; Nakagami, 2016). Bardoxolone methyl (CDDO-Me) showed pharmacodynamic activity in humans (ARE-gene induction in tumor biopsies; renal function improvements), but its BEACON Phase 3 trial in advanced CKD was halted for cardiovascular adverse events—an outcome that did not negate class activity but highlighted the need for indication-specific risk management and exclusion criteria (e.g., high BNP, poor baseline eGFR) (Masullo et al., 2017; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Subsequent controlled studies in rarer CKD-associated diseases continued under tighter cardiometabolic selection, while medicinal-chemistry efforts generated second-generation analogs including fluorinated scaffolds (e.g., omaveloxolone) to tune reactivity and PK/PD (Sun et al., 2017).

For omaveloxolone specifically, preclinical pharmacology established Nrf2-dependent induction of glutathione homeostasis genes and improvements in mitochondrial respiration; systemic PK in primates/humans showed dose proportionality and measurable tissue distribution (including liver, lung, brain), with PBMC and tissue Nrf2 target-gene induction at clinically achievable exposures (Reisman et al., 2019). In oncology, a first-in-human dose-escalation study in advanced solid tumors reported acceptable tolerability with pharmacodynamic evidence of Nrf2 pathway activation in PBMCs; in dermatology, topical RTA-408 lotion activated Nrf2 in human skin and was well tolerated (Creelan et al., 2017; Reisman et al., 2019). In neurology, omaveloxolone advanced through the MOXIe program for Friedreich’s ataxia with evidence of neurologic benefit at clinical doses ≥80 mg and exposures concordant with preclinical pharmacology (Naidu & Dinkova-Kostova, 2020; Reisman et al., 2019; Zahir et al., 2025).

Ocularly, multiple oleanane triterpenoid derivatives have shown benefit in retinal oxidative-stress models: dh404 induced canonical Nrf2 target genes (NQO1, HO-1, GCLM), reduced inflammatory mediators, and decreased retinal vascular leakage; CDDO-TFEA and CDDO-EA activated NQO1 in photoreceptor-derived 661W cells and CDDO-TFEA reduced light-induced retinal degeneration (Cheng et al., 2021). RS9, an OA-derived analog generated via microbial transformation, showed superior potency versus CDDO-Me in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) protection, increased retinal HO-1/NQO1 at low doses, and suppressed neovascularization and blood-brain barrier hyperpermeability in vivo, supporting the generalizable ocular protective potential of optimized oleanane triterpenoids (Cheng et al., 2021). Critically for translational relevance, omaveloxolone itself has documented protective activity in human fetal RPE at low-nanomolar concentrations (≤100 nM), where it prevents H₂O₂-induced apoptosis/necrosis by shifting the Bcl-2:Bax ratio and reducing protein glutathionylation—biomarkers linked to oxidative damage and barrier compromise in RPE (Cheng et al., 2021). Moreover, RTA-408 is the only oleanolic acid analogue noted to have entered clinical trials in ocular indications (cataract-surgery–related pain/inflammation and corneal endothelial cell loss), demonstrating sponsor commitment to ophthalmic development and an initial tolerability signal for ocular use (Cheng et al., 2021). No clinical reports were found in the provided context for omaveloxolone in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) specifically, nor in geographic atrophy; thus, this is a repurposing proposal grounded in mechanistic and preclinical ocular convergence rather than direct AMD clinical precedent (Cheng et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
The KEAP1–NRF2 node is a cysteine-centric electrophile sensor system that orchestrates the phase-2 antioxidant and cytoprotective response. Under basal conditions, KEAP1 recruits NRF2 to the CUL3 E3 ligase complex for ubiquitination and proteasomal turnover. Electrophiles such as cyano-enone triterpenoids react with KEAP1 cysteine sensors—most prominently Cys151 in the BTB domain—to disrupt CUL3 docking and/or alter KEAP1 conformation, thereby stabilizing NRF2, allowing nuclear translocation, heterodimerization with small Maf proteins, and binding to antioxidant response elements (ARE) to induce a transcriptional battery including NQO1, HO-1 (HMOX1), glutathione biosynthesis enzymes (GCLC, GCLM), thioredoxin and thioredoxin reductase (Txn1, Txnrd1), sulfiredoxin (Srxn1), and other detoxifying/antioxidative genes (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Reisman et al., 2019). Oleanane cyano-enone triterpenoids are among the most potent NRF2 activators known, with structure–activity relationships showing strong correlations between the presence/geometry of Michael acceptors and both iNOS suppression and NQO1 induction across series; mechanistic profiling indicates covalent yet reversible conjugation to protein thiols underlies this pharmacology (Naidu & Dinkova-Kostova, 2020).

Within this class, omaveloxolone is an electrophilic Michael acceptor–bearing, difluoro-propanamide oleanane that activates Nrf2 at nanomolar concentrations in reporter assays and upregulates canonical ARE-target genes (NQO1, HO-1, GCLM, TxnR1), consistent with its cyano-enone pharmacophore engaging KEAP1 Cys151 and allied redox sensors (Sun et al., 2017; Cuadrado et al., 2019). In systemic models, omaveloxolone increases glutathione concentrations, supports mitochondrial respiration, and normalizes metabolic/energetic parameters downstream of Nrf2 activation—effects mechanistically rationalized by Nrf2-driven induction of NADPH-generating enzymes and mitochondrial support genes, which collectively bolster reductive and ATP capacity in stressed cells (Reisman et al., 2019). In immunologic contexts, oleanane triterpenoids suppress IFN-γ–induced nitric oxide signaling in macrophages, reduce reactive oxygen and nitrotyrosine production by myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), and can inhibit IKKβ/NF-κB signaling (demonstrated for CDDO-Me), contributing to anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory actions that are secondary but complementary to NRF2-mediated cytoprotection (Creelan et al., 2017; Sporn et al., 2007). The class is bifunctional: low-to-moderate exposures favor NRF2-dependent cytoprotection and redox quenching, whereas higher exposures can increase oxidative burden and trigger apoptosis—an important consideration when targeting delicate ocular tissues (Liby et al., 2007).

For ocular cell types relevant to dry AMD, multiple lines of evidence anchor Nrf2/ARE biology. In the retina, oleanane triterpenoids (dh404, CDDO derivatives) induce NQO1/HO-1/GCLM, reduce inflammatory mediators and vascular leakage, and protect photoreceptors and retinal structure in oxidative-stress models; RS9 dosing increases retinal NQO1/HO-1 in vivo (Cheng et al., 2021). In human fetal RPE, omaveloxolone prevents H₂O₂-induced apoptosis and necrosis at ≤100 nM, shifts Bcl-2:Bax pro-survival balance, and reduces protein S-glutathionylation, a reversible oxidative modification implicated in disruption of cytoskeletal and junctional complexes that maintain barrier integrity (Cheng et al., 2021). Taken together, these data support that omaveloxolone, via KEAP1 cysteine sensing and Nrf2 activation in RPE and adjacent retinal cells, can rapidly enhance the endogenous antioxidant program, elevate glutathione/NADPH buffering, mitigate protein oxidative adducts, and suppress inflammatory amplification—biomechanistic axes directly relevant to RPE survival and barrier function under oxidative stress (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Cheng et al., 2021).

Pharmacologically, omaveloxolone exhibits high plasma protein binding and broad tissue distribution preclinically, with oral dosing in primates/humans yielding exposures that induce Nrf2 targets in PBMCs and distribute to metabolically active tissues; topical dermal dosing in humans activates cutaneous Nrf2 without untoward safety signals (Reisman et al., 2019). For ocular dosing, clinical testing of RTA-408 in cataract-surgery contexts (ocular pain/inflammation, corneal endothelial protection) establishes feasibility of achieving pharmacologically relevant ocular exposure with acceptable tolerability in humans, though detailed ocular PK has not been published in the provided excerpts (Cheng et al., 2021).

Expected Effect  
Assay and hypothesis: In a human RPE monolayer model subjected to H₂O₂-induced oxidative injury, omaveloxolone is expected to covalently and reversibly modify KEAP1 cysteines (notably Cys151), stabilize and activate Nrf2, and robustly induce the ARE-regulated antioxidant gene set (NQO1, HO-1, GCLM, TXNRD1, SRXN1), thereby increasing cellular glutathione, NADPH-dependent antioxidant enzyme activity, and mitochondrial resilience; these changes should reduce protein S-glutathionylation, prevent loss of perijunctional actomyosin integrity, and preserve tight-junction belts, culminating in restoration of transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and reduction of paracellular flux (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Reisman et al., 2019; Cheng et al., 2021). Mechanistic support for each step:

- Target engagement and Nrf2 activation in RPE: Cyano-enone triterpenoids are sensed by KEAP1 Cys151, stabilizing Nrf2; omaveloxolone activates Nrf2 at nanomolar concentrations and induces NQO1/HO-1/GCLM/TxnR1 in human cells, and has shown protection in human fetal RPE at ≤100 nM against H₂O₂-induced death with suppression of protein glutathionylation—an oxidative adduct linked to structural protein dysfunction and barrier failure (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Cheng et al., 2021).

- Evidence that ocular cells mount an ARE program: In retinal models, dh404 and CDDO derivatives upregulate NQO1, HO-1, and GCLM; RS9 increases retinal NQO1/HO-1 in vivo, confirming that ARE-responsive gene expression is present and inducible in ocular tissues relevant to barrier function and oxidative injury (Cheng et al., 2021).

- Mitochondrial and redox effects: Omaveloxolone increases glutathione and promotes mitochondrial respiration in preclinical systems, and Nrf2 regulates a broad antioxidative and bioenergetic program that supplies reductive capacity (NADPH) and detoxifying enzymes, supporting RPE energy-demanding barrier maintenance under stress (Reisman et al., 2019).

- Barrier functional correlates in vivo and in vitro: Oleanane triterpenoids reduce retinal vascular leakage in models of inflammation/oxidative stress, and RTA-408 decreases oxidative protein glutathionylation in RPE—a mechanistic event that plausibly preserves junctional complexes and TEER under H₂O₂ stress, even though explicit TEER data for RTA-408 in RPE are not provided here (Cheng et al., 2021).

Operationally, we anticipate a biphasic exposure–response: low nanomolar concentrations should maximize cytoprotective Nrf2 signaling without triggering the pro-oxidant/apoptotic bifurcation observed at higher exposures for this class (Liby et al., 2007). In line with available RPE data, we would start at 1–100 nM omaveloxolone, quantify early ARE-gene induction (1–6 h), glutathione/NADPH pools, protein S-glutathionylation, and image ZO-1/occludin belts, then assess TEER and fluorescein (or 70 kDa dextran) paracellular flux after H₂O₂ challenge; photoreceptor-derived 661W and co-culture systems can be used to evaluate paracrine rescue (Cheng et al., 2021).

As a translational bridge, we would prioritize in vivo models where oleanane triterpenoids have shown benefit (light-induced retinal damage; ischemia–reperfusion; BRB leakage models) to confirm retinal/RPE exposure and barrier readouts, leveraging prior triterpenoid ocular pharmacology experience (Cheng et al., 2021).

Drug delivery considerations: Given lipophilicity and protein binding typical of this class, formulation will influence retinal/RPE exposure. Approaches used for related triterpenoids—e.g., amorphous solid dispersions for oral delivery (CDDO-Me) or nanoparticle carriers for ocular delivery (demonstrated for ursolic acid)—illustrate feasible strategies to reach ocular tissues while minimizing systemic exposure; the fact that RTA-408 has entered ocular clinical trials (post-cataract endpoints) supports translatable tolerability of ophthalmic administration (Cheng et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Mechanistic fit to dry AMD biology: Oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central to RPE degeneration in dry AMD; omaveloxolone engages KEAP1 cysteine sensors to activate Nrf2 and induce a comprehensive, rapid-acting ARE program that elevates glutathione/NADPH, upregulates HO-1/NQO1/GCL-enzymes, and improves mitochondrial bioenergetics—changes expected to blunt H₂O₂-triggered barrier loss and death in RPE (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2017; Reisman et al., 2019). The oleanane scaffold’s larger, conformationally constrained electrophile is argued to offer improved selectivity and controllable PK/PD versus small electrophiles, potentially reducing off-target liabilities at therapeutic concentrations (Cuadrado et al., 2019).

- Direct RPE evidence and ocular translational precedent: RTA-408 protects human fetal RPE from H₂O₂-induced apoptosis/necrosis at ≤100 nM and reduces protein S-glutathionylation, a lesion consistent with cytoskeletal/junctional dysfunction; related oleanane triterpenoids induce Nrf2 targets in retina, reduce BRB leak, and attenuate oxidative-stress retinal damage in vivo (Cheng et al., 2021). RTA-408 is the only OA analogue documented to have entered ocular clinical trials (post-cataract endpoints), supporting feasibility of ophthalmic development (Cheng et al., 2021).

- Clinical-stage agent with known human PK/PD: Omaveloxolone has extensive preclinical and early clinical characterization, including primate/human PK with tissue distribution and PBMC Nrf2 target induction, topical proof of mechanism in human skin, and multiple oral clinical programs (oncology, FA), reducing translational uncertainty compared to earlier chemical matter (Reisman et al., 2019; Creelan et al., 2017; Zahir et al., 2025).

- Class potency and breadth: Oleanane cyano-enones are among the most potent known Nrf2 activators; RS9’s superior retinal potency and CDDO tethered analogs’ efficacy in retinal models argue that the scaffold class, optimized for ocular delivery, can achieve pharmacodynamic effects in the eye at low doses (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Cheng et al., 2021).

Risks and weaknesses  
- Electrophile-driven bifunctionality and narrow window: The same α,β-unsaturated carbonyls that confer high potency can, at higher exposures, increase oxidative stress and trigger apoptosis; dose selection and exposure control will be critical in the eye (Liby et al., 2007; Cheng et al., 2021).

- Class safety history: Bardoxolone methyl’s cardiovascular signal in late-stage CKD underscores the need for indication- and formulation-specific safety strategies; while not probative for ocular topical/intraocular dosing, it motivates cautious systemic exposure limits and cardiovascular exclusion if systemic routes are used (Nakagami, 2016; Sun et al., 2017).

- Incomplete AMD-specific evidence: The provided literature does not report omaveloxolone in dry AMD or geographic atrophy models; most ocular data derive from oxidative-stress/retinal injury and postoperative inflammation paradigms, which are supportive but not definitive for the multifactorial dry AMD pathobiology (Cheng et al., 2021).

- Delivery and exposure uncertainties: Omaveloxolone’s lipophilicity and strong protein binding complicate prediction of ocular distribution; although ocular clinical testing exists for RTA-408, detailed ocular PK/PD are not included in the excerpts, and tailored ophthalmic formulations may be required to achieve RPE/retinal exposure without anterior-segment sequestration (Reisman et al., 2019; Cheng et al., 2021).

Program recommendations  
- In vitro RPE barrier program: Establish a standardized H₂O₂-induced barrier disruption assay in human RPE monolayers with readouts for TEER, large-molecule paracellular flux, ZO-1/occludin belt integrity, protein S-glutathionylation, and apoptosis/caspase activation. Titrate omaveloxolone at 1–100 nM to define the cytoprotective plateau and the onset of bifurcation, and confirm KEAP1–NRF2 mechanism using pharmacologic/CRISPR Nrf2 blockade (Cheng et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2017; Liby et al., 2007).

- Ocular in vivo models: Utilize light-induced photoreceptor injury and retinal I/R models, where the class has shown benefit, to benchmark efficacy and establish exposure–response (retinal NQO1/HO-1 induction, BRB leakage suppression), followed by NaIO₃-induced RPE injury to approximate dry AMD-relevant oxidative RPE loss (Cheng et al., 2021). Include RS9 and a non-electrophilic control to contextualize class effects (Cheng et al., 2021).

- Delivery strategy: Develop an ophthalmic formulation (e.g., micelles, lipid nanoparticles) guided by prior triterpenoid formulation successes (amorphous dispersion for CDDO-Me; UA nanoparticles) to target posterior-segment delivery via topical, suprachoroidal, or intravitreal routes depending on PK modeling and in vivo biodistribution; minimize systemic absorption to mitigate class-related CV risk (Cheng et al., 2021).

- Safety pharmacology: Delineate the therapeutic index around ocular exposures, including ERG and OCT endpoints, and histopathology for photoreceptors, RPE, and ganglion cells; monitor inflammatory and angiogenic pathways to rule out unanticipated pathway cross-talk at sustained Nrf2 activation (Liby et al., 2007).

Conclusion  
On balance, omaveloxolone is a mechanistically well-aligned, clinically de-risked Nrf2 activator with direct protective activity in human RPE and supportive in vivo retinal pharmacology from its chemical class, making it a strong repurposing candidate for dry AMD focused on RPE barrier preservation under oxidative stress (Cheng et al., 2021; Cuadrado et al., 2019). The primary development challenges are exposure control to avoid electrophile-mediated bifunctionality, demonstration of efficacy in AMD-relevant RPE injury models and barrier assays (including TEER), and optimization of ocular delivery to achieve posterior-segment pharmacodynamics with minimal systemic exposure (Liby et al., 2007; Cheng et al., 2021; Reisman et al., 2019). Given the magnitude of unmet need in dry AMD and the centrality of oxidative injury to RPE pathology, a staged program beginning with RPE barrier assays and retinal oxidative stress models, followed by formulation-enabled ocular PK/PD and safety, is justified and has a reasonable probability of technical success based on the assembled evidence (Cheng et al., 2021; Reisman et al., 2019).
