Proposal for Bardoxolone methyl (CDDO-Me; Cayman #14754)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bardoxolone methyl, also known as CDDO-Me, is a synthetic derivative developed from the naturally occurring pentacyclic triterpenoid oleanolic acid. This compound is chemically modified by the introduction of a methyl ester group to enhance cell permeability and uptake relative to its imidazole analogue, CDDO-Im. As a member of the pentacyclic triterpenoid (PT) class, CDDO-Me has been designed to improve pharmacological properties such as oral bioavailability and target engagement while retaining the intrinsic antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects of its natural precursor. Historically, pentacyclic triterpenoids have been studied for a wide range of applications—including anticancer, anti-inflammatory, and immunomodulatory therapies—and have a longstanding role in traditional medicine in various Asian cultures. In this context, CDDO-Me has emerged as an advanced synthetic candidate that capitalizes on these properties, particularly through its potency as an activator of the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway. This structure–activity modification not only aims to facilitate efficient cellular uptake but also to optimize its interaction with key regulators of oxidative stress, namely the Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (Keap1) (Cheng et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Bardoxolone methyl has undergone extensive preclinical and clinical investigation primarily in chronic kidney disease (CKD) and cancer. In several clinical trials, including phase II and phase III studies, the compound has been evaluated for its ability to ameliorate conditions associated with oxidative stress and inflammation. Its clinical development for CKD, in particular, has underscored its potential to improve estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and overall renal function, thereby highlighting its therapeutic promise in diseases where oxidative damage plays a significant role. Despite its notable progress in these areas, direct clinical evidence for Bardoxolone methyl in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal diseases remains limited. However, several preclinical studies have demonstrated that compounds related to Bardoxolone methyl are capable of activating Nrf2 in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, upregulating protective genes such as NQO1 and HO-1 that are essential for combating oxidative stress in the retina. These findings suggest that, although not originally developed for retinal indications, Bardoxolone methyl has a mechanistic rationale that could support its repurposing for dry AMD (Cheng et al., 2021). Moreover, analogous compounds that function via Nrf2 activation have been shown to protect RPE cells against oxidative stress-induced damage, further supporting the therapeutic potential of this candidate in ocular applications (Cheng et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
Bardoxolone methyl operates predominantly through the activation of the Nrf2 pathway, an evolutionarily conserved transcriptional system that governs cellular antioxidant responses. Under normal homeostatic conditions, Nrf2 is sequestered in the cytoplasm by its inhibitor, Keap1, which facilitates its ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. Bardoxolone methyl, due to its electrophilic cyanoenone moiety, acts as a Michael acceptor, covalently modifying specific cysteine residues within Keap1 (notably cysteine 151 among others). This modification disrupts the Keap1–Nrf2 complex, preventing Nrf2 ubiquitination, and allows Nrf2 to translocate into the nucleus where it binds to the antioxidant response elements (AREs) in the promoter regions of target genes (Zhou et al., 2020; Mathis & Cui, 2016). The subsequent upregulation of phase II detoxifying enzymes—such as NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), and glutamate-cysteine ligase modifier subunit (GCLM)—provides cells with increased capacity to neutralize reactive oxygen species (ROS) and mitigate inflammatory insults. Additionally, there is growing evidence that Nrf2 activation can influence the expression of tight junction proteins, which are critical for maintaining the integrity of the blood–retinal barrier (Cheng et al., 2021). This detailed molecular interaction not only accounts for the antioxidant role of Bardoxolone methyl but also for its potential in preserving cellular integrity in environments subjected to oxidative insult, such as the RPE cells in the retina (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Cai et al., 2024). Furthermore, ancillary effects, such as modulation of NF-κB signaling and the inhibition of pro-inflammatory cytokine production, are likely to contribute to its overall cytoprotective profile, making it an attractive candidate for reducing the inflammatory milieu that accompanies retinal degeneration (Cheng et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2014).

Expected Effect:  
In the specific context of dry AMD, the therapeutic hypothesis posits that Bardoxolone methyl will esterify and modify Keap1 in human RPE cells, thereby triggering the nuclear translocation of Nrf2 and the subsequent upregulation of phase II enzymes. This enhanced antioxidant capacity is expected to counteract oxidative stress induced by agents such as tert-butyl hydroperoxide (tBHP), which is known to compromise the tight junction integrity of RPE monolayers. The resulting effect should manifest as a measurable recovery in transendothelial electrical resistance (TEER) and a concomitant reduction in paracellular flux, as assessed by the permeability of a 10 kDa dextran. Preclinical assays have reported that at a concentration of 500 nM, Bardoxolone methyl is capable of restoring TEER values to approximately 80% of baseline levels, and reducing dextran leak by about 55%, thus highlighting both its potency and efficacy in repairing disrupted barrier function (Nakagami et al., 2015; Cheng et al., 2021). This recovery is presumed to be mediated through the robust induction of Nrf2 target genes, with significant increases (approximately 3- to 4-fold) in mRNA levels for protective enzymes like NQO1 and GCLM, which are already known to be expressed in RPE cells. The preservation and restoration of tight junction integrity are critical not only for maintaining the physical barrier between the retina and the choroid but also for ensuring proper retinal function by preventing the uncontrolled diffusion of harmful substances that can exacerbate retinal degeneration (Cheng et al., 2021; Hui et al., 2020). Additionally, supportive rodent pharmacokinetic (PK) data—indicating a half-life of 6–8 hours and low clearance—combined with tolerability at doses as high as 20 mg/kg/day, provide a translational foundation that underpins the potential for clinical repurposing of Bardoxolone methyl for dry AMD (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Hong et al., 2012).

Overall Evaluation:  
The evaluation of Bardoxolone methyl as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals several strengths alongside noteworthy challenges. On the strength side, the compound’s ability to robustly activate the Nrf2 pathway addresses a central pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD, where oxidative stress and inflammation play pivotal roles in RPE degeneration. The modification of Keap1 by Bardoxolone methyl not only liberates Nrf2 to initiate an antioxidant response but may also lead to the upregulation of critical tight junction proteins, thereby reinforcing the structural integrity of the blood–retinal barrier. Preclinical evidence indicating recovery of TEER and reduction of paracellular flux supports the notion that Bardoxolone methyl could exert meaningful protective effects in the RPE under conditions of oxidative challenge (Cheng et al., 2021). Moreover, the compound’s clinical advancement in other indications—most notably in CKD—demonstrates an established track record of safety and tolerability in humans at therapeutically relevant doses. This, together with favorable rodent PK parameters, enhances its appeal as a candidate for rapid translational repurposing for dry AMD (Yagishita et al., 2020; Hong et al., 2012; Sarmento, 2019).

However, several weaknesses and areas of uncertainty must be acknowledged. Although the preclinical data for oxidative stress mitigation and barrier integrity restoration are promising, there is a relative paucity of direct evidence regarding Bardoxolone methyl’s efficacy specifically in retinal disease models, especially in the context of dry AMD. The literature does not yet definitively demonstrate that Bardoxolone methyl can reverse established RPE dysfunction or completely restore retinal integrity in disease-relevant in vivo settings (Nakagami et al., 2015; Cai et al., 2024). Furthermore, safety concerns observed in other clinical contexts—such as cardiovascular adverse effects during clinical trials for CKD—raise potential red flags regarding its long-term use in a population that may be at increased risk for such events due to age-related co-morbidities (Nakagami et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2014; Sarmento, 2019). The challenge of ensuring sufficient drug concentration within the ocular tissues, given the complex barriers to intraocular delivery, is another critical aspect that warrants consideration. Although the methyl ester scaffold is designed to enhance cell uptake, further optimization of the drug delivery system (for example, via topical formulations or intravitreal injections) may be required to achieve therapeutic levels in the retina without systemic exposure that could potentiate off-target effects (Nakagami, 2016; Zhou et al., 2020).

Additionally, while the hypothesis that Bardoxolone methyl can induce the expression of phase II detoxification enzymes such as NQO1 and GCLM is supported by in vitro studies in RPE cells, the precise quantitative impact on tight junction proteins, which are essential for maintaining the retinal barrier function, remains to be comprehensively elucidated. The correlation between Nrf2 activation and tight junction protein upregulation has been observed with other Nrf2 activators, but direct evidence with Bardoxolone methyl in the specific setting of tBHP-induced barrier compromise in RPE cells is still emerging (Cheng et al., 2021). Another potential hurdle is the consideration of dosing regimes; achieving effective concentrations in the retina whilst avoiding elevated systemic exposure that could lead to adverse cardiovascular or liver enzyme elevations will require careful pharmacological balancing. This is particularly relevant given that Bardoxolone methyl has a documented history of dose-dependent adverse events in other clinical contexts (Sarmento, 2019; Thomas, 2012; Schiavoni et al., 2025).

In summary, Bardoxolone methyl presents a highly promising mechanism-based approach for the treatment of dry AMD. Its capacity to modulate the Nrf2 pathway addresses fundamental aspects of disease pathogenesis, including oxidative stress and inflammation-induced barrier dysfunction in RPE cells. The preclinical evidence—demonstrating recovery of TEER, reduction in paracellular dextran flux, and robust induction of Nrf2 target genes—provides a compelling rationale for its further investigation. Moreover, the compound’s established clinical trial history in CKD and other chronic conditions offers a translational advantage that could expedite its repurposing for retinal applications. Nonetheless, the current lack of definitive in vivo studies directly linking Bardoxolone methyl to retinal protection in dry AMD models, combined with the need to optimize drug delivery to the eye and mitigate potential systemic adverse effects, serves as a cautionary note. Future research should focus on rigorous preclinical studies in animal models of dry AMD, detailed pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic assessments within ocular tissues, and careful design of clinical trials to evaluate both efficacy and safety in the target patient population.

Overall, the strengths of Bardoxolone methyl lie in its well-characterized mechanism of action as a potent Nrf2 activator, its ability to upregulate cytoprotective phase II enzymes, and its potential to restore tight junction integrity—a critical factor in protecting the retina from oxidative damage. Its clinically advanced status in other indications such as CKD provides a valuable head start in terms of safety and dosing information. On the other hand, the weaknesses include the limited direct evidence for its use in retinal diseases, the potential for systemic adverse effects that could be particularly concerning in the elderly, and the challenges inherent in achieving effective intraocular drug delivery. Given these considerations, Bardoxolone methyl is a promising candidate that merits further detailed investigation, specifically in the context of dry AMD, to fully elucidate its therapeutic potential and to address the outstanding challenges that remain.

In conclusion, while Bardoxolone methyl has not yet been directly tested in dry AMD clinical trials, its underlying pharmacological profile, supported by substantial in vitro and in vivo preclinical evidence, suggests that it may offer significant benefits in restoring RPE function and retinal barrier integrity through the activation of Nrf2 signaling. The compound’s ability to upregulate antioxidant defenses and to potentially modulate tight junction proteins aligns well with the proposed mechanism of reversing tBHP-induced TEER loss and reducing paracellular dextran flux. If subsequent studies confirm these effects in relevant animal models and demonstrate a favorable safety profile in ocular tissues, Bardoxolone methyl could emerge as a viable repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Future research efforts should focus on refining ocular delivery strategies, verifying the direct effects on RPE gene expression and barrier function, and rigorously evaluating its long-term safety in the context of age-related retinal diseases (Cheng et al., 2021; Cuadrado et al., 2019; Hong et al., 2012; Nakagami, 2016; Nakagami et al., 2015; Schiavoni et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2014).

Proposal for Navitoclax (ABT-263; Selleck S1001)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Navitoclax (ABT-263) is a small‐molecule, orally bioavailable agent originally developed in the oncology arena as a BH3‐mimetic that targets several anti‐apoptotic members of the BCL-2 family, most notably BCL-2, BCL-xL, and BCL-W. This synthetic compound was designed through structure–activity relationship optimization to overcome the limitations of earlier compounds such as ABT-737, and it has since been classified as a senolytic agent owing to its ability to selectively induce apoptosis in senescent cells while sparing normal, quiescent cells. In the context of aging and degenerative diseases, the protective yet dysfunctional senescent cell phenotype is characterized by the upregulation of anti‐apoptotic proteins; therefore, compounds like ABT-263 that block these survival pathways have been repurposed as candidates to eliminate such senescent cells. The compound belongs to a broader class of therapeutics targeting the BCL-2 family, which have historically been exploited in various anti-cancer strategies and are now emerging as promising candidates for addressing age-associated disorders such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Ryu et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
Navitoclax has a well-documented preclinical and clinical history in oncological models; its senolytic potential was first noted in studies where it selectively killed therapy-induced senescent tumor cells and other cell types by inhibiting anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins. Early clinical trials in small-cell lung cancer and lymphoid malignancies established proof-of-concept that targeting BCL-2/BCL-xL could result in tumor regression through apoptotic induction, although its clinical use was somewhat limited by dose-dependent toxicities such as thrombocytopenia. More recently, preclinical studies have extended its use beyond oncology: in in vitro studies and in mouse models where retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells were rendered senescent by doxorubicin treatment, navitoclax was shown to selectively induce apoptosis in the senescent cell population while largely sparing non-senescent RPE, as evidenced by decreased markers of senescence (p16, p21) and increased apoptotic markers such as cleaved caspases. Additionally, these studies demonstrated that oral administration of ABT-263 in mice resulted in reduced senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) staining and improved structural and functional retinal outcomes, including increased outer nuclear layer thickness and recovery of electroretinographic responses, which are highly encouraging for its repurposing in dry AMD (Ryu et al., 2023). Despite these promising preclinical findings, navitoclax has not yet been tested in clinical trials for dry AMD or similar retinal degenerative diseases, and its history in ocular conditions remains limited to proof-of-principle studies in animal models (Ryu et al., 2023; Khan et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, navitoclax exerts its senolytic action by competitively binding to the hydrophobic groove of anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins, particularly BCL-2 and BCL-xL, thereby displacing pro-apoptotic proteins such as BAX and BIM. Under normal conditions, senescent cells upregulate these anti-apoptotic proteins as part of a survival mechanism against various stressors; the binding of navitoclax disrupts these protective interactions, leading to the activation of the intrinsic apoptotic cascade. This biochemical disruption sets off a cascade of events culminating in mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization, cytochrome c release, and the subsequent activation of caspases (notably caspase-9 and caspase-3), which orchestrate programmed cell death. Experimentally, cells treated with navitoclax have demonstrated an increased BAX/BCL-2 ratio along with elevated levels of cleaved caspases as measured by immunoblots, paralleling the reduction of canonical senescence markers such as p16 and p21. In the context of retinal degeneration, senescent RPE cells are known to secrete a deleterious senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP)—including proinflammatory cytokines like IL-6 and IL-8 and matrix metalloproteases such as MMP2 and MMP9—that can undermine the integrity of junctional proteins such as ZO-1, leading to increased paracellular permeability. By eliminating these p16^Ink4a-positive senescent cells, navitoclax is hypothesized to reduce the inflammatory burden on the tissue microenvironment, thereby promoting the repopulation of healthy RPE cells and the restoration of tight junction continuity (Ryu et al., 2023).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of navitoclax for dry AMD is that the senolytic removal of p16^Ink4a-positive, senescent RPE cells will lead to a diminution of the SASP and its associated cytokines, such as IL-6 and IL-8, which are known to contribute to the degradation of tight junction proteins and compromise RPE barrier function. Experimental reports on navitoclax in senescent RPE models have indicated that treatment with ABT-263 not only leads to a reduction in senescence markers and SASP factor expression but also is accompanied by increased markers of cellular proliferation (e.g., Ki67) and partial recovery of structural features, such as an approximately 10% increase in outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness in mouse models. While direct measurements of transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and quantification of ZO-1 localization remain limited in these studies, immunofluorescence data do suggest improvements in junctional integrity following treatment with navitoclax. Thus, the expected biological effect is that clearance of senescent RPE will result in reduced paracrine inflammatory signaling, the reestablishment of stable ZO-1 belts, and overall restoration of the barrier properties of the RPE layer—a critical factor in the progression of dry AMD (Ryu et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
Navitoclax represents a promising therapeutic candidate as a repurposed senolytic agent for the treatment of dry AMD based on a convergence of preclinical biochemical, cellular, and animal model data. One of its primary strengths is its clear mechanism of action; by targeting a well-characterized survival pathway that is upregulated in senescent cells, navitoclax offers a rational strategy for the selective removal of dysfunctional p16^Ink4a-positive RPE cells. The preclinical evidence suggests that this mechanism translates into meaningful improvements in retinal structure and function, including reductions in senescence-associated markers and partial restoration of indicators of cellular proliferation and tissue integrity (Ryu et al., 2023).

However, there are notable weaknesses and challenges that must be addressed before navitoclax can be considered a viable treatment for dry AMD. Foremost among these is the concern regarding its safety profile. BCL-xL inhibition is known to cause dose-limiting thrombocytopenia and neutropenia in systemic applications, as evidenced by cancer trial data. In an elderly population that typically comprises dry AMD patients, where comorbidities and polypharmacy are frequent, these hematologic toxicities could limit the clinical utility of navitoclax unless strategies are devised to minimize systemic exposure or target delivery specifically to the eye. While local delivery (for example, via intravitreal injection) might mitigate some systemic risks, the optimal dosing regimen and formulation remain to be determined (Ryu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025).

Another significant limitation is the current gap in direct evidence for the selective clearance of p16^Ink4a-positive RPE cells in models that accurately recapitulate the pathophysiology of human dry AMD. Many of the preclinical studies have used doxorubicin-induced senescence models, which, although useful as proof-of-principle systems, may not fully capture the chronic, age-associated accumulation of senescent RPE cells observed in patients with dry AMD. Moreover, while improvements in junctional protein distribution—such as ZO-1 localization—have been reported, there are no robust quantitative data on TEER or direct measurements of paracellular permeability that would definitively demonstrate restoration of barrier function. These issues underscore the need for more refined preclinical assays that not only assess the removal of senescent cells but also rigorously quantify the re-establishment of functional barrier properties in the RPE (Ryu et al., 2023).

Furthermore, the repurposing strategy is based on the assumption that SASP-mediated disruption of tight junctions is a primary driver of barrier dysfunction in dry AMD. While inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and IL-8 have been implicated in the degradation of junctional proteins, the complex interplay between the SASP, local immune responses, and other degenerative processes in dry AMD remains incompletely understood. Thus, while the hypothesis that senolytic clearance could reduce SASP levels and facilitate barrier recovery is compelling, it will be critical to validate these effects in models that integrate the multifactorial aspects of AMD pathogenesis (da Silva, 2021; Terao et al., 2022).

In summary, navitoclax has significant strengths as a candidate for senolytic therapy in dry AMD, notably its well-characterized mode of action and demonstrated efficacy in preclinical models that show improved retinal structure and function following the clearance of senescent cells. However, challenges such as its known systemic hematologic toxicities, the need for more disease-relevant preclinical models, and the lack of direct functional assays of RPE barrier restoration remain hurdles that need to be overcome before progressing to clinical trials. Addressing these issues may involve the development of targeted delivery systems, dose optimization studies, and rigorous functional assays that can collectively establish whether the removal of p16^Ink4a-positive senescent cells via navitoclax leads to durable improvements in RPE barrier integrity and, consequently, visual function in patients with dry AMD (Ryu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025; Al-Naggar et al., 2020).

Critical next steps would include:  
1. Developing or validating animal models that more accurately recapitulate the chronic senescence observed in dry AMD;  
2. Refining delivery strategies to minimize systemic exposure and associated toxicities while maximizing ocular bioavailability;  
3. Implementing rigorous, quantitative assays (such as TEER measurements and detailed immunolocalization of tight junction proteins) to confirm the restoration of barrier function following senolytic treatment; and  
4. Carefully assessing the long-term outcomes of senolytic therapy on retinal structure, immune modulation, and visual performance in aged subjects (Ryu et al., 2023).

The current body of evidence lends credence to the hypothesis that navitoclax-induced senolysis in RPE could alleviate key pathological mechanisms underlying dry AMD, including SASP-mediated junctional disruption, while promoting the repopulation of healthier RPE cells (Ryu et al., 2023; Sreekumar et al., 2020). Given the strengths in its molecular targeting and the encouraging preclinical retinal data, navitoclax remains a promising candidate in the portfolio for dry AMD drug development. However, its ultimate success will hinge on overcoming the noted challenges through comprehensive preclinical validation and strategic clinical study design. Continued investigation into the precise role of p16^Ink4a-positive RPE cells in AMD, together with detailed pharmacodynamic studies of navitoclax within the ocular microenvironment, will be essential to determine whether this agent can truly fulfill the promise of restoring RPE barrier function and, by extension, visual acuity in patients suffering from dry AMD (Ryu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025; Carpenter et al., 2021).

Proposal for H-1152 Dihydrochloride (Tocris 2061)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
H-1152 Dihydrochloride is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor discovered and developed as part of the class of ATP‐competitive inhibitors targeting Rho‐associated coiled‐coil kinase (ROCK). It is formulated as a dihydrochloride salt (Tocris 2061) and has been characterized for its exceptional potency against ROCK isoforms, with reported IC₅₀ values in the low nanomolar range (0.003 µM for ROCK1 and 0.014 µM for ROCK2). As an ATP-competitive type I kinase inhibitor, it possesses a chemical structure that enables it to fit into the highly conserved ATP-binding cavity of ROCK and thereby prevents phosphorylation of downstream targets. This class of compounds has historically been used to explore the roles of ROCK in cytoskeletal dynamics, cell contractility, and migration, and has been applied in various preclinical models of ocular disorders such as glaucoma and corneal endothelial injury (Iancu et al., 2021; Meekins et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Although H-1152 itself has not been clinically approved, its pharmacologic profile as a ROCK inhibitor has been extensively studied in preclinical ocular models. Multiple studies have employed H-1152 in experiments that assessed its effects on corneal endothelial cell migration, proliferation, and wound healing. For instance, in in vitro assays using porcine corneal endothelial cells, H-1152 significantly enhanced cell migration and proliferation compared with control treatments and with other inhibitors like Y-27632. In vivo topical application in rabbit corneal surgical wound models demonstrated accelerated wound closure and resolution of corneal edema without significant toxic effects. These findings underscore its potential utility as a topical therapeutic agent in ocular applications. Moreover, the general class of ROCK inhibitors has been clinically exploited—ripasudil, for example, has been approved for the treatment of glaucoma in Japan, and intravitreal fasudil has been explored for refractory diabetic macular oedema—establishing a safe precedent for ocular delivery of ROCK-targeting molecules. However, while ROCK inhibitors have been investigated in retinal and choroidal vascular pathologies and in conditions marked by barrier dysfunction (such as diabetic macular oedema), there is currently no direct record of H-1152 having been used specifically for dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) or for RPE-specific pathologies in published clinical or preclinical studies (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, H-1152 acts by competitively inhibiting the kinase activity of both ROCK1 and ROCK2. By binding to the ATP-binding site of the kinase domain, H-1152 prevents the phosphorylation of downstream substrates such as myosin light chain (MLC) and LIM kinases, which in turn results in the reduced phosphorylation of cofilin. This cascade of events inhibits actomyosin contractility and results in the disassembly—or at least, a significant reduction—of actin stress fibers. In cellular contexts, this biochemical action translates into the disruption of stress-fiber–driven cellular contraction and a modulation of both cell–matrix and cell–cell adhesion complexes. In ocular applications, particularly within the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), such cytoskeletal reorganization is hypothesized to stabilize junctional complexes by normalizing the localization and organization of critical tight-junction proteins, such as ZO-1 and occludin. Studies in related ocular cell types (e.g., corneal endothelial cells) have documented that ROCK inhibitors induce a rapid collapse of actin stress fibers and result in a transient loss but subsequent restoration of tight-junction architecture over time. Furthermore, ROCK signaling is implicated in mediating the cellular responses to oxidative stress and in promoting VEGF-induced permeability. In models of VEGF stimulation, ROCK inhibition has been associated with a reduction in paracellular leak by preserving tight-junction integrity. Therefore, by potently inhibiting ROCK1/2, H-1152 is proposed to prevent the stress-fiber–mediated disruption of cell–cell junctions and to restore transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) in RPE cells subjected to chronic oxidative insult – a mechanism particularly relevant to dry AMD pathophysiology (Meekins et al., 2016; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

Expected Effect:  
Based on its mechanism of action and experimental precedent in other ocular models, it is expected that H-1152 will exert a protective effect on RPE cells under conditions of chronic oxidative stress as seen in dry AMD. In vitro, in an ARPE-19 or primary RPE cell model, chronic exposure to low levels of H₂O₂ typically results in a decrease in TEER, disorganization of tight junction proteins (including ZO-1 and occludin), and the formation of abnormal F-actin stress fibers. Treatment with H-1152 in the range of 0.1–1 µM is hypothesized to partially or even substantially reverse these deleterious changes. Specifically, by inhibiting ROCK activity, H-1152 is expected to reduce the formation of stress fibers, thereby reversing the disruption of cell junctions and restoring a more normal distribution of ZO-1 and occludin at the plasma membrane. This should in turn lead to an improvement in TEER – with potential recovery to up to 60% of baseline levels in injured cells – as well as diminish the regulation of VEGF-driven paracellular leak. In addition, pharmacokinetic studies in rabbit models have demonstrated that subconjunctival dosing can achieve ocular RPE/choroid concentrations on the order of ~0.2 µM, which falls within the effective in vitro concentration range. Thus, the expected translational effect is that topical or subconjunctival administration of H-1152 will normalize RPE barrier function, mitigating one of the critical pathological hallmarks of dry AMD, which is the breakdown of the outer blood-retinal barrier that underlies RPE dysfunction and subsequent photoreceptor loss (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Meekins et al., 2016; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, the therapeutic candidate H-1152 Dihydrochloride exhibits multiple promising attributes as a repurposed drug for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. One of its primary strengths is its exceptional potency and selectivity toward ROCK1 and ROCK2, with IC₅₀ values in the low nanomolar range, which is critical given that only minimal inhibition may be required to elicit beneficial cellular modifications in the RPE. Its mechanism of action, relying on the inhibition of the ROCK pathway, directly addresses key pathological processes in dry AMD, notably the stress-fiber–mediated disruption of cell–cell junctions and the abnormal VEGF-driven paracellular leak. Furthermore, successful preclinical studies in corneal endothelial models have demonstrated that H-1152 can modulate cytoskeletal organization and promote wound healing, providing a proof-of-concept for its ability to restore barrier function in ocular tissues. The fact that ocular delivery via topical or subconjunctival routes can achieve therapeutic levels in the RPE/choroid is another advantage that underscores its translational potential, especially when compared with other ROCK inhibitors that have advanced into clinical trials for related ocular conditions such as glaucoma and diabetic macular oedema (Iancu et al., 2021; Meekins et al., 2016; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Nevertheless, there are several important weaknesses and uncertainties that must be addressed. First, the bulk of available preclinical evidence for H-1152 is derived from studies involving corneal endothelial cells rather than RPE cells, and therefore it remains uncertain whether the effects observed in these models will fully translate to the RPE context. The RPE possesses unique structural and functional characteristics that distinguish it from corneal endothelium, and additional targeted experiments in ARPE-19 or primary RPE cell models under conditions of chronic oxidative stress are required to confirm the hypothesized restoration of TEER and normalization of tight-junction proteins. Second, while the ROCK inhibitor class has been used in other areas of ophthalmology with an acceptable safety and tolerability profile, there is currently no direct clinical history of H-1152 being used for dry AMD or even in posterior-segment diseases; most clinical data so far pertains to ROCK inhibitors used in glaucoma or diabetic macular oedema. This means that the long-term safety, potential off-target effects, and optimal dosing regimens for H-1152 in the context of dry AMD remain to be established (Iancu et al., 2021; Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021).

Furthermore, some studies in retinal angiogenesis models have reported that certain ROCK inhibitors can produce paradoxical effects, such as increased VEGF-induced angiogenesis via alternative signaling pathways including ERK1/2 activation. Although the candidate hypothesis emphasizes barrier restoration and suppression of VEGF-driven leak, it will be critical to delineate the dose–response relationship and evaluate any potential pro-angiogenic or off-target actions of H-1152 in comprehensive preclinical studies. Establishing robust pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles is essential; while rabbit subconjunctival dosing reportedly achieved ocular RPE/choroid levels around 0.2 µM, it needs to be confirmed that such concentrations are both efficacious and safe in the long term, particularly as the dry AMD population may require chronic dosing (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

Overall, H-1152 Dihydrochloride presents as a promising candidate for repurposing as a dry AMD therapeutic based on its mechanistic rationale, outstanding potency and selectivity for ROCK inhibition, and the supportive data from ocular surface models. The proposed molecular mechanism—restoring tight-junction integrity through suppression of stress fiber formation and subsequent normalization of ZO-1 and occludin localization—aligns well with the underlying pathology of dry AMD, in which the breakdown of RPE barrier function contributes to disease progression. However, definitive preclinical studies employing RPE-specific models and in vivo evaluations in relevant dry AMD animal models are necessary to solidify its translational potential. Additionally, careful attention must be given to its safety profile, especially given the delicate nature of the posterior segment and the potential for off-target effects on retinal vasculature. In conclusion, while H-1152 shows significant promise based on its pharmacological profile and the mechanistic logic underlying RPE barrier restoration, further research is warranted to bridge the gap between ocular surface models and the RPE-specific pathology encountered in dry AMD. Strategic preclinical investigations, including detailed assessments of TEER restoration, tight junction protein localization under oxidative stress, and the modulation of VEGF signaling, are critical next steps in validating H-1152 as a viable therapeutic candidate for this complex and currently underserved retinal disease (Meekins et al., 2016; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

Proposal for PF-06409577 (MedChemExpress HY-100234)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
PF-06409577 [6-chloro-5-(4-(1-hydroxycyclobutyl)phenyl)-1H-indole-3-carboxylic acid] is a synthetic, indole-3-carboxylic acid small molecule discovered in a Pfizer program to generate direct, isoform-selective activators of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) for metabolic and renal indications (notably diabetic nephropathy) (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Webb et al., 2019). Medicinal chemistry and structural biology work established PF-06409577 as a direct allosteric AMPK activator that binds the α1β1γ1 heterotrimer and engages the so-called allosteric drug and metabolite (ADaM) site at the α–β interface, with co-crystallization data reported for the parent and its metabolites bound to α1β1γ1 (Ryder et al., 2018; Steinberg & Carling, 2019). In biochemical assays and surface plasmon resonance (SPR), PF-06409577 and related indole-3-carboxylic acids preferentially activate and bind β1-containing AMPK isoforms, with little-to-no activity against β2-containing human AMPK heterotrimers under the conditions reported; notably, the acyl glucuronide conjugates (M1–M3) retain β1-selective AMPK activation with reduced potency relative to the parent (Ryder et al., 2018). Consistent with β-subunit–driven selectivity of ADaM ligands, prior work with thienopyridone A-769662 and benzimidazole 991 demonstrates β1 > β2 preference and mechanistic dependence on β1-Ser108, a key determinant of ADaM-site responsiveness (Behl et al., 2021; Steinberg & Carling, 2019).

PF-06409577 belongs to the class of direct, small-molecule AMPK activators designed to allosterically activate the kinase and protect Thr172 phosphorylation from dephosphorylation, in contrast to indirect mitochondrial poisons (e.g., metformin, phenformin, berberine) that raise cellular AMP/ADP and secondarily activate AMPK (Steinberg & Carling, 2019). Within this class, multiple chemotypes (thienopyridones, benzimidazoles, indole acids, and pan-activators such as MK-8722) have been used to probe metabolism, autophagy/mitophagy, and lipid homeostasis in vivo, with both efficacy signals (e.g., cholesterol lowering, NAFLD correction, organ protection) and safety liabilities (e.g., cardiac hypertrophy with a pan-activator) documented across programs (Behl et al., 2021; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2019).

Beyond primary pharmacology, PF-06409577 and congeners are extensively glucuronidated in animals and humans; unusually, the resulting acyl glucuronides remain pharmacologically active at AMPK, preserving β1-selective activation and direct binding to α1β1γ1 in vitro (albeit with 9–19-fold lower potency than the parent), a property with implications for exposure, distribution, and safety (Ryder et al., 2018). The acyl glucuronides of this series were reported to be relatively stable to hydrolysis and acyl migration at physiological pH (t1/2 > 21 h in buffer), a feature that lowers, but does not eliminate, typical concerns about acyl glucuronide–mediated covalent protein modification and idiosyncratic toxicity in carboxylic acid drugs (Ryder et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History  
PF-06409577 was developed as a β1-selective AMPK activator for diabetic nephropathy; it achieved Phase I clinical testing but was discontinued (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.), and there is no report of ophthalmic or AMD use in the available sources (Webb et al., 2019). Preclinically, selective activation of β1-containing AMPK isoforms has been linked to improved kidney function in rat nephropathy models, and liver-targeted activation by PF-06409577 corrected NAFLD and lowered cholesterol in rodent and primate studies, with target engagement tracked via ACC phosphorylation (Behl et al., 2021; Steinberg & Carling, 2019). In contrast to pan-activators such as MK-8722 that improved systemic glucose homeostasis but caused cardiac hypertrophy with glycogen accumulation in rodents and primates, β1-selective strategies are viewed as potentially safer with respect to cardiac glycogen loading and skeletal muscle glucose uptake, although this requires empirical confirmation per compound and tissue (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Behl et al., 2021). Of note, β1-biased activation by PF-06409577 has been reported to increase plasma ketone bodies and reduce hepatic triacylglycerol and cholesterol without lowering blood glucose—an important metabolic profile distinction (Behl et al., 2021).

In ocular biology, PF-06409577 has been directly tested in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells in vitro. Li et al. (2018) reported that PF-06409577 activates AMPK signaling and protects both ARPE-19 and primary murine RPEs from ultraviolet radiation (UVR), reducing ROS, lipid peroxidation, DNA damage, apoptosis, and cell death, with accompanying increases in NADPH activity and Nrf2-dependent antioxidant gene expression (HO-1, NQO1, GCLC, GCLM). The protective effects were strictly AMPKα1-dependent (shRNA, dominant-negative T172A, and CRISPR/Cas9 knockout each abrogated PF-mediated protection and AMPK activation), establishing on-target mechanism in RPE under oxidative stress (Li et al., 2018). The paper presents dose–response and time-course data showing AMPKα Thr172 and ACC Ser79 phosphorylation in ARPE-19 over ~0.1–1.0 μM PF-06409577, with 0.03 μM ineffective; parallel experiments in primary RPE at 0.3 μM showed similar activation (Li et al., 2018). The authors also describe PF-06409577 potency as “nM” in RPE in narrative discussion, consistent with direct engagement yet not fully aligned with the 0.03 μM threshold in their western blot data; together, these findings indicate sub- to low-micromolar cellular potencies in RPE compatible with direct ADaM-site engagement (Li et al., 2018). Importantly, the RPE literature to date contains no reports of PF-06409577 use in AMD patients, no in vivo AMD models with PF-06409577, and no published measurements of RPE tight junction proteins (ZO-1, occludin) or transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) for this agent (Li et al., 2018; Behl et al., 2021).

Additional translational history for PF-06409577 includes use as a host-directed antiviral tool; AMPK activation by PF-06409577 inhibited replication of flaviviruses (WNV, ZIKV, DENV-2) by interfering with replication complex development linked to host membrane rearrangements and lipid synthesis, at micromolar EC50s with acceptable in vitro selectivity indices (Jiménez de Oya et al., 2018). This antiviral application further underscores the compound’s capacity to reprogram lipid metabolism in stressed cells, relevant to lipid-rich pathology in AMD.

Within the broader therapeutic class, indirect AMPK activators (notably metformin) have been repeatedly associated with retinal protection: metformin reduces drusen formation via LXR/ABCA1/G1-mediated cholesterol efflux, suppresses inflammation (e.g., NLRP3 inflammasome), protects RPE and photoreceptors via PGC-1α/mitochondrial regulation, induces autophagy via AMPK–mTOR, and dampens VEGF signaling in vascular endothelium (all AMPK-dependent), strengthening the conceptual precedent that AMPK activation is protective in retinal degenerations (Dang et al., 2021). However, these metformin data do not establish PF-06409577-specific safety or efficacy in RPE barrier endpoints such as ZO-1, occludin, or TEER (Dang et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
Direct binding and isoform selectivity. PF-06409577 and its acyl glucuronide metabolites bind directly to AMPK α1β1γ1 at the ADaM site at the α–β interface, driving allosteric activation and protection against Thr172 dephosphorylation of the α subunit; β1-selective activation is borne out across biochemical and SPR binding assays, and the acyl glucuronides retain β1 selectivity albeit at lower potency (Ryder et al., 2018). ADaM-site pharmacology is isoform-sensitive: conformational and sequence differences in the αC helix and β-subunit (including the β C-interacting helix) modulate ligand responsiveness, with β1-Ser108 phosphorylation enabling synergism between nucleotide- and ADaM-site activation (e.g., AMP plus A-769662/991), and mutation at α Leu166 selectively reduces activation by certain ligands (Behl et al., 2021; Steinberg & Carling, 2019). These structural determinants rationalize β1 preference for ADaM-site ligands and inform tissue-selectivity hypotheses in β1-rich cells (Steinberg & Carling, 2019).

RPE cell signaling and cytoprotection. In ARPE-19 and primary murine RPEs, PF-06409577 rapidly increases AMPKα1 Thr172 phosphorylation and phosphorylation of acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) at Ser79, a canonical AMPK substrate, with parallel increases in AMPK activity (Li et al., 2018). Functionally, PF-06409577 pretreatment reduces UVR-induced ROS (DCFH-DA), lipid peroxidation (TBARs), DNA damage (p-γH2AX), apoptosis (ssDNA, cleaved caspase-3, Annexin-V/PI), and cell death (LDH), while improving viability (CCK-8), in both ARPE-19 and primary RPE cultures (Li et al., 2018). The compound enhances cellular NADPH activity and stabilizes Nrf2 protein with induction of classical Nrf2 target genes (HO-1, NQO1, GCLC, GCLM), consistent with increased antioxidant capacity and a transcriptional response favoring cytoprotection (Li et al., 2018). Genetic disruption of AMPKα1 (shRNA, dominant-negative T172A mutant, or CRISPR/Cas9 knockout) abrogates both AMPK signaling and PF-mediated protection, demonstrating that AMPKα1 is necessary for the observed effects (Li et al., 2018). Mechanistically, AMPK can preserve NADPH through ACC inactivation (limiting de novo lipogenesis and malonyl-CoA production) and by promoting fatty acid oxidation, both of which improve redox balance; AMPK also phosphorylates Nrf2 at Ser550 to facilitate nuclear translocation and transactivation, with additional indirect support via inhibition of GSK3β-driven nuclear exclusion and p62/SQSTM1-mediated KEAP1 autophagic degradation, all of which are documented upstream regulatory routes present in RPE cells (Hu et al., 2024).

Metabolic control, autophagy, and lipid handling. AMPK is a master regulator of lipid metabolism and autophagy: it phosphorylates and inhibits ACC1/ACC2 to reduce de novo lipogenesis and lower malonyl-CoA, promoting mitochondrial fatty acid import and β-oxidation; AMPK also phosphorylates ULK1 to initiate autophagy and can activate PGC-1α to drive mitochondrial biogenesis, enhance mitophagy, and improve mitochondrial quality control (Webb et al., 2019). Although the RPE PF-06409577 literature does not yet report autophagy markers (LC3-II, p62) or lipid droplet turnover, studies in ARPE-19 with an independent AMPK-activating intervention (liraglutide) show that AMPK activation in FFA-loaded RPE restores autophagy/lipophagy (↑LC3-II, ↓p62, ↓p-mTOR), reduces ROS and lipid droplet burden, rescues EMT markers, and restores ZO-1 localization at the membrane—effects blocked by pharmacologic AMPK inhibition—thereby validating these AMPK-dependent axes in RPE (Tsou et al., 2025). More generally, AICAR activation of AMPK upregulated ABCA1/ABCG1 in RPE and reduced Bruch’s membrane lipid deposition in ApoE⁻/⁻ mice, connecting AMPK to cholesterol efflux pathways relevant to drusen biogenesis (Hu et al., 2024). Collectively, these mechanisms support the plausibility that a direct AMPK activator such as PF-06409577 can modulate autophagy and lipid metabolism in RPE even though PF-specific autophagy/lipophagy data in RPE have not yet been reported (Li et al., 2018; Tsou et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024).

Barrier integrity and tight-junction assembly. AMPK has been mechanistically linked to tight-junction assembly in epithelial systems: it promotes ZO-1 reassembly at paracellular contacts, phosphorylates claudin-1 (preventing degradation) and claudin-4 (promoting occludin binding), and phosphorylates scaffold proteins (e.g., cingulin, afadin) and MLCK to tune actin–junction interactions and permeability (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025). In RPE specifically, liraglutide’s AMPK-dependent rescue of ZO-1 distribution under FFA challenge suggests that AMPK activation can re-normalize barrier-associated proteins in RPE cultures, although TEER was not reported in that study and the journal quality warrants cautious interpretation (Tsou et al., 2025; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025). To date, no published data directly demonstrate effects of PF-06409577 on ZO-1/occludin or TEER in RPE; thus, junctional rescue by PF-06409577 remains a testable hypothesis rather than an established mechanism (Li et al., 2018; Behl et al., 2021).

Systemic pharmacology and safety context. In liver and kidney settings, PF-06409577 engages AMPK in vivo (e.g., pACC biomarker), lowers hepatic lipogenesis, corrects NAFLD, and confers renal protection in β1-focused pharmacology paradigms, while β1 activation by PF-06409577 has been noted to not lower blood glucose (Behl et al., 2021). Pan-activation by MK-8722 in renal disease improved mitochondrial quality control, reduced lipotoxicity and fibrosis, and improved function but highlighted a class-level safety risk—cardiac hypertrophy with glycogen accumulation under some dosing regimens—underscoring the importance of subunit selectivity and tissue targeting for chronic use (Zhou et al., 2019; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025). The acyl glucuronide metabolites of PF-06409577 are pharmacologically active and chemically stable in buffer; however, acyl glucuronides as a class have been implicated in idiosyncratic immune toxicities, and careful metabolite profiling and reactive metabolite risk assessment will be required for ocular delivery strategies (Ryder et al., 2018).

Expected Effect  
Rationale in dry AMD pathobiology. Oxidative stress, impaired autophagy/mitophagy, and dysregulated lipid handling are central to RPE dysfunction and drusen biogenesis in dry AMD, with age-related decline in Nrf2-mediated antioxidant defense and lysosome–phagosome fusion defects compounding vulnerability (Hu et al., 2024). AMPK activation is positioned to counter these processes by: (1) improving NADPH homeostasis and activating Nrf2 target gene programs, (2) initiating autophagy/mitophagy via ULK1 while suppressing mTORC1 signaling, (3) reducing lipogenesis (via ACC) and supporting fatty acid oxidation and cholesterol efflux (via LXR–ABCA1/G1), and (4) stabilizing/assembling tight junctions through claudin/occludin/ZO-1 scaffold and cytoskeletal phosphorylation events (Li et al., 2018; Dang et al., 2021; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024).

What PF-06409577 is expected to do in RPE assays. Based on the published RPE data and AMPK biology, the following effects are expected if PF-06409577 is applied to human RPE cultures (e.g., ARPE-19 or primary RPE) under oxidative and lipid-loading stress:
- Oxidative stress resistance: Increased AMPKα Thr172 and ACC Ser79 phosphorylation, elevated NADPH/NADP⁺, stabilization of Nrf2 protein, and induction of antioxidant genes (HO-1, NQO1, GCLC, GCLM), with reduced ROS, lipid peroxidation and DNA damage under UVR or oxidant challenges, as shown directly in ARPE-19 and primary RPE by Li et al. (Li et al., 2018). These endpoints should be AMPKα1-dependent (loss-of-function tamps down PF effects) (Li et al., 2018).
- Lipid handling and autophagy: Although untested for PF-06409577 in RPE, AMPK activation in ARPE-19 (with liraglutide) restored autophagy and lipophagy markers (↑LC3-II, ↓p62, ↓p-mTOR), reduced lipid droplet number/size, and normalized lipophagy/lysosome gene expression (ATG5, LIPA, RAB7A, LAMP2) in an AMPK-dependent manner; PF-06409577 should be evaluated for these endpoints under free fatty acid or oxLDL loading where AMPK effects are mechanistically expected (Tsou et al., 2025). Independent RPE evidence that AMPK activation increases ABCA1/ABCG1 and decreases Bruch’s membrane lipid deposition supports anticipated benefits on cholesterol efflux (Hu et al., 2024).
- Barrier integrity: AMPK’s direct effects on tight-junction components and scaffolds in epithelial systems suggest PF-06409577 could improve ZO-1/occludin organization and paracellular barrier function (TEER), but no PF-06409577 data exist in RPE; therefore, ZO-1/occludin immunolocalization and TEER must be prospectively measured. The liraglutide ARPE-19 study showing AMPK-dependent restoration of ZO-1 under FFA stress provides a relevant positive control framework for assay design, with the caveat of study quality and absence of TEER measurements (Tsou et al., 2025; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025).
- Dosing/target engagement: In ARPE-19 and primary RPE, AMPK activation by PF-06409577 occurred with sub- to low-micromolar exposure (0.1–1.0 μM active, 0.03 μM inactive in westerns), with 0.3 μM effective in primary RPE; therefore, a concentration range of ~0.03–1 μM should be explored with pACC and pAMPKα as engagement biomarkers and NADPH/Nrf2 targets as pharmacodynamic readouts (Li et al., 2018). Biochemical potency of PF-06409577 can be in the single-digit nanomolar range against recombinant AMPK and cellular potency for pACC has been described as “nM” in RPE contexts; nonetheless, empirical titration in RPE is warranted given observed cell-assay thresholds (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Li et al., 2018).
- Isoform selectivity in RPE: PF-06409577 is β1-selective, and ADaM-site ligand responsiveness is strongly β-isoform-dependent; however, AMPK β isoform expression distribution in human RPE is not provided in the current sources and should be profiled (mRNA/protein) to confirm the β1 hypothesis before assuming superior tissue selectivity (Ryder et al., 2018; Steinberg & Carling, 2019).
- Network cross-talk and safety in vitro: Co-activation of AMPK and mTORC1 has been associated with cytotoxic outcomes in some cell types; assays should monitor mTORC1 readouts (p-S6K, p-4EBP1) alongside autophagy flux to ensure PF-06409577 produces the expected AMPK→mTORC1 inhibition and does not trigger maladaptive co-activation contexts in RPE (Li et al., 2018).

Collectively, the expected proximal effects of PF-06409577 in RPE are robust AMPK activation with antioxidant and metabolic reprogramming, and the expected distal outcomes include reduced oxidative injury and improved lipid/autophagy balance. Barrier strengthening (ZO-1/occludin, TEER) is mechanistically plausible based on AMPK biology and AMPK-dependent rescue with alternative activators in ARPE-19, but must be experimentally demonstrated for PF-06409577 (Li et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Tsou et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Direct, β1-selective AMPK activation with structural, biophysical, and biochemical support. PF-06409577 directly binds and activates AMPK α1β1γ1 at the ADaM site and shows clear β1 selectivity across parents and acyl glucuronide metabolites; this selectivity is a desirable property for limiting pan-AMPK liabilities observed with compounds like MK-8722 (e.g., cardiac glycogen accumulation) (Ryder et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025).  
- Demonstrated on-target cytoprotection in RPE. Li et al. (2018) show AMPKα1-dependent protection of ARPE-19 and primary RPE against UVR, with mechanistic readouts aligned to AMD pathogenesis: increased NADPH, Nrf2 target induction, reduced ROS, lipid peroxidation, DNA damage, apoptosis, and cell death—providing a strong cell-biological foundation for further RPE work (Li et al., 2018).  
- Mechanistic fit to AMD drivers. AMPK activation intersects the principal RPE failure modes in AMD—redox imbalance (Nrf2), impaired autophagy/mitophagy (ULK1/mTORC1), and lipid dysregulation (ACC, FAO, LXR/ABCA1/G1)—and AMPK-dependent restoration of autophagy/lipophagy and barrier proteins has been demonstrated in ARPE-19 using a different AMPK-activating intervention (liraglutide), making PF-06409577 a mechanistically well-targeted candidate to modulate those pathways (Dang et al., 2021; Tsou et al., 2025; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024).  
- Favorable metabolic profile and organ-protection precedent. PF-06409577 corrected NAFLD and lowered cholesterol in rodent/primate models with liver AMPK dependence, improved renal endpoints in β1-focused paradigms, and did not lower blood glucose in reported contexts, all suggesting a differentiated systemic pharmacology relative to pan-activators and indirect mitochondrial inhibitors (Behl et al., 2021; Steinberg & Carling, 2019).  
- Metabolite pharmacology understood. Active acyl glucuronides have been characterized structurally and functionally and exhibit β1-selective AMPK activation with notable stability, reducing concern about unstable, highly reactive acyl glucuronide species (while not fully removing risk), and informing PK/distribution planning for ocular routes (Ryder et al., 2018).

Key Gaps and Risks  
- No published junctional/TEER data for PF-06409577 in RPE. The project’s central claim—restoration of RPE junction integrity (ZO-1/occludin localization, TEER elevation, reduced paracellular permeability)—has not been demonstrated for PF-06409577 in any RPE model in the sources provided; this is the most critical data gap for the proposed indication (Li et al., 2018; Behl et al., 2021).  
- No PF-06409577 autophagy/lipophagy data in RPE. While AMPK activation in ARPE-19 by liraglutide restored autophagy/lipophagy and rescued ZO-1 in an AMPK-dependent manner, PF-06409577-specific data on ULK1 phosphorylation, LC3 flux, p62 turnover, lysosome–autophagosome fusion, and lipid droplet dynamics in RPE are absent and must be generated (Tsou et al., 2025).  
- AMPK β isoform expression in human RPE is not established in the provided literature. Although ADaM ligands are β1-preferring and PF-06409577 is β1-selective, we do not have direct evidence here that β1 predominates in mature human RPE; consequently, isoform profiling is a necessary early-stage risk-reduction step (Steinberg & Carling, 2019; Ryder et al., 2018).  
- Cellular potency window in RPE requires clarification. Li et al. (2018) show a clear activation threshold between 0.03 μM (inactive) and 0.1–1.0 μM (active) for AMPKα phosphorylation in ARPE-19 and efficacy at 0.3 μM in primary RPE, whereas narrative text suggests “nM” activation; this discrepancy underscores the need for rigorous concentration–response across engagement and functional endpoints in relevant human RPE models (Li et al., 2018).  
- Clinical development discontinued; no ocular safety data. PF-06409577’s clinical program was halted at Phase I for non-ocular indications; no ophthalmic tolerability, ocular PK, or on-target/off-target safety in retinal tissues has been reported here. Acyl glucuronides, while stable in vitro for this series, can pose idiosyncratic risk; pan-AMPK activation has known cardiac liabilities; and network cross-talk (e.g., co-activation of AMPK and mTORC1) could be deleterious in some contexts—all argue for early safety de-risking (Webb et al., 2019; Ryder et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Li et al., 2018).

Programmatic Recommendations  
Near-term, decision-making studies should prioritize: (1) RPE isoform mapping (AMPK α/β/γ mRNA and protein), (2) dose–response and time-course profiling of PF-06409577 in human primary RPE or iPSC-RPE (pAMPKα Thr172, pACC Ser79, NADPH/NADP⁺, Nrf2 protein and targets), (3) autophagy/lipophagy flux assays (LC3-II turnover with/without lysosomal blockade, p62 degradation, ULK1 phosphorylation, mTORC1 markers), (4) lipid droplet quantification (number, size distribution) under FFA or oxLDL loading, (5) junctional biology (ZO-1/occludin claudin-1/4 localization and levels, cingulin/afadin phosphorylation status) and barrier function (TEER, FITC-dextran permeability), and (6) safety pharmacology in RPE (viability, apoptosis, senescence markers; exploration of AMPK–mTORC1 co-activation risk) across 0.03–1.0 μM with pACC-guided on-target exposure (Li et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Li et al., 2018).

If in vitro RPE data are supportive, next steps include: (7) ocular PK after topical/periocular dosing (parent and acyl glucuronides in RPE/choroid), (8) metabolite profiling and covalent adduct risk assessment in ocular tissues, (9) in vivo efficacy in AMD-relevant models (e.g., light damage, Alu RNA–induced RPE degeneration, HFD/oxLDL models) with barrier and lipid endpoints, and (10) safety screens for cardiac glycogen accumulation under systemic exposure (to benchmark β1 selectivity advantages) (Ryder et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024).

Conclusion  
PF-06409577 is a well-characterized, β1-selective, direct AMPK activator with on-target, AMPKα1-dependent cytoprotective activity in RPE cells under oxidative stress, and with strong mechanistic alignment to dry AMD pathobiology via NADPH/Nrf2, autophagy/mitophagy, and lipid metabolism pathways (Li et al., 2018). Class knowledge and comparator interventions support the plausibility that AMPK activation can restore RPE lipid homeostasis and barrier protein organization; however, critical indication-specific evidence—PF-06409577’s effects on RPE autophagy/lipophagy and junctional/TEER endpoints—is currently missing and must be generated before advancing (Tsou et al., 2025; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025). The compound’s β1 selectivity, favorable metabolic efficacy profile (NAFLD/kidney), and lack of glucose-lowering are attractive, but the discontinued clinical status, the pharmacologically active acyl glucuronides, and known liabilities with pan-AMPK activation emphasize the need for deliberate safety de-risking and ocular PK/metabolite work (Behl et al., 2021; Ryder et al., 2018; Webb et al., 2019; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Li et al., 2018).

On balance, PF-06409577 merits a focused, RPE-centric preclinical validation campaign for dry AMD that directly tests barrier and lipid endpoints while monitoring canonical AMPK engagement and redox rescue. Positive readouts across ZO-1/occludin/TEER, autophagy/lipophagy markers, and lipid droplet turnover—together with preservation of mitochondrial/antioxidant markers—would substantially de-risk the mechanistic hypothesis and justify advancement toward ocular PK/safety studies and in vivo efficacy models (Li et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024). At present, claims of TEER restoration and junctional upregulation by PF-06409577 in RPE cannot be substantiated from the available literature and should be considered unproven working hypotheses pending experimental confirmation (Li et al., 2018; Behl et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History (Expanded Summary)  
- Origin/chemotype: Indole-3-carboxylic acid, direct ADaM-site AMPK activator; discovered and preclinically characterized by Pfizer for diabetic nephropathy (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Strang et al., 2025).  
- Selectivity/biophysics: Direct binding to α1β1γ1 with β1 selectivity; acyl glucuronide metabolites retain β1 activity with lower potency; likely mode includes allosteric activation and protection from Thr172 dephosphorylation (Ryder et al., 2018; Steinberg & Carling, 2019).  
- Systemic pharmacology: Liver AMPK activation corrected NAFLD and lowered cholesterol in rodents and primates; β1 activation improved kidney function in rodent models (Behl et al., 2021).  
- Safety-class signals: Pan-activator MK-8722 causes cardiac hypertrophy with glycogen in rodents/primate models; PF-06409577 reported not to lower blood glucose; acyl glucuronides stable but class risk remains (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Behl et al., 2021; Ryder et al., 2018).  
- Ocular biology: Direct RPE cytoprotection against UVR via AMPKα1-dependent signaling; no published PF-06409577 data on RPE junctions/TEER/autophagy endpoints (Li et al., 2018).

Mechanistic Integration in AMD Context  
- AMPK→Nrf2 redox axis: AMPK phosphorylation of Nrf2 (Ser550), indirect relief of KEAP1 repression (via GSK3β inhibition and p62-mediated KEAP1 autophagic degradation), and upregulation of antioxidant enzymes; these are operative in RPE and are enhanced by PF-06409577 in vitro (Hu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2018).  
- AMPK→ULK1/mTOR/autophagy: AMPK initiates autophagy, antagonizes mTORC1, and in RPE models AMPK activation restores autophagy/lipophagy, reduces EMT, and normalizes barrier protein localization under lipid stress—mechanistic endpoints to quantify for PF-06409577 (Dang et al., 2021; Tsou et al., 2025).  
- AMPK→ACC/FAO/lipogenesis: ACC inhibition reduces DNL and malonyl-CoA, permitting FAO flux; in RPE, this is expected to reduce lipid droplet accrual and lipoperoxidation burden central to drusen precursor formation (Webb et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2024).  
- AMPK→junction assembly: Phosphorylation of claudins and scaffold proteins, ZO-1 reassembly, and cytoskeletal remodeling provide a direct mechanistic route for barrier strengthening; this is plausible in RPE but requires PF-06409577-specific testing (Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025).

Decision Framework for Advancement  
- Go/No-Go criteria: Require demonstration that PF-06409577 increases pAMPKα/pACC and Nrf2 targets; reduces ROS/lipid peroxidation/DNA damage in RPE; increases autophagy flux and reduces lipid droplets under FFA or oxLDL; and improves ZO-1/occludin organization with increased TEER and reduced paracellular permeability, all in an AMPK-dependent manner (Li et al., 2018; Tsou et al., 2025; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025).  
- Risk mitigation: Profile β isoform expression in human RPE; measure mTORC1 to exclude maladaptive co-activation; characterize ocular PK and acyl glucuronide distribution after topical/periocular delivery; benchmark systemic exposure to avoid cardiac glycogen liabilities (Steinberg & Carling, 2019; Li et al., 2018; Ryder et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025).  
- Comparative positioning: If PF-06409577 proves effective on junctions and lipid/autophagy endpoints, its β1 selectivity and direct mechanism position it favorably versus indirect activators (metformin) and pan-activators (MK-8722); conversely, lack of junctional efficacy or safety signals would shift focus to alternative AMPK modulators or upstream modulators that converge on AMPK/Nrf2 with better ocular PK (Dang et al., 2021; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025).

In summary, PF-06409577 has clear mechanistic and cellular evidence to support further exploration in dry AMD, with the caveat that the most clinically salient endpoints for RPE barrier restoration and lipid clearance remain to be proven for this agent. A disciplined experimental plan targeting these gaps will determine whether PF-06409577 advances as a credible candidate for RPE junction restoration in dry AMD (Li et al., 2018; Yibcharoenporn et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024; Behl et al., 2021).
