Proposal for Saroglitazar (Cayman 19606)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Saroglitazar is a novel, fully synthetic small‐molecule compound that functions as a dual agonist of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors, specifically targeting both the α and γ isoforms, with a pharmacological profile that heavily favors PPAR-α activation. Initially synthesized by Zydus Cadila (also referred to as Cadila Healthcare Limited) in Ahmedabad, India, saroglitazar was designed as a new chemical entity (NCE) – a groundbreaking achievement as it is regarded as India’s first NCE to reach the market (Sharma et al., 2015; Sosale et al., 2015). Chemically, it is defined as (S)-α-ethoxy-4-{2-[2-methyl-5-(4-methylthio)phenyl]-1H-pyrrol-1-yl]ethoxy}-benzenepropanoic acid magnesium salt, a structure that confers the necessary lipophilic and acidic characteristics common among PPAR agonists (Jain et al., 2015; Sharma et al., 2015). Being a member of the glitazar class, this drug group historically aimed to combine the lipid-lowering benefits of fibrates (PPAR-α agonists) with the insulin-sensitizing and anti-inflammatory effects of thiazolidinediones (PPAR-γ agonists), yet previous attempts with similar dual compounds were marred by safety concerns, including adverse cardiovascular and renal outcomes (Chatterjee et al., 2015; Derosa et al., 2018). Saroglitazar distinguishes itself by presenting a predominantly PPAR-α profile with moderate PPAR-γ activity, a fine-tuning that aims to harness the metabolic benefits while mitigating the classical side effects associated with pure PPAR-γ agonism, such as weight gain and edema (Jain et al., 2015; Chhabra et al., 2022; Sosale et al., 2015). Its synthetic origin, coupled with a well-characterized chemical structure that includes key functional groups (in particular, an α-ethoxy carboxylic acid moiety that forms hydrogen bonds with amino acid residues in the receptor binding domain), has enabled a robust mechanistic foundation from which to understand its systemic pharmacology (Joshi, 2015; Sharma et al., 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, saroglitazar has been approved by India’s Drug Controller General (DCGI) for the treatment of diabetic dyslipidemia and hypertriglyceridemia in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) who are not adequately managed by statin therapy alone (Sosale et al., 2015; Lange et al., 2022). Extensive preclinical studies have demonstrated its lipid-lowering, insulin-sensitizing, and anti-inflammatory effects in multiple animal models, ranging from diabetic rodents (db/db mice, Zucker fa/fa rats) to nonhuman primates; these studies laid the groundwork for phase I human trials, the results of which indicated favorable pharmacokinetics and safety margins (Jain et al., 2015; Joshi, 2015; Jani et al., 2013). Subsequent phase III clinical trials—among them the PRESS V and PRESS VI studies—confirmed its efficacy in reducing serum triglyceride levels by approximately 45–47% and improving other dyslipidemic parameters in the target patient population (Joshi, 2015; Honda et al., 2021). Beyond its use in diabetic dyslipidemia, recent research efforts have extended its potential application into metabolic liver diseases such as nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) (Honda et al., 2021; Vuppalanchi et al., 2022). Despite the substantial body of literature supporting its use in metabolic disorders, none of the documented clinical or preclinical studies to date have directly tested saroglitazar in ocular conditions such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar retinal pathologies (Tan et al., 2017; Kaul et al., 2019). However, the robust clinical validation of saroglitazar’s dual PPAR-α/γ effects in liver disease and diabetic dyslipidemia provides an important translational basis for its repurposing, especially given that both chronic inflammation and disordered lipid metabolism have been recognized as central drivers in the progression of dry AMD (Sharma et al., 2015; Sosale et al., 2015).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, saroglitazar acts as a ligand for the nuclear receptor superfamily member PPAR. Once bound, the compound facilitates the heterodimerization of the activated receptor with the retinoid X receptor (RXR), and this heterodimer subsequently binds to specific peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs) in the promoter regions of target genes, thus initiating transcriptional regulation (Chudiwal & Mujeeb, n.d.; Joshi, 2015). The activation of PPAR-α by saroglitazar leads to an upregulation of genes involved in hepatic fatty acid oxidation pathways, including enzymes responsible for β-oxidation, which results in decreased triglyceride synthesis and secretion while enhancing the clearance of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins (Patel et al., 2018a; Patel et al., 2018b). This mechanism is especially relevant for reducing systemic lipid levels—a property exploited in the treatment of diabetic dyslipidemia. Concurrently, the PPAR-γ component, though moderate in its activation by saroglitazar, plays an important role in modulating inflammatory responses and improving insulin sensitivity. Activation of PPAR-γ results in the repression of pro-inflammatory cytokine genes (including IL-6 and IL-8) and the promotion of genes associated with adipocyte differentiation and lipid storage, while also inhibiting the expression of inflammatory mediators in immune cells (Gawrieh et al., 2021). Structural biology studies indicate that the α-ethoxy carboxylic acid portion of saroglitazar forms hydrogen bonds with key amino acid residues within the ligand-binding domains of both PPAR-α and PPAR-γ, thereby stabilizing the receptor conformation for optimal transcriptional activity (Sharma et al., 2015; Joshi, 2015; Honda et al., 2021). This dual receptor engagement enables a coordinated response where lipid metabolism is corrected via PPAR-α activation while a parallel anti-inflammatory effect is mediated through PPAR-γ, ultimately leading to improved metabolic homeostasis (Honda et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2017).

In the context of dry AMD, the chronic low-grade inflammation observed within the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) along with the abnormal accumulation of lipids (drusen formation) are thought to contribute significantly to disease progression. PPAR-γ has been implicated in the modulation of inflammatory responses in various tissues, including ocular tissues, and its activation can result in the suppression of inflammatory cytokines and a reduction in oxidative stress (Kaul et al., 2019; Honda et al., 2021). In parallel, PPAR-α activation is associated with increased fatty acid oxidation and improved lipid clearance, a function that could potentially counteract the deposition of lipid-rich drusen in the outer retina (Patel et al., 2018a; Patel et al., 2018b). Thus, saroglitazar’s dual activation of these receptors offers a mechanistic rationale for addressing both inflammation and dysregulated lipid metabolism in the RPE. Given that barrier integrity in the RPE, as measured by transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), is closely linked to the expression and organization of tight junction proteins such as zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin, the anti-inflammatory actions of PPAR-γ may be critical in preserving these junctional complexes under inflammatory stress, as evidenced by experimental models where TNF-α exposure leads to barrier compromise (Chudiwal & Mujeeb, n.d.; Chhabra et al., 2022). The structural and molecular interactions described in the literature provide a detailed understanding of how saroglitazar can modulate these pathways at the transcriptional level, potentially offering both immediate and long-term benefits in maintaining RPE barrier function (Joshi, 2015; Sosale et al., 2015).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis under investigation is that dual PPAR-α/γ activation by saroglitazar will exert a synergistic effect on RPE cells under conditions of inflammatory stress—a condition that mirrors the pathophysiology of dry AMD. In an in vitro model employing the ARPE-19 cell line (a well-established human RPE cell model), exposure to the pro-inflammatory cytokine tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) is known to compromise the integrity of the RPE monolayer by reducing TEER and disrupting the organization of critical tight junction proteins, specifically ZO-1 and occludin (Tan et al., 2017; Sosale et al., 2015). Preliminary data provided by the research team indicate that treatment with 1 µM saroglitazar is capable of restoring TEER by approximately 55% and significantly reducing the release of the inflammatory cytokines interleukin-6 (IL-6) and interleukin-8 (IL-8) in TNF-α-challenged ARPE-19 monolayers. This robust effect is postulated to be mediated via the activation of PPAR-γ, which leads to the suppression of inflammatory mediator expression, while the concurrent activation of PPAR-α enhances lipid catabolism and clearance. Such dual action is particularly relevant, given that chronic inflammation and impaired lipid metabolism are two principal drivers in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Sosale et al., 2015; Chudiwal & Mujeeb, n.d.).

Moreover, the molecular basis for this anticipated benefit is supported by prior evidence in non-ocular models. For instance, in hepatic and adipose tissues, saroglitazar has been shown to enhance the expression of genes involved in fatty acid oxidation and to downregulate inflammatory pathways—effects that translate into improved metabolic profiles and reduced systemic inflammation (Gawrieh et al., 2021; Derosa et al., 2018). Although these results originate from studies primarily focused on metabolic syndrome and diabetic dyslipidemia, there is a strong mechanistic rationale that similar pathways may be operative in the RPE. It is known that PPARs are expressed in ocular tissues, including the RPE, and that their activation can modulate local inflammatory responses and cellular lipid metabolism (Gawrieh et al., 2021; Sosale et al., 2015). Thus, in the proposed experimental context, saroglitazar is expected to restore RPE monolayer integrity by preserving the ZO-1 and occludin architecture and recovering TEER—in turn, this could prevent the leakage of toxic substances and inflammatory mediators that exacerbate RPE dysfunction in dry AMD.

In addition to its effects on the RPE barrier, the anti-inflammatory properties conferred by PPAR-γ activation may also counteract the paracrine signaling that contributes to chronic inflammation in the retina; reduced secretion of IL-6 and IL-8 will likely diminish local immune cell recruitment and activation, thereby alleviating the inflammatory milieu that predisposes to cell damage and drusen formation (Chudiwal & Mujeeb, n.d.; Sosale et al., 2015). The enhanced lipid clearance mediated by PPAR-α activation may further reduce intracellular lipid accumulation, a factor closely linked to oxidative stress and subsequent RPE cell apoptosis. Consequently, the combined effects of saroglitazar could contribute to the stabilization—and potentially the restoration—of retinal homeostasis in the setting of dry AMD (Patel et al., 2018a; Patel et al., 2018b).

Overall Evaluation:  
Taken together, saroglitazar emerges as a promising repurposing candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration based on its dual pharmacological actions. Its primary strengths lie in its well-defined mechanism of action that combines robust lipid-lowering effects with potent anti-inflammatory properties. The predominant activation of PPAR-α is particularly advantageous in enhancing fatty acid oxidation and reducing lipid deposition, which may help in curbing the formation of drusen—a hallmark of dry AMD—while the moderate activation of PPAR-γ minimizes the risk of adverse effects such as weight gain and edema that have historically accompanied other PPAR-γ-targeted therapies (Sharma et al., 2015; Sosale et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2017). The fact that saroglitazar has already undergone extensive clinical validation in metabolic disorders provides a strong translational foundation for its potential application in ocular diseases. Its established safety profile, favourable pharmacokinetic characteristics, and therapeutic efficacy in non-ocular settings imply that, with appropriate formulation adjustments to ensure adequate retinal bioavailability, saroglitazar could be repurposed with relatively low developmental risk.

However, the candidate also has notable weaknesses. Currently, there is no direct evidence from preclinical ocular models or clinical trials that explicitly investigate the efficacy of saroglitazar in dry AMD or related retinal conditions. The pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic parameters optimized for systemic metabolic control may not automatically translate to effective intraocular drug levels, and the unique immunological and biochemical environment of the retina could pose challenges that are not encountered in hepatic or adipose tissue (Chatterjee et al., 2015). Thus, there exists an imperative need for thorough preclinical testing in relevant ocular models to establish dosing regimens, evaluate retinal safety, and confirm that the molecular targets of saroglitazar are effectively engaged in the RPE.

Another potential challenge lies in drug delivery. Given that saroglitazar was developed for oral administration with systemic effects in mind, repurposing for dry AMD may require the development of novel delivery approaches. This could include exploring topical eye drop formulations, intravitreal injections, or even sustained-release implants to ensure that therapeutic concentrations are achieved in the retina while minimizing systemic side effects. The pharmacological properties documented in the metabolic studies (such as rapid absorption and predominant hepatobiliary clearance) must be re-evaluated in the context of ocular tissue penetration and retention (Patel et al., 2018b; Vuppalanchi et al., 2022).

On the strength side, the dual action on inflammation and lipid metabolism is uniquely relevant for dry AMD, where both chronic, low-grade inflammation and aberrant lipid accumulation play critical roles in disease progression. In vitro data showing that 1 µM saroglitazar can restore TEER by 55% in TNF-α–compromised ARPE-19 monolayers and decrease pro-inflammatory cytokine release (IL-6, IL-8) provide promising initial proof-of-concept evidence that warrants further investigation (Sosale et al., 2015; Chudiwal & Mujeeb, n.d.). These findings suggest that saroglitazar may not only halt the progression of RPE barrier dysfunction but might also reverse some of the deleterious cellular processes induced by chronic inflammatory cytokine exposure. Such dual benefits, if reproducible in more advanced ocular models, would represent a significant therapeutic advance in managing dry AMD—a condition for which current treatment options remain limited.

In summary, saroglitazar’s established safety and efficacy in metabolic diseases, together with its molecular capacity to modulate both inflammatory cascades and lipid metabolism, render it an attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. The proposed mechanism—that dual PPAR-α/γ activation can restore RPE barrier integrity by preserving tight junction proteins (ZO-1, occludin) and enhancing transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) while simultaneously reducing inflammatory cytokine output—addresses two key pathogenic drivers implicated in the progression of dry AMD. Importantly, the translational feasibility of repurposing a drug that has already been clinically validated in humans accelerates the potential developmental timeline, provided that ocular pharmacokinetics and local target engagement are confirmed in specialized preclinical studies.

It is recommended that further studies be designed to (1) characterize the expression and functionality of PPAR-α and PPAR-γ receptors in primary human RPE cells and in animal models of dry AMD; (2) adapt the formulation of saroglitazar to optimize intraocular delivery and retention; (3) conduct detailed mechanistic studies that elucidate the molecular pathways through which saroglitazar modulates tight junction integrity and inflammatory signaling in the RPE; and (4) perform in vivo proof-of-concept studies using established animal models of dry AMD to evaluate both efficacy and safety in the ocular context (Sosale et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2017; Gawrieh et al., 2021). Addressing these points would greatly strengthen the rationale for clinical trials investigating saroglitazar as a novel therapeutic option for dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
Strengths of saroglitazar as a repurposed candidate for dry AMD include its thoroughly characterized dual agonist activity, which confers both an enhanced lipid-clearing effect via PPAR-α activation and a potent anti-inflammatory effect via PPAR-γ activation. The compound’s safety profile and clinical validation in metabolic disorders, such as diabetic dyslipidemia and NAFLD, provide a robust foundation for potential repurposing, leveraging existing pharmacokinetic and toxicological data (Sharma et al., 2015; Sosale et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2017). Additionally, the preliminary in vitro evidence indicating improvements in RPE barrier function—with measurable restoration of TEER and reduction in key inflammatory markers like IL-6 and IL-8—are highly encouraging, as they suggest that saroglitazar may help halt or even reverse the RPE dysfunction that is central to dry AMD pathology (Chudiwal & Mujeeb, n.d.; Sosale et al., 2015).

Nonetheless, the weaknesses of this approach cannot be overlooked. The current literature does not offer any direct evidence of saroglitazar’s efficacy or safety in ocular applications, nor is there any previous usage of this compound (or closely related glitazars) specifically in dry AMD. The unique microenvironment of the retina, characterized by its blood-retina barrier and distinct immunologic landscape, may influence both drug delivery and receptor responsiveness in ways that differ substantially from systemic tissues such as the liver or adipose tissue (Chatterjee et al., 2015). Moreover, given its original development for oral administration targeting systemic metabolic conditions, modifications in the drug’s formulation may be necessary to achieve effective concentrations within the retinal tissues without provoking off-target systemic effects. These uncertainties emphasize the critical need for comprehensive preclinical studies focused on ocular pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and efficacy in animal models that recapitulate dry AMD pathology (Patel et al., 2018b; Vuppalanchi et al., 2022).

In conclusion, saroglitazar presents a scientifically compelling and mechanistically plausible candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its dual PPAR-α/γ agonism offers an integrated approach to addressing both fundamental pathogenic mechanisms of dry AMD—namely, chronic inflammation and impaired lipid clearance. While the preexisting clinical validation in metabolic diseases confers significant translational advantages, targeted ocular studies remain essential to confirm that the drug’s pharmacological actions can be effectively harnessed in the retina. Should the hurdles of ocular formulation and local target engagement be overcome, saroglitazar could offer a novel means to preserve RPE barrier integrity, reduce inflammatory damage, and ultimately slow or reverse the progression of dry AMD. Given these considerations, the proposed repurposing of saroglitazar merits further investigation through detailed preclinical ocular studies and, pending positive results, subsequent clinical trials tailored for patients with dry AMD (Sosale et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2017; Gawrieh et al., 2021).

Overall, saroglitazar’s repurposing for dry AMD is supported by a strong mechanistic rationale and promising preliminary in vitro data; however, significant challenges remain regarding its intraocular delivery, pharmacokinetic optimization, and direct demonstration of efficacy in ocular models. A balanced research strategy that addresses these issues through systematic preclinical evaluation and formulation development is warranted to fully elucidate the therapeutic potential of saroglitazar in managing dry AMD.

Proposal for Bexarotene (Selleckchem S1572)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bexarotene is a fully synthetic retinoid analog classified as a rexinoid, specifically acting as a pan–retinoid X receptor (RXR) agonist. It was originally developed through structure–activity relationship studies aimed at mimicking the natural ligand 9-cis retinoic acid, while providing greater receptor selectivity, improved potency, and a pharmacological profile amenable to therapeutic use. Its synthesis and subsequent discovery were driven by the need to harness RXR‐mediated gene regulation, and it subsequently became the only FDA-approved synthetic RXR ligand to date (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021). As a member of the retinoid drug class, bexarotene has been primarily used in the oncological setting, specifically for the treatment of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, and its chemical design reflects modifications that impart high lipophilicity and receptor specificity (Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018). This synthetic derivation distinguishes it from naturally occurring retinoids and underpins its utility across a number of experimental and clinical contexts.

Therapeutic History:  
Bexarotene’s clinical history is marked by its approval as a second-line therapy for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, which provided a strong basis for its safety and efficacy in a human disease setting (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021). In addition to its primary use in oncology, preclinical and early clinical research has investigated bexarotene for applications in neurodegenerative diseases, most notably Alzheimer’s disease and multiple sclerosis. These studies have demonstrated that RXR activation by bexarotene can influence the clearance of pathological protein aggregates and promote remyelination, respectively (Gaunt, 2020; Behl et al., 2022). However, despite the broad mechanistic appeal of RXR agonism in modifying lipid metabolism and neuroinflammation, there is little to no established clinical or veterinary precedent for employing bexarotene in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar ocular degenerative conditions. In fact, while several RXR agonists have been considered in various models of ocular disease, the role of RXR in the diseased retina remains underexplored, with only sparse reports such as a study with the RXR agonist PA024 in retinal degeneration models (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014). This gap in therapeutic history presents both a challenge and an opportunity in repurposing bexarotene for dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action:  
Bexarotene exerts its pharmacological effects primarily by binding to the ligand-binding domain of RXR isoforms (RXRα, RXRβ, and RXRγ) with nanomolar potency, inducing conformational changes that favor the recruitment of coactivators and subsequent transcriptional activation of targeted genes (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021). RXR is a promiscuous nuclear receptor that forms obligate heterodimers with several other nuclear receptors, most notably the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs) such as PPARγ. In doing so, the bexarotene-induced RXR/PPARγ heterodimer binds to specific peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs) in the genome, thereby upregulating target genes involved in lipid metabolism and transport. One key target is ABCA1, an ATP-binding cassette transporter implicated in cholesterol efflux from cells, which plays a central role in maintaining intracellular lipid homeostasis (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Choudhary & Malek, 2016).

In the context of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, the activation of the RXR/PPARγ pathway is particularly compelling. RPE cells are highly involved in the processing and clearance of lipids, including cholesterol, and in modulating the structural integrity of the outer blood-retinal barrier via tight junction proteins such as claudin-1 and occludin. When under stress—such as exposure to cytotoxic mediators like 7-ketocholesterol (7KCh), which disrupts normal junctional organization and reduces transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER)—the activation of RXR offers a potential therapeutic avenue. Bexarotene’s ability to stimulate RXR signaling is expected to upregulate ABCA1 expression, thereby enhancing cholesterol efflux, while also promoting the transcription of genes that lead to the re-expression of claudin-1 and occludin, which are critical for restoring barrier integrity (Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Choudhary & Malek, 2016).

The biochemical interactions following RXR activation by bexarotene include a cascade of events where the ligand-receptor complex alters the transcriptional landscape of the cell. This process entails the heterodimerization of RXR with its partner receptor, binding to DNA response elements, and initiating the recruitment of transcriptional coactivators, which together drive the expression of genes that modulate lipid metabolism, inflammatory responses, and cell junction integrity. The specificity of bexarotene for RXR, as opposed to broader retinoic acid receptor (RAR) activity, allows for a more targeted enhancement of these pathways—a factor that is crucial in tissues like the RPE, where precise regulation of lipid handling and barrier properties is essential for retinal health (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Choudhary & Malek, 2016).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis underlying the repurposing of bexarotene for dry AMD is that its activation of RXR in RPE cells will facilitate heterodimerization with PPARγ, driving the transcriptional upregulation of lipid-handling genes, most notably ABCA1. In vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells have provided compelling preliminary data indicating that exposure to 0.5 µM bexarotene in the presence of 7-ketocholesterol stress is capable of restoring TEER to approximately 85% of baseline values and significantly increasing ABCA1 mRNA levels. This restoration of TEER suggests that bexarotene not only promotes cholesterol efflux by upregulating ABCA1 but also exerts a beneficial influence on the expression of key tight junction proteins, such as claudin-1 and occludin, which are essential for maintaining the integrity of the RPE barrier (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014).

The expected molecular effect in the assay is thus twofold. First, through its molecular interaction with RXR, bexarotene reinforces the RXR/PPARγ heterodimer formation, triggering a cascade of gene transcription events that culminate in enhanced cholesterol efflux via ABCA1. This effect directly addresses the accumulation of lipid deposits that contribute to RPE dysfunction in dry AMD. Second, by re-inducing the expression of claudin-1 and occludin, bexarotene is anticipated to improve cellular junctional integrity, thereby reducing paracellular leakage and restoring the overall barrier function of the RPE as measured by TEER. The use of ocular gel formulations for local delivery promises to concentrate the therapeutic effect within the eye, circumventing the systemic adverse effects that are typically associated with bexarotene’s unfavorable physicochemical properties, such as high lipophilicity and low systemic solubility (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of bexarotene as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is founded upon a robust mechanistic rationale and promising preliminary in vitro data, yet it also presents several challenges that must be addressed through rigorous further research. One of the primary strengths of this candidate lies in its well-established mode of action as a selective RXR agonist. Its ability to promote heterodimerization with PPARγ and subsequently upregulate genes such as ABCA1 is well supported by a substantial body of research in other disease contexts, including neurodegeneration and oncology (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Gaunt, 2020). This receptor specificity not only underscores bexarotene’s potential to modulate RPE lipid metabolism but also suggests that similar pharmacological principles could translate into the restoration of tight junction integrity—a key therapeutic goal in dry AMD.

Another significant strength is its prior clinical approval for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. This provides a substantial amount of safety data and experience in human use, which could expedite the repurposing process under a drug repositioning strategy. Moreover, the observed in vitro effects—namely the partial restoration of TEER and the increase in ABCA1 mRNA in stressed ARPE-19 cells—lend direct support to the hypothesis that RXR agonism can counteract 7-ketocholesterol-induced disruptions in RPE function (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014). The concept of using ocular gel formulations to achieve localized delivery and thereby minimize systemic side effects is another innovative aspect that addresses one of the traditional limitations of bexarotene, namely its adverse systemic metabolic disturbances, which include dyslipidemia and hypothyroidism (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021).

However, there are notable weaknesses that temper this optimism. First, bexarotene’s unfavorable physicochemical properties—its high lipophilicity and low solubility—pose a significant formulation challenge, especially when transitioning from systemic oncology applications to local ocular delivery. While gel formulations offer a potential solution, achieving the precise pharmacokinetics and adequate tissue penetration in the retina will require meticulous formulation development and validation. Second, despite the extensive research on RXR agonism in other tissues, there is very limited precedent for the use of bexarotene or similar compounds in the treatment of dry AMD or related ocular diseases. In other words, while the underlying nuclear receptor biology in the retina is compelling, the absence of prior clinical or even robust preclinical ocular studies increases the risk associated with translational uncertainty (Dorofeeva et al., 2023; Malek & Lad, 2014).

Moreover, systemic side effects associated with bexarotene have been well documented in its approved indications. Although the strategy of localized ocular delivery aims to mitigate these adverse effects, any leakage from the ocular compartment into systemic circulation could potentially re-expose patients to these risks. Additionally, the complexity of dry AMD as a multifactorial disease—with contributions from oxidative stress, inflammation, and complex extracellular matrix alterations—means that modulating only lipid handling and tight junction integrity might not be sufficient to arrest or reverse disease progression. Thus, while the mechanistic hypothesis is sound, it should ideally be integrated into a broader therapeutic strategy that also addresses other pathological mechanisms in dry AMD.

In summary, the proposed use of bexarotene for dry AMD is supported by a strong mechanistic foundation based on RXR agonism and its downstream effects on lipid metabolism and cellular junction integrity. The preliminary in vitro evidence in ARPE-19 cells under 7-ketocholesterol stress is promising, particularly with the reported restoration of TEER and upregulation of ABCA1. The strengths of this candidate include its specificity for RXR, the translational potential backed by its FDA–approved status for an unrelated indication, and the innovative strategy of local ocular delivery through gel formulations. On the other hand, challenges related to its physicochemical properties, potential for systemic side effects, and the overall gaps in preclinical ocular data necessitate further rigorous research. Preclinical studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD and careful formulation optimization will be essential next steps to validate the therapeutic potential of bexarotene in this context (Willems, Zaienne, & Merk, 2021; Watanabe & Kakuta, 2018; Choudhary & Malek, 2016; Malek & Lad, 2014).

Proposal for 4-Octyl Itaconate (4-OI; Sigma SML2192)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
4‐Octyl Itaconate (4‐OI) is a cell‐permeable derivative of itaconate, a naturally occurring immunometabolite generated in activated macrophages during inflammatory responses. 4‐OI has been synthesized by chemically modifying itaconate to improve its lipophilicity and enhance its cellular uptake, which in turn facilitates its electrophilic reactivity. This improved cell permeability enables 4‐OI to effectively modulate intracellular targets such as Keap1. As a member of the electrophilic compounds class, 4‐OI belongs to a group of therapeutics that are designed to exploit the redox-sensing molecular machinery of cells. Historically, compounds in this class have been used to induce antioxidant and cytoprotective responses by activating the nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway. In its commercial form (Sigma SML2192), 4‐OI offers a reproducible and standardized reagent for preclinical studies and drug development, making it an attractive candidate for repurposing in conditions where oxidative stress plays a central pathophysiological role, such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–6; Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6).

The therapeutic candidate is particularly intriguing given the significant role of oxidative stress and inflammation in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, especially within the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). The RPE is highly susceptible to oxidative damage due to its high metabolic demand, continuous exposure to light, and abundance of polyunsaturated fatty acids. Dysregulation of the redox balance in these cells has been directly tied to barrier dysfunction, including loss of transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and increased permeability to molecules such as FITC-dextran. By design, 4‐OI aims to exploit its electrophilic nature to alkylate reactive cysteine residues on the Keap1 protein, thereby liberating Nrf2 and triggering its stabilization and nuclear translocation. Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 upregulates various antioxidant genes and possibly genes that maintain tight junction integrity, thus promoting cytoprotection and barrier restoration. This profile makes 4‐OI a promising candidate in the context of dry AMD, where restoration of RPE barrier function is a critical therapeutic goal (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–6; Cai et al., 2021, pp. 5–6).

Therapeutic History:  
The use of itaconate derivatives, including 4‐OI, has been widely investigated across several biomedical fields, particularly in studies focused on modulating the cellular response to oxidative stress and inflammation. Preclinical studies in various cell types have demonstrated that 4‐OI can potently activate the Nrf2 pathway, leading to increased transcription of phase II detoxification enzymes and antioxidant proteins. For instance, in human retinal pigment epithelium cells exposed to angiotensin II (Ang II), 4‐OI was shown to significantly reduce reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation and malondialdehyde (MDA) levels while concomitantly enhancing superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity. Such findings provide concrete evidence of its ROS-scavenging potential and anti-inflammatory efficacy (Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6).

Outside the ocular context, 4‐OI has been evaluated in models of renal ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI), where it was observed to reduce tubular injury scores, lower inflammatory cytokine levels, and improve overall kidney function through activation of the Nrf2 pathway. Similar protective effects have been recorded in lung transplantation models under cold ischemia/reperfusion conditions, wherein 4‐OI treatment improved epithelial cell viability and donor lung function (Gao et al., 2025, pp. 1–2; Li et al., 2023, pp. 3–5, 9–11). The mechanism underlying these benefits consistently centers on the electrophilic activation of the Nrf2 pathway via alkylation of Keap1 cysteines.

Regarding ocular diseases, while the direct use of 4‐OI in dry AMD has yet to be fully evaluated in clinical settings, several studies have established the general importance of the Keap1/Nrf2 axis in maintaining retinal health. Agents that stimulate this pathway, including dimethyl fumarate, quercetin, and various itaconate derivatives, have shown promising results in protecting RPE cells from oxidative and inflammatory insults (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–7). Preliminary investigations using 4‐OI in RPE cell models have indicated improvements in antioxidant responses and cell viability, suggesting that compounds of this class may offer therapeutic benefits similar to those seen in other tissues challenged by oxidative stress (Fu et al., 2021, pp. 6–8).

In addition, the therapeutic history of similar electrophilic Nrf2 activators highlights their dual role both in mitigating inflammatory responses and in bolstering barrier functions via tight junction stabilization. This is particularly relevant when considering the pathogenesis of dry AMD, which is marked by compromised RPE barrier integrity and chronic oxidative injury (Cai et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Falcão et al., 2025, p. 20). Thus, although the direct clinical application of 4‐OI in AMD is still in its early stages, the compound has a well-documented history in preclinical models of oxidative injury and barrier dysfunction, which supports its repurposing for dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action:  
The central mechanism by which 4‐OI exerts its therapeutic effects is through its electrophilic modification of Keap1, a regulatory protein that normally sequesters Nrf2 in the cytoplasm and promotes its proteasomal degradation. Under basal conditions, Keap1 binds to Nrf2 and facilitates its ubiquitination, thereby maintaining low intracellular levels of Nrf2. 4‐OI covalently modifies key cysteine residues on Keap1, which disrupts the Keap1/Nrf2 interaction and prevents the ubiquitination and subsequent degradation of Nrf2. This post-translational modification allows Nrf2 to accumulate in the cytoplasm and eventually translocate into the nucleus (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–6; Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6).

Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds to the antioxidant response element (ARE) located in the promoter region of various cytoprotective genes. This binding leads to the transcriptional activation of genes encoding a host of antioxidant enzymes and protective proteins, including heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), and various glutathione biosynthetic enzymes. Through this coordinated induction of antioxidant defenses, cells can effectively neutralize ROS, restore redox homeostasis, and mitigate the harmful effects of chronic oxidative stress (Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6; Camelo, 2025, pp. 6–7).

In addition to its antioxidant role, Nrf2 activation has been implicated in the regulation of inflammatory signaling pathways. By promoting the expression of anti-inflammatory mediators and by interfering with the nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) pathway—through competition for transcriptional co-activators—Nrf2 activation can lead to decreased secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-8 (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–7). It is worth noting that the effects of 4‐OI on inflammatory cytokine production can be dose-dependent; while low concentrations typically suppress cytokine transcription and inflammation, higher doses have been associated with unintended pro-inflammatory outcomes, such as enhanced IL-1β release and inflammatory apoptosis in certain cell types (Muri et al., 2020, pp. 2–3, 5–7). Such dual effects necessitate careful titration of the dose to ensure that the therapeutic window is maximized for protective outcomes while minimizing potential cytotoxicity.

Furthermore, evidence from studies on endothelial cells and Caco-2 monolayers indicates that similar electrophilic Nrf2 activators can protect and restore barrier function, as measured by transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER). In these models, activation of Nrf2 has been linked to the upregulation of tight junction proteins and the maintenance of paracellular integrity (Cai et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Gao et al., 2025, pp. 1–2). Although direct studies of TEER in RPE cells treated with 4‐OI are limited, the underlying molecular logic suggests a similar beneficial impact on RPE barrier function. This is particularly relevant given the hypothesis that 4‐OI treatment will restore TEER and decrease FITC-dextran permeability in oxidative stress or A2E plus blue-light injury models by both reducing oxidative stress and enhancing the expression of tight junction proteins that are regulated by Nrf2 (Camelo, 2025, pp. 6–7; Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6).

Additionally, the specificity of 4‐OI for Keap1’s cysteine residues, along with its favorable cell permeability, positions the compound as a modulatory switch that can trigger a host of downstream protective pathways. This multifaceted mechanism of action, encompassing direct antioxidant effects, anti-inflammatory activity, and preservation of barrier function, underpins the potential clinical utility of 4‐OI in conditions marked by oxidative damage and barrier dysfunction, such as dry AMD (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–6; Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6).

Expected Effect:  
The proposed hypothesis for employing 4‐OI in dry AMD is that by alkylating Keap1 cysteines in RPE, it will stabilize and induce the nuclear accumulation of Nrf2, thereby upregulating antioxidant defenses and tight junction proteins. The expected outcome in an in vitro model is a restoration of TEER and a decrease in FITC-dextran permeability under conditions of oxidative stress or when RPE cells are challenged with A2E and blue-light exposure. Precedent for this predicted effect is found in studies where 4‐OI’s electrophilic activation of Nrf2 has led to robust antioxidant responses, including the upregulation of genes encoding detoxifying enzymes and the suppression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (Camelo, 2025, pp. 6–7; Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6).

Specifically, the anticipated activation of Nrf2 in RPE cells is expected to result in increased expression of key cytoprotective genes such as HO-1 and NQO1, which play crucial roles in combating ROS-mediated cellular damage. In addition, Nrf2 activation has been linked to the expression of genes associated with maintaining tight junction integrity—an essential aspect of the RPE’s barrier function (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–6; Cai et al., 2021, pp. 5–6). Given that reduced TEER and increased FITC-dextran permeability are hallmarks of RPE barrier disruption in dry AMD, the modulation of these parameters by 4‐OI is a central goal of the proposed intervention.

Experimental data from studies in other cell types, such as endothelial cells challenged with endotoxin, have shown that electrophilic Nrf2 activators can rescue TEER to levels exceeding 95%, suggesting that similar outcomes may be achievable in RPE cells (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–6; Cai et al., 2021, pp. 5–6). In parallel, research using 4‐OI in human primary RPE models has demonstrated a reduction in ROS production, decreased inflammation, and improved cellular viability in the context of oxidative stress induced by agents like angiotensin II (Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6, 7–8). These findings lend credence to the expectation that 4‐OI will counteract A2E plus blue-light-induced oxidative damage in RPE cells, thereby reestablishing normal barrier properties.

Moreover, given that oxidative stress and inflammation are intimately intertwined in the progression of dry AMD, the multitargeted action of 4‐OI is expected to yield a comprehensive protective effect. By dampening inflammatory cytokine release (including IL-6, IL-8, and MCP-1) and reducing oxidative biomarkers such as malondialdehyde, 4‐OI should mitigate the deleterious microenvironment that contributes to RPE dysfunction (Camelo, 2025, pp. 6–7; Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6). The net result would be a restoration of cellular homeostasis, improved barrier integrity, and a reduction in the secondary effects of chronic oxidative injury, which collectively translate into a potential therapeutic benefit for dry AMD.

Finally, the anticipated outcomes are supported by the observation that Nrf2 is expressed in RPE cells and is critical for their survival under stress conditions (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–6; Cai et al., 2021, pp. 2–3). Activation of Nrf2 by 4‐OI, therefore, is expected to counteract the pathophysiological mechanisms that precipitate RPE degeneration in dry AMD. These effects could be quantified both by measuring restored TEER values as a proxy for tight junction integrity and by assessing decreased FITC-dextran permeability as an indicator of improved barrier function (Cai et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6).

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall evaluation of 4‐Octyl Itaconate as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is decidedly positive, though not without certain challenges that must be addressed in subsequent investigations. One of the most significant strengths of 4‐OI is its strong mechanistic rationale: by targeting Keap1 via electrophilic alkylation, 4‐OI effectively liberates Nrf2, triggering a cascade of antioxidant and cytoprotective responses that are crucial for maintaining RPE health. This mode of action is consistent with a broad body of preclinical evidence across several tissue models, including renal, pulmonary, and endothelial systems (Gao et al., 2025, pp. 1–2; Li et al., 2023, pp. 3–5, 9–11). The ability of 4‐OI to restore barrier function, as evidenced by its reported rescue of TEER in endotoxin-challenged endothelial cells, provides an additional layer of validation for its potential use in RPE models, where barrier dysfunction is a hallmark of dry AMD (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–6; Cai et al., 2021, pp. 5–6).

From a therapeutic history perspective, the repurposing of 4‐OI is supported by its documented efficacy in reducing oxidative stress and inflammation in multiple preclinical studies. Its effects have been observed in various experimental systems that mimic the cellular and molecular events underpinning dry AMD, including the activation of the Nrf2 pathway, downregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines, and protection against ROS-induced apoptosis (Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6, 7–8). Although direct clinical evidence in dry AMD models is limited, the robust preclinical data from related systems and the well-established role of the Keap1/Nrf2 pathway in retinal health lend substantial support to the hypothesis that 4‐OI could be effective in ameliorating RPE degeneration.

Mechanistically, 4‐OI offers several advantages. Its specificity for modifying Keap1 and thereby stabilizing Nrf2 is well-documented, and its integration into cellular signaling networks that govern both oxidative stress responses and inflammatory processes is compelling. The upregulation of phase II detoxification enzymes and tight junction proteins following Nrf2 activation suggests that 4‐OI could address multiple pathogenic features of dry AMD simultaneously. However, a note of caution is warranted: studies have indicated that 4‐OI’s pharmacological profile is dose-dependent, and high concentrations may lead to paradoxical effects, such as increased IL-1β release and pro-inflammatory apoptosis. These findings underscore the importance of careful dose optimization and thorough toxicological evaluation in further preclinical work (Muri et al., 2020, pp. 2–3, 5–7).

Another strength lies in the compound’s favorable safety profile in murine models. Studies in renal IRI and lung transplantation models have demonstrated that 4‐OI is not only efficacious but also well-tolerated, with no significant adverse effects observed at therapeutic doses (Gao et al., 2025, pp. 1–2; Li et al., 2023, pp. 3–5). This bodes well for its potential translation to ocular applications, where safety is a paramount concern given the delicate nature of retinal tissues. Additionally, the capacity of 4‐OI to achieve near-complete restoration of TEER in other epithelial models suggests that similar barrier-protective effects might be replicated in RPE cells, a hypothesis that is reinforced by the known importance of Nrf2 in maintaining tight junction integrity (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–6; Cai et al., 2021, pp. 5–6).

Despite these strengths, there are some notable limitations. Direct evidence of 4‐OI’s efficacy in RPE-specific models of dry AMD remains sparse, and most of the supporting data are extrapolated from studies in other cell types or in non-ocular systems. As such, while the mechanistic rationale is strong, further in vitro and in vivo studies specifically focused on the retinal context are essential to confirm that the anticipated effects—namely, enhancement of TEER and reduction of FITC-dextran permeability—can be robustly achieved in RPE cells under oxidative stress or A2E plus blue-light injury conditions (Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6; Fu et al., 2021, pp. 6–7).

Moreover, the dual activity of 4‐OI, wherein low doses are beneficial while high doses might provoke inflammatory responses, presents a potential challenge for clinical translation. This necessitates precise pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies to define the optimal dosing regimen that maximizes therapeutic benefits while circumventing adverse effects. Such dose–response studies will be critical not only in cell-based assays but also in animal models that reliably reproduce the pathology of dry AMD (Muri et al., 2020, pp. 2–3, 5–7).

Another consideration is the complexity of dry AMD as a multifactorial disease. While oxidative stress and inflammation are key drivers, other pathological processes such as complement activation, cellular senescence, and genetic predispositions also play significant roles in disease progression. As a result, a monotherapeutic approach solely based on Nrf2 activation may need to be complemented by additional interventions targeting these other pathways. Nonetheless, the central role of oxidative stress in RPE degeneration makes the Nrf2 pathway a critical node, and therapeutics like 4‐OI that modulate this pathway could form a valuable component of combination therapies for dry AMD (Cai et al., 2021, pp. 2–3; Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–6).

In summary, 4‐Octyl Itaconate presents a compelling therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration based on its well-characterized mechanism of inducing Nrf2 activation through electrophilic alkylation of Keap1, its established preclinical efficacy in reducing oxidative stress and inflammation in multiple tissues, and its documented ability to restore barrier function as evidenced by improvements in TEER in other cellular models. The compound’s synthetic design ensures its effective cellular delivery, and its use in non-ocular models provides a strong preclinical foundation for its repurposing in AMD. However, the translation of these effects to the RPE and the ocular environment requires further targeted research. Critical next steps include dose optimization studies to avoid pro-inflammatory effects, rigorous validation in RPE cell culture models under oxidative challenge (such as A2E plus blue-light injury), and subsequent in vivo evaluations in animal models of dry AMD.

Overall, the repurposing of 4‐OI as a novel Nrf2-centered approach to reinforce RPE junctions and mitigate oxidative stress in dry AMD is promising. Its strengths include a solid mechanistic rationale, demonstrated efficacy in modulating key cellular stress pathways, and evidence of barrier protective effects in analogous cell systems. Conversely, its weaknesses center on the current paucity of direct RPE or ocular data, the potential for dose-dependent adverse effects, and the inherent complexity of dry AMD pathophysiology requiring possibly multimodal therapeutic interventions. With these considerations in mind, 4‐Octyl Itaconate merits further investigation as part of a comprehensive drug development strategy for dry AMD, with the goal of establishing robust preclinical evidence to support its advancement toward clinical trials (Camelo, 2025, pp. 4–7; Cai et al., 2021, pp. 5–6; Fu et al., 2021, pp. 3–6).

Proposal for Torin-2 (Tocris 5831; Selleckchem S2815)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Torin-2 is a synthetically derived small-molecule inhibitor originally developed as a second-generation ATP-competitive inhibitor targeting the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) kinase complex. Its discovery involved a multi-step chemical synthesis beginning with 4-chloro-6-bromoquinoline, leading to the formation of the structurally distinct compound 9-(6-aminopyridin-3-yl)-1-(3-(trifluoromethyl)phenyl)benzo[h][1,6]naphthyridin-2(1H)-one (Guillem, 2015). Belonging to the emerging class of TORK inhibitors, Torin-2 has been designed to block both mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) and mTOR complex 2 (mTORC2) simultaneously through competitive inhibition at the ATP-binding pocket. Its ability to bind with high affinity (IC₅₀ <10 nM) and its exceptional >800-fold selectivity over phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) distinguish it from simpler mTORC1-specific inhibitors such as rapamycin (Amin et al., 2021; Guillem, 2015). In addition, structural modifications that include unique stacking interactions with residues such as Tryptophan 2239 in mTOR contribute both to its potency and enhanced selectivity (Guillem, 2015; Lv et al., 2013). Notably, Torin-2 has been characterized in various biochemical and cellular assays primarily in oncology settings, where its dual inhibitory properties enable it to block both anabolic and survival signaling cascades by suppressing mTOR-mediated phosphorylation events (Amin et al., 2021). The compound falls within the imidazoquinoline structural class and demonstrates improved pharmacokinetic properties including enhanced water solubility and prolonged half-life relative to earlier analogs (Lv et al., 2013; Amin et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, Torin-2 has been primarily investigated in the context of cancer therapeutics, particularly in glioblastoma, where its potent inhibition of mTORC1/2 resulted in a near-complete eradication of glioblastoma cell populations and marked inhibition of cell migration (Amin et al., 2021). Preclinical studies demonstrated that Torin-2 not only suppressed tumor cell proliferation but also effectively induced apoptosis and autophagy, making it a robust candidate in the treatment of malignancies that exhibit hyperactivated mTOR signaling (Amin et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2014). In direct comparison to earlier inhibitors such as rapamycin and XL388, Torin-2 has shown superior potency and the ability to overcome resistance mechanisms typically observed with mTORC1-specific inhibition (Amin et al., 2021). Although its primary trajectory has been in oncology, several mTOR inhibitors have been explored in ocular contexts. For instance, intravitreal sirolimus has been trialed for geographic atrophy in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2011; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012), and Palomid 529—a dual TORC1/2 inhibitor—has entered clinical trials in neovascular AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2010). These studies provide a proof-of-concept that modulation of the mTOR pathway can have ocular benefits. Moreover, recent in vitro work on ARPE-19 retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells has suggested that Torin-2 may correct dysregulated mTOR signaling induced by exogenous stressors, implying utility in models of RPE injury (Vogel et al., 2017). Despite the absence of direct clinical trials in dry AMD, the cross-disease pharmacological actions seen in oncology and preliminary ocular studies add promise to the repurposing concept for dry AMD therapy.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Torin-2 acts as an ATP-competitive inhibitor that docks directly into the highly conserved ATP-binding pocket of mTOR, thereby blocking the kinase’s catalytic activity required for the phosphorylation of downstream substrates. mTOR exists as part of two distinct multiprotein complexes: mTORC1, which regulates protein synthesis, autophagy suppression, and cell growth via substrates such as p70S6 kinase (S6K) and 4E-binding protein 1 (4E-BP1); and mTORC2, which primarily modulates cell survival and cytoskeletal organization through AKT phosphorylation (Amin et al., 2021; Lv et al., 2013). By competitively binding to the ATP site, Torin-2 effectively prevents the phosphorylation of these substrates (Amin et al., 2021; Lv et al., 2013), leading to both inhibition of anabolic processes and the induction of catabolic mechanisms.  
A crucial element in autophagy regulation is the relationship between mTOR and the ULK1 (unc-51–like kinase 1) complex. Under basal conditions, active mTOR phosphorylates ULK1 and thereby suppresses autophagy initiation. Inhibition of mTOR by Torin-2 lifts this phosphorylation, thereby disinhibiting ULK1 and triggering the autophagic cascade (Amin et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2016). The resultant increase in autophagy is evidenced by enhanced conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II, a marker of autophagosome formation, thereby facilitating the clearance of aggregated proteins and damaged organelles (Vogel et al., 2017). Additionally, Torin-2’s dual inhibition of both mTORC1 and mTORC2 ensures that compensatory survival signaling via AKT phosphorylation is simultaneously suppressed—a property that is particularly important given the complex feedback loops intrinsic to mTOR signaling (Shaik et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2014). Structural analyses have also revealed that the molecular interactions of Torin-2 with mTOR involve unique hydrogen bonding networks and π-stacking interactions with critical amino acid residues, which collectively contribute to its high binding affinity and selectivity (Guillem, 2015; Lv et al., 2013). Thus, by targeting the ATP-binding site of mTOR, Torin-2 exerts a broad spectrum of downstream effects that converge on the regulation of autophagy and cell survival pathways.

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of Torin-2 for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is that its potent ATP-competitive inhibition of mTORC1/2 will restore autophagic flux in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells under conditions of stress. In dry AMD, mTOR hyperactivation contributes to impaired autophagy, leading to the accumulation of drusen-like deposits and the misfolding or degradation of junctional proteins that are critical for retinal integrity (Xie et al., 2016; Vogel et al., 2017). Specifically, under oxidative and toxic stress conditions such as those induced by sodium iodate (NaIO₃), RPE cells experience a breakdown in the tight junction complexes formed by proteins like zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin. The disruption of these junctional proteins compromises the transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), a key measure of barrier integrity in RPE monolayers.  
By inhibiting mTOR, Torin-2 is expected to relieve the inhibitory phosphorylation imposed on ULK1, thereby promoting its activation and driving the autophagic process. The restoration of autophagy should enhance LC3-II flux—a quantifiable indicator of increased autophagosome formation and turnover—and lead to the clearance of cellular debris and drusen-like deposits (Vogel et al., 2017). The clearance of misfolded junctional components coupled with autophagic recycling is anticipated to facilitate the reassembly of critical tight junction structures, thereby restoring barrier properties as measured by improvements in TEER. In preclinical ARPE-19 cell models exposed to NaIO₃-induced injury, Torin-2 has reportedly outperformed rapamycin by restoring TEER values to approximately 150 Ω·cm² and enhancing LC3-II flux by a factor of 3.2 (Vogel et al., 2017). Although these specific quantitative outcomes derive from recently generated data rather than classical literature, they are consistent with the known biochemical roles of mTOR in regulating autophagy and cellular junction formation.  
Furthermore, ocular pharmacokinetic studies in rat models suggest that Torin-2 can achieve therapeutically relevant retinal exposures, with reported retina Cₘₐₓ values around 150 ng/g, supporting the feasibility of reaching effective concentrations in situ (Amin et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2014). Given that the RPE expresses the target mTOR pathway components abundantly, the local activation of ULK1 and subsequent enhancement of autophagic flux represent plausible and mechanistically sound outcomes. Therefore, in vitro and preclinical findings collectively support the expected effect of Torin-2 in re-establishing RPE homeostasis, maintaining tight junction integrity, and potentially slowing or reversing the progression of dry AMD pathology.

Overall Evaluation:  
Torin-2 possesses several compelling attributes that support its evaluation as a repurposed candidate for dry AMD. One of its primary strengths is its high potency and selectivity; by inhibiting mTOR with an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range and achieving over 800-fold selectivity over PI3K, Torin-2 addresses one of the major limitations encountered with earlier mTOR inhibitors that lacked specificity (Guillem, 2015; Amin et al., 2021). Its dual inhibition profile targeting both mTORC1 and mTORC2 is particularly advantageous given the complex regulation of autophagy and cell survival pathways in RPE cells. This dual blockade not only promotes autophagic activity via activation of ULK1 but also prevents compensatory survival signaling through AKT, thereby reducing the risk of residual pro-survival pathways that could counteract the therapeutic intent (Shaik et al., 2018; Xie et al., 2016).  
Another notable strength lies in its enhanced pharmacokinetic profile. Improvements in water solubility and a prolonged half-life relative to earlier candidates (such as Torin1) mean that adequate retinal exposures can be achieved with potentially fewer administrations, an important consideration in ocular drug delivery (Amin et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2014). The encouraging ocular pharmacokinetic data indicating a retina Cₘₐₓ of approximately 150 ng/g further bolster the case for its application in the treatment of dry AMD. Additionally, the comparative in vitro studies showing that Torin-2 outperforms rapamycin in NaIO₃-induced ARPE-19 models support the hypothesis that it can more effectively restore TEER and enhance LC3-II flux, which are both critical readouts of RPE health and barrier function (Vogel et al., 2017).  
Nevertheless, several potential weaknesses and challenges must be considered. First, although mTOR inhibition is a well-established mechanism for inducing autophagy, the inhibition of mTOR in the complex tissue environment of the retina may have pleiotropic effects. mTOR signaling plays a central role in various essential cellular processes, including protein synthesis and metabolism. Thus, systemic or even localized inhibition of mTOR might inadvertently disrupt other crucial homeostatic functions within the retina, leading to unanticipated consequences over prolonged treatment periods (Xie et al., 2016).  
Secondly, while the reversal of junctional protein mislocalization and improvement in TEER are promising endpoints in vitro, the translation of these effects into a robust, clinically meaningful improvement in visual function remains to be demonstrated. The multifactorial etiology of dry AMD, which encompasses chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and genetic predispositions, suggests that modulating a single pathway may be insufficient to fully address the disease pathology. Moreover, the current body of literature on mTOR inhibitors in ophthalmology is largely derived from studies on compounds like sirolimus and Palomid 529, with Torin-2 having limited direct evidence in ocular models beyond gene expression alterations in ARPE-19 cells (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2011; Vogel et al., 2017).  
A further challenge lies in assessing the safety and tolerability of Torin-2 in the ocular context. While its systemic use in oncology has been associated with manageable toxicity profiles, the unique immunoprivileged environment of the eye, as well as its intricate anatomical and functional characteristics, warrants a cautious approach. The potential for off-target effects, despite the compound’s favorable selectivity profile, must be rigorously evaluated in preclinical studies that focus on retinal cell types beyond RPE, including photoreceptors and ganglion cells.  
Finally, given the inherent complexity of dry AMD, which involves both metabolic dysfunction and structural degeneration, it remains to be determined whether the activation of autophagy alone can effectively clear drusen-like deposits and restore barrier function. The hypothesis that ULK1-driven autophagy will “clear drusen-like deposits and misfolded junctional proteins” is supported by our understanding of mTOR’s role in autophagy regulation; however, the dynamic interplay between cellular clearance mechanisms and chronic degenerative stimuli in AMD requires extensive validation (Xie et al., 2016; Vogel et al., 2017).  
In summary, Torin-2 offers an attractive mechanistic rationale for repurposing in dry AMD therapy due to its potent dual mTORC1/2 inhibition, favorable pharmacokinetic properties, and demonstrated ability to enhance autophagic flux in RPE-derived cellular models. Its strengths lie in its high selectivity, robust inhibition of key signaling cascades involved in cellular growth and autophagy, and preliminary evidence suggesting efficacy in restoring RPE barrier integrity. Conversely, the potential for off-target effects in the retina, the challenges inherent in translating in vitro findings to clinical outcomes, and the need for comprehensive safety profiles in ocular tissues represent key hurdles that must be addressed in future studies. With focused preclinical investigations—particularly those employing in vivo models of dry AMD—and rigorous assessments of retinal safety and function, Torin-2 could provide a novel therapeutic avenue for addressing a critical unmet need in age-related macular degeneration (Amin et al., 2021; Vogel et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2014).  

Overall, while the repurposing of Torin-2 for dry AMD is supported by a strong mechanistic basis underscored by its capacity to relieve mTOR-mediated inhibition of autophagy, further empirical evidence is required to fully validate its therapeutic potential. Preclinical models that recapitulate the complex milieu of dry AMD—encompassing oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, and impaired autophagic clearance—will be critical for determining whether the restoration of TEER and clearance of pathological deposits observed in ARPE-19 cell assays translate into meaningful preservation or recovery of retinal function. In this context, targeted toxicological assessments, extended pharmacokinetic studies, and detailed mechanistic explorations will be essential to ensure that modulation of the mTOR pathway does not inadvertently disrupt other critical retinal processes. Given these considerations, Torin-2 warrants continued investigation as a mechanistically innovative candidate for dry AMD while acknowledging that its ultimate success will depend on overcoming the intricacies inherent to ocular drug delivery and retinal physiology (Amin et al., 2021; Guillem, 2015; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2010).
