Proposal for BIRB 796 (Doramapimod; Selleck S1076)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
BIRB 796 (doramapimod) is a small-molecule p38 MAP kinase inhibitor discovered at Boehringer Ingelheim as part of a diaryl urea/pyrazolyl-urea medicinal chemistry effort to exploit an inactive, DFG-out conformation of p38 and thereby achieve high potency and kinase-family selectivity via an allosteric binding site adjacent to the ATP pocket (type II binding) (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Bagley et al., 2010; Xing, 2016; Coulthard et al., 2009). In contrast to classical ATP-site inhibitors (e.g., pyridinyl-imidazoles such as SB203580) that anchor in the hinge region and remain in the DFG-in active conformation, BIRB 796 engages a selectivity pocket opened by flipping the Asp-Phe-Gly (DFG) motif to a DFG-out state; this binding mode is incompatible with ATP binding and additionally disrupts the interaction between p38α and its upstream activators MKK3/MKK6 (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Bagley et al., 2010). Structural features include deep insertion of a t-butyl group into the hydrophobic “Phe-pocket” created by the DFG-out rearrangement, naphthyl contacts, favorable packing of a tolyl group in a Glu71-containing hydrophobic pocket, a morpholino that H-bonds with Met109, and a diaryl urea NH that forms an H-bond with Glu71 analogous to the adenine N1 interaction in ATP binding (Bagley et al., 2010). Kinetically, BIRB 796 is a prototypical slow-binding, slow-dissociating p38 inhibitor: association is ~500-fold slower and dissociation ~10^6-fold slower than the ATP-site pyridinyl-imidazole SK&F 86002, consistent with a major conformational rearrangement upon binding and prolonged target residence time (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012). Biophysically, reported potency is sub-nanomolar in binding assays (Kd ~0.1–<0.8 nM) with functional enzymatic or cellular IC50 values on the order of tens of nanomolar (e.g., ~63 nM), and the compound inhibits all p38 isoforms to varying degrees (pan-p38), with context-dependent reports of minimal or dual activity on JNK2 (Xing, 2016; Bagley et al., 2010; Yong et al., 2009; Coulthard et al., 2009). A microwave-assisted route to BIRB 796 was reported (aminopyrazole formation from pivaloylacetonitrile and p-tolylhydrazine; carbamate and aminonaphthol intermediates; DMSO coupling at 100°C), enabling improved yields for preclinical supply and mechanistic studies (Bagley et al., 2010).

As a chemotype, diaryl/urea-type type II kinase inhibitors that exploit DFG-out conformations were developed to expand selectivity beyond hinge-binding ATP mimetics, often achieving slow off-rates and high apparent affinity; within the p38 field, BIRB 796 became the best-characterized example of this allosteric/selectivity-pocket strategy and served as a clinical tool compound for inflammatory indications (Xing, 2016; Coulthard et al., 2009).

Therapeutic History  
BIRB 796 advanced through Phase I and Phase II programs and was reported as having reached Phase II/III development for autoimmune and inflammatory diseases including rheumatoid arthritis (RA), Crohn’s disease (CD), and psoriasis; a human endotoxemia model was used to demonstrate pharmacodynamic target engagement (suppression of TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-8, and effects on coagulation/fibrinolysis/endothelial activation) (Yong et al., 2009; Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Coulthard et al., 2009; Xing, 2016). Oral dosing regimens included 5–30 mg twice daily (RA) and 10–60 mg twice daily (CD); in endotoxemia, single doses up to 600 mg were tested and showed robust biomarker modulation (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Yong et al., 2009). Despite clear pharmacodynamic effects, randomized trials failed to demonstrate durable clinical efficacy in Crohn’s disease and psoriasis, and RA efficacy was not substantiated; development was discontinued after Phase II, with repeated administration associated with elevated liver transaminases (class-typical hepatotoxicity) (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012). Mechanistic work implicated a reactive naphthalene-epoxide metabolite (glutathione-conjugated) in the ALT elevations observed in CD patients, supporting on-drug hepatotoxicity as a liability for the chemotype (Machado et al., 2021). More broadly, many clinical p38 inhibitor programs (including BIRB 796) showed a stereotyped pattern of early biomarker suppression (e.g., CRP, soluble TNF receptor) that returned to near baseline by week 12, coincident with a lack of sustained clinical benefit, pointing to network compensation under chronic p38 blockade (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Xing, 2016). These outcomes, together with dose-limiting toxicities seen across the class, drove a field-wide shift toward alternative strategies (substrate-selective or docking-site inhibitors) rather than pan-p38 catalytic inhibition (Burton et al., 2021).

In preclinical and translational settings, BIRB 796 has been widely used as a pharmacological probe: it reduces LPS-induced TNF-α and other cytokines in vitro and in vivo; in a human endotoxemia model a 600 mg dose suppressed coagulation/fibrinolysis and endothelial activation; in tumor-associated contexts it inhibited IL-6 secretion and reduced tumor cell proliferation (Yong et al., 2009). In macrophage-centric COPD studies, BIRB-class inhibitors sometimes failed to suppress IL-8, underscoring cell-type-specific differences in p38 control of cytokine outputs; however, at very low concentrations (1 nM) BIRB-0796 exhibited synergistic cytokine suppression when combined with corticosteroids, reflecting complementary mechanisms (steroids do not block p38-HSP27 phosphorylation) (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012). In epithelial barrier biology, doramapimod protected the Sertoli cell tight-junction barrier against cadmium-induced injury, preserving localization of ZO-1, claudin-11, occludin, and adherens junction components and rescuing transepithelial electrical resistance (TER), while selectively blocking p38 phosphorylation (without suppressing JNK, CREB, or Akt activation) (Wang et al., 2023).

No registered clinical trials of p38 MAPK inhibitors (including doramapimod) for age-related macular degeneration (AMD) are listed on ClinicalTrials.gov under the queried terms, indicating no formal AMD program has been conducted in this class to date (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Mechanistically, p38 signaling has been implicated in retinal vascular and AMD-relevant processes (e.g., VEGF induction, matrix remodeling via MMP-2/MMP-14 and basigin, inflammasome activation, endothelial dysfunction and barrier leakage), which supports biological plausibility but not direct clinical translation for AMD (Burton et al., 2021). There is no RPE- or AMD-specific preclinical study of doramapimod in the provided materials, and none of the cited clinical programs tested dry AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Burton et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
p38 MAPKs (α/β/γ/δ) are stress-activated serine/threonine kinases that integrate inflammatory cues and drive transcriptional and post-transcriptional control of cytokines including TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-8; downstream effectors include MK2/MK3 (MAPKAPK2/3), MSK1/2, and HSP27, which regulate mRNA stability, translation, and cytoskeletal dynamics (Machado et al., 2021; Coulthard et al., 2009; Burton et al., 2021). Canonical activation proceeds via MKK3 and MKK6 phosphorylation of the Thr-Gly-Tyr activation loop, but atypical, TAB1-dependent activation on endosomes also occurs in response to GPCR/cytokine stimuli, fueling vascular inflammation and barrier dysfunction; p38 pathway activity is further modulated by MAPK phosphatases (DUSPs) feeding back on p38 dephosphorylation (Burton et al., 2021).

BIRB 796 binds in a selectivity pocket adjacent to the ATP site and induces a DFG-out conformation that is catalytically incompetent, sterically and conformationally precluding ATP binding and preventing interaction with upstream kinases (MKK3/MKK6) (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Bagley et al., 2010). Structural contacts include insertion of a tert-butyl group into the DFG-derived Phe-pocket, hydrophobic contacts by a naphthyl group, a tolyl group accommodated in a Glu71-containing hydrophobic cavity, and a morpholino ring that H-bonds to Met109; importantly, a diaryl urea NH forms a hydrogen bond with Glu71 that mimics the adenine N1 interaction in ATP, highlighting how selectivity-pocket binders can spare classical hinge contacts yet achieve high affinity (Bagley et al., 2010). The kinetic signature of BIRB 796—extremely slow dissociation and slow association—reflects the energetic barrier to reorganize the DFG motif and surrounding activation loop, and is thought to confer prolonged target occupancy in cells (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012). As a result, BIRB 796 has sub-nanomolar binding affinity to non-activated p38α (Kd ~0.1–<0.8 nM) with functional inhibitory potency in the low- to mid-nanomolar range in biochemical/cellular assays (Xing, 2016; Bagley et al., 2010).

Isoform and pathway coverage is broad: multiple sources report inhibition of all p38 isoforms (α/β/γ/δ), a property linked to the allosteric binding mode, which avoids the Met109-dependent hinge interaction exploited by ATP-site inhibitors that often lack activity on γ/δ (Coulthard et al., 2009; Xing, 2016). Some profiling described BIRB 796 as selective against JNK2, whereas other reports noted dual p38/JNK activity—differences likely arise from assay format, activation state, and concentration ranges, but the possibility of JNK2 inhibition exists and complicates mechanistic attribution in certain systems (Yong et al., 2009; Bagley et al., 2010). Functionally, BIRB 796 suppresses LPS-induced TNF-α and lowers IL-6 and IL-8 in human endotoxemia, reduces p38 readouts such as phosphorylated HSP27 (a sensitive pharmacodynamic biomarker), and decreases phosphorylation of MK2, consistent with dampened pro-inflammatory transcription and mRNA stabilization (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Yong et al., 2009; Burton et al., 2021). In immortalized Werner syndrome fibroblasts, BIRB 796 prevents p38 activation, reduces pp38 and pHSP27, and thereby modifies senescence-associated phenotypes, reinforcing its activity on the p38→MK2/HSP27 axis in stressed/aged cells (Bagley et al., 2010). In primary Sertoli cells exposed to cadmium, doramapimod specifically blocked p38 phosphorylation, preserved junctional protein localization (e.g., ZO-1, occludin, claudin-11, JAM-A), and maintained barrier function (TER), while not suppressing parallel stress signals (pJNK, p-c-Jun, p-CREB, p-Akt), indicating target-pathway selectivity in vitro (Wang et al., 2023).

Clinical pharmacology confirms human anti-inflammatory effects: a 600 mg dose of BIRB-796BS in endotoxemia suppressed LPS-induced coagulation, fibrinolysis, and endothelial activation (Yong et al., 2009). However, in chronic inflammatory diseases, repeated dosing produced only transient biomarker suppression and limited clinical benefits; repeated administration caused liver-enzyme elevations, and mechanistic toxicology implicated a reactive naphthalene-epoxide metabolite (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Machado et al., 2021). These observations align with broader p38 inhibitor experience: pan-p38 blockade can interrupt beneficial anti-inflammatory signaling (e.g., MSK1/2-mediated) and distort feedback circuits, while disinhibiting upstream kinases (e.g., TAK1, MLK2/3) and activating JNK or NF-κB crosstalk, conferring dose-limiting toxicities and short-lived efficacy (Coulthard et al., 2009).

Expected Effect  
Assay hypothesis: In senescent retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), pharmacologic p38α/β inhibition with BIRB 796 will suppress SASP-like cytokines (particularly IL-6 and IL-8), reducing paracrine/autocrine downregulation of junctional proteins and preserving tight junction belts (e.g., ZO-1) and transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER).

Mechanistic rationale: p38 controls transcriptional and post-transcriptional programs that elevate IL-6 and IL-8 across multiple inflamed tissues and cell types; BIRB 796 lowers IL-6/IL-8 in human endotoxemia and tumor-cell paracrine models, and at low nanomolar concentrations can synergize with corticosteroids to suppress cytokines in macrophage systems, consistent with broad suppression of p38-driven inflammatory outputs (Yong et al., 2009; Albrecht & Laufer, 2012). Downstream, p38→MK2 phosphorylates HSP27 and RNA-binding proteins (e.g., tristetraprolin/TTP), which increases mRNA stability and translation of cytokine transcripts; BIRB 796 reduces pp38 and pHSP27 in senescence models, matching the predicted SASP attenuation mechanism (Burton et al., 2021; Bagley et al., 2010). In epithelial barrier contexts, doramapimod rescued tight-junction integrity and TER in primary Sertoli monolayers under toxic stress while maintaining junctional protein localization, providing a functional precedent that p38 inhibition can preserve epithelial-like barrier structure and function via junctional/cytoskeletal stabilization (Wang et al., 2023).

RPE disease-context rationale: Although no RPE-specific BIRB 796 data are provided here, p38 signaling is implicated in AMD-relevant processes (e.g., VEGF induction and angiogenesis, MMP-driven matrix remodeling, inflammasome activation, vascular endothelial dysfunction and barrier leakage), making p38 a plausible node in retinal inflammation and barrier pathology (Burton et al., 2021). Given that p38 activity drives IL-6/IL-8 production broadly, and that these cytokines can downregulate junctional proteins and disrupt epithelial barriers in many systems, it is reasonable to expect that BIRB 796 will lower MK2/HSP27 pathway activity, reduce IL-6/IL-8 secretion from senescent RPE, and preserve ZO-1 belts and TEER if p38-dependent SASP is operative in this cell type (Coulthard et al., 2009; Xing, 2016; Burton et al., 2021). Atypical (TAB1-mediated) p38 activation has been linked to endothelial barrier disruption; while not demonstrated in RPE here, such noncanonical activation could also contribute to epithelial stress responses and might be sensitive to allosteric type II inhibition (Burton et al., 2021).

Assay execution considerations: To test the hypothesis rigorously in senescent RPE, readouts should include (1) p38 pathway activity markers (pp38, pMK2, pHSP27), (2) secreted SASP cytokines (IL-6, IL-8), and (3) barrier metrics (continuous ZO-1 belts by immunofluorescence; TER dynamics over time), with BIRB 796 concentration–response spanning low nanomolar to low micromolar given reported cellular potencies and the 10 µM concentration that preserved Sertoli barrier function (Wang et al., 2023; Xing, 2016; Bagley et al., 2010). Given steroid independence of p38 signaling (p-HSP27 is not reduced by steroids), testing BIRB 796 alone and in combination with a glucocorticoid could probe pharmacologic additivity and compensatory pathways in RPE SASP (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012). Because IL-8 may be variably p38-dependent across cell types, the assay should be powered to detect partial suppression and explore time-dependent compensation (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012). Finally, inclusion of controls that assess atypical activation (e.g., TAB1–p38 engagement) and post-transcriptional endpoints (TTP phosphorylation status) could sharpen mechanistic attribution (Burton et al., 2021).

Translational considerations: Systemic doramapimod exposure is constrained by hepatotoxicity and lack of durable efficacy in chronic inflammation, plausibly due to network adaptation; any clinical path in dry AMD would require local ocular delivery to minimize systemic exposure and to bypass compensatory systemic responses, a principle consistent with proposed niches for p38 inhibitors in localized/short-term settings (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Coulthard et al., 2009). At present, there are no registered AMD trials of p38 inhibitors, so translational validation must proceed from RPE/retinal preclinical models (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Mechanistic fit: p38 MAPK is a master regulator of inflammatory cytokines, including IL-6 and IL-8, with well-defined downstream effectors (MK2/MK3, HSP27) that also interface with cytoskeletal and junctional integrity; BIRB 796 potently and durably engages this pathway, reduces p38 phosphorylation readouts, and suppresses IL-6/IL-8 in human endotoxemia and other systems (Machado et al., 2021; Coulthard et al., 2009; Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Yong et al., 2009). The proposed RPE SASP-barrier mechanism is therefore biochemically coherent (Burton et al., 2021).  
- High potency and residence time: sub-nanomolar affinity, nanomolar functional inhibition, and extremely slow off-rate support strong target engagement at low free concentrations, which may be advantageous for intraocular dosing strategies designed to minimize systemic exposure (Xing, 2016; Albrecht & Laufer, 2012).  
- Allosteric type II mode and pan-p38 coverage: by stabilizing DFG-out, BIRB 796 inhibits α/β/γ/δ isoforms, potentially covering non-α p38 activity that could contribute to epithelial senescence or retinal inflammation; the allosteric site is exploited with favorable structural interactions and a defined pharmacophore (Coulthard et al., 2009; Bagley et al., 2010; Xing, 2016).  
- Barrier-protection precedent in epithelia: doramapimod preserved ZO-1/occludin/claudin-11 localization and TER in primary Sertoli monolayers under toxic injury while selectively blocking p38 phosphorylation, an effect directionally aligned with the goal of preserving RPE tight junctions and barrier function (Wang et al., 2023).  
- PD biomarkers to guide development: pHSP27 and pMK2 provide sensitive pathway engagement readouts, facilitating translational bridging from in vitro RPE to in vivo ocular models and potentially to human aqueous/vitreous sampling (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Burton et al., 2021).  
- Combination potential: BIRB-class inhibitors can synergize with corticosteroids at very low concentrations in cytokine suppression assays, reflecting complementary mechanisms of action and offering a combination path to mitigate compensation (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012).

Weaknesses and risks  
- Lack of RPE-specific data: No direct evidence in the provided materials demonstrates doramapimod effects on senescent RPE SASP, IL-6/IL-8, ZO-1 belts, or TEER; AMD- or RPE-specific proof of concept remains to be generated (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Burton et al., 2021).  
- Clinical class history of transient efficacy: Across chronic inflammatory indications, p38 inhibitors showed early biomarker suppression followed by reversion toward baseline and lack of durable benefit by ~12 weeks, likely reflecting pathway compensation and complex feedback/crosstalk that may also occur in chronic retinal disease (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Xing, 2016).  
- Hepatotoxicity and metabolic liability: Repeated systemic dosing raised liver enzymes, and mechanistic toxicology implicated a reactive naphthalene-epoxide metabolite for BIRB 796 specifically; while intraocular delivery could mitigate systemic exposure, any repurposing must address ocular-specific safety and formulation (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Machado et al., 2021).  
- Potential dual JNK2 activity: Reports vary on BIRB 796 selectivity; dual p38/JNK2 inhibition has been described, complicating mechanistic interpretation and potentially adding pathway liabilities in some cellular contexts (Bagley et al., 2010; Yong et al., 2009).  
- Isoform- and context-specific cytokine control: In alveolar macrophages and COPD models, IL-8 can be relatively resistant to p38 inhibition, cautioning against assuming uniform suppression of IL-8 in senescent RPE; parallel drivers (e.g., NF-κB) may require combination strategies (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012).  
- Strategic alternatives may be preferable: Substrate-selective p38 pathway interventions (e.g., ED-site inhibitor UM101) that spare beneficial MSK1 signaling, or inhibitors that block atypical TAB1-mediated activation, have shown preclinical advantages and may reduce compensation/toxicity risks compared with pan-p38 catalytic inhibition (Burton et al., 2021).

Decision-oriented assessment for dry AMD  
- Biological plausibility: Strong. p38 controls IL-6/IL-8 and MK2/HSP27 signaling that plausibly drive SASP and barrier dysfunction; doramapimod has repeatedly demonstrated suppression of these axes and preserved epithelial-like barrier function in vitro (Machado et al., 2021; Coulthard et al., 2009; Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Wang et al., 2023).  
- Translational tractability: Conditional. Systemic use is precluded by hepatotoxicity and lack of durable efficacy; however, local ocular delivery could deliver high intraocular drug levels while limiting systemic exposure, and the slow off-rate may support infrequent dosing, pending ocular PK/toxicity profiling (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Coulthard et al., 2009).  
- Evidence gaps: Critical. No RPE-focused or AMD-model data exist here; there are no registered AMD clinical trials for p38 inhibitors; demonstration in senescent RPE models is essential before advancing (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Recommended next steps  
- In vitro RPE senescence studies: Evaluate BIRB 796 concentration–response (1 nM–10 µM) on pp38/pMK2/pHSP27, IL-6/IL-8 secretion, ZO-1/occludin belt continuity, and TEER in primary human RPE and iPSC-RPE rendered senescent (e.g., replicative or stress-induced senescence) (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Burton et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023).  
- Mechanistic dissection: Assess TTP phosphorylation and mRNA decay of IL-6/IL-8; interrogate atypical TAB1-dependent activation signatures; compare to a substrate-selective p38 modulator where possible to benchmark compensation (Burton et al., 2021).  
- Combination testing: Explore additivity with a glucocorticoid and/or NF-κB modulation to overcome potential IL-8 resistance in RPE; measure durability after washout to probe rebound signaling (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012).  
- Ocular safety and delivery: Conduct ex vivo/in vivo ocular tolerability (ERGs, histology) and intraocular PK in relevant species; leverage the slow target off-rate to test low-dose intravitreal delivery designed to minimize systemic exposure (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Coulthard et al., 2009).  
- Prioritize de-risking strategies: If doramapimod exhibits ocular or systemic liabilities, consider pathway-refined alternatives (e.g., MK2 inhibitors; ED-site p38α inhibitors sparing MSK1; TAB1-site blockers) that may retain anti-SASP efficacy with reduced toxicity and compensation (Burton et al., 2021; Coulthard et al., 2009).

Conclusion  
On mechanistic grounds, BIRB 796 is well-suited to test the SASP-barrier hypothesis in senescent RPE: it is a potent, slow-off, allosteric type II inhibitor that suppresses IL-6/IL-8 outputs and p38→MK2/HSP27 signaling, and it preserves epithelial-like junctional integrity and TER in a primary Sertoli barrier model (Xing, 2016; Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; Yong et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2023). The absence of RPE- or AMD-specific evidence and the class’s clinical history of transient efficacy and hepatotoxicity are significant liabilities that limit immediate translational prospects; nonetheless, a local-delivery, RPE-focused preclinical program is justified to generate the missing data and to determine whether p38 suppression can stabilize RPE barrier function and SASP in dry AMD models (Albrecht & Laufer, 2012; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Coulthard et al., 2009). If positive, doramapimod could serve as a powerful chemical probe for isoform- and pathway-specific dissection in RPE senescence, while parallel exploration of pathway-refined or substrate-selective p38 modulators may offer a more sustainable clinical trajectory for chronic ocular disease (Burton et al., 2021; Coulthard et al., 2009).

Proposal for Spermidine (Sigma S3266)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Spermidine is a naturally occurring polyamine that has been extensively characterized over the last several decades as a key endogenous modulator of cellular homeostasis. Chemically, spermidine is classified as a small aliphatic polyamine with the structure H₂N(CH₂)₃NH(CH₂)₄NH₂, and it is biosynthesized from precursor amino acids such as ornithine and arginine via enzymatic steps involving decarboxylation reactions. Its discovery, dating back to early biochemical studies, has led to its isolation from various natural sources, including soybeans, aged cheese, mushrooms, and citrus fruits, and it is now commercially available as a highly purified compound (Sigma S3266). As a member of the polyamine family, spermidine is well known for its roles in modulating cell growth, autophagy, DNA stability, and the regulation of ion channels. These characteristics have fostered significant interest in its application as a dietary supplement with potential anti-aging properties, and more recently, its use has been explored in the context of ocular diseases due to its ability to induce autophagy and mitigate oxidative stress (Han et al., 2022; Hassani et al., 2022). Notably, the compound has exhibited a relatively favorable safety profile in dietary contexts, permitting rapid translation from bench research to potential clinical application, an attribute that is particularly attractive when repurposing drugs for complex diseases such as dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Han et al., 2022; Rivera et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History:  
Spermidine’s therapeutic history spans a broad array of biomedical investigations, including diverse preclinical studies in ocular as well as non‐ocular contexts. Initially, its anti‐aging and autophagy‐inducing properties were recognized through studies that linked its supplementation to longevity and enhanced cellular survival under stress conditions. This foundational work, while largely performed in non‐ocular systems, subsequently prompted researchers to explore its use in neuroprotection and the management of chronic conditions associated with oxidative damage. In ocular models, particularly, spermidine has been examined for its potential to mitigate oxidative stress in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), which are critical cell types for retinal function and vision. For instance, several in vitro and preclinical studies have demonstrated that spermidine can mitigate oxidative stress, suppress apoptotic pathways, and promote survival in retinal cells through the chelation of excess calcium and upregulation of antioxidant enzymes (Han et al., 2022). Preclinical animal models of glaucoma and optic nerve injury have provided evidence that spermidine can facilitate optic nerve regeneration and improve RGC survival, suggesting beneficial neuroprotective effects that may be relevant to retinal degenerative diseases (Han et al., 2022).

More specifically, in the context of retinal degenerative diseases such as age‐related macular degeneration, studies have shown that spermidine supplementation may protect RPE cells from oxidative insults by restoring calcium homeostasis and enhancing the expression of intrinsic antioxidant enzymes, thereby preserving cellular integrity (Han et al., 2022). However, these studies also highlight a critical caveat: the effects of spermidine are dose‐dependent, with excessive concentrations leading to oxidative stress and cytotoxicity that may exacerbate retinal damage (Han et al., 2022). In addition to its direct cellular effects, spermidine has been implicated in modulating immune responses in the ocular environment, including influencing the polarization of retinal microglia and T cell differentiation—a factor that could have implications not only for neurodegenerative processes but also for inflammatory disorders such as dry eye syndrome and autoimmune uveitis (Han et al., 2022). Despite promising preclinical data, direct evidence supporting spermidine’s therapeutic efficacy specifically in dry AMD remains limited, thus necessitating further targeted studies; some reviews have advocated for its potential given the broad spectrum of its bioactivities and safety as a dietary supplement, even as they call for careful dose optimization (Han et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
The hypothesis central to the current proposal is that spermidine mediates EP300 inhibition, thereby facilitating the deacetylation of autophagy-related proteins in RPE cells. EP300 (also known as p300) is a well-characterized histone acetyltransferase that plays a critical role in mediating acetylation on both histone and non-histone proteins, which in turn influences chromatin remodeling, gene expression, and multiple cellular processes including autophagy. Hyperacetylation of autophagy-related proteins by EP300 is thought to impair autophagic flux—a process essential for the removal of damaged organelles and misfolded proteins in RPE cells. By inhibiting EP300, spermidine is hypothesized to reverse this block, thereby facilitating the deacetylation of key autophagy mediators such as ATG proteins and LC3, which are essential for the formation and maturation of autophagosomes (Han et al., 2022; Luo et al., 2025).

At the molecular level, the inhibition of EP300 by spermidine may restore a balance between acetylation and deacetylation events within the RPE cell cytoplasm. This rebalancing is expected to promote autophagosome formation and enhance the clearance of cytotoxic substrates such as A2E (a component of lipofuscin) that accumulate in the RPE over time, particularly under conditions of chronic oxidative stress. Notably, the accumulation of lipofuscin and its toxic byproducts is a hallmark of dry AMD, contributing to RPE dysfunction and subsequent photoreceptor degeneration. In addition, proper autophagic clearance is essential for maintaining the integrity of intercellular junctions within the RPE layer. The junctional proteins ZO-1 and occludin are central to preserving the barrier function in the RPE, which is quantitatively measured using transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER). Spermidine-mediated EP300 inhibition is expected to reduce the acetylation-mediated impairment of autophagic proteins, thereby facilitating the removal of damaged junctional components and bolstering the structural integrity of the ZO-1/occludin belts (Han et al., 2022).

In vitro studies have documented that spermidine acts not only as an inducer of autophagy but also as a modulator of inflammatory and apoptotic pathways, particularly under oxidative challenge. Its function as a calcium chelator further contributes to its protective effects in RPE cells by reducing intracellular calcium overload—a condition that can precipitate apoptosis and cellular dysfunction. Moreover, previous work has suggested that autophagy induced by spermidine can also lead to improvements in mitochondrial function and energy metabolism, which are crucial for maintaining RPE cell viability during chronic oxidative stress common in dry AMD (Rivera et al., 2024; Han et al., 2022). Thus, the proposed mechanism of action—selective inhibition of EP300 to enhance autophagic clearance and preserve junctional integrity—integrates multiple lines of evidence regarding the protective and rejuvenating effects of spermidine in cellular systems exposed to oxidative and metabolic stress (Luo et al., 2025; Han et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
Within the framework of the proposed experimental design, spermidine is anticipated to yield several beneficial outcomes when applied to lipofuscin/chloroquine-challenged RPE cultures. Chloroquine is known to perturb autophagic flux by impairing lysosomal function, while the accumulation of lipofuscin represents a chronic stressor that simulates conditions similar to those observed in dry AMD. Under these circumstances, spermidine is expected to initiate a cascade of molecular events that restore the autophagic clearance of damaged cellular components. Specifically, its EP300 inhibitory action is hypothesized to result in the deacetylation of key autophagic proteins, thus reactivating lysosome-dependent degradation pathways. This reactivation should, in turn, lead to the clearance of accumulated A2E and other toxic lipofuscin components, mitigating their deleterious effects on RPE cell function (Han et al., 2022).

Furthermore, by enhancing autophagosome formation and clearance, spermidine is posited to have a direct effect on the maintenance and repair of the RPE’s intercellular junctions. The preservation of ZO-1 and occludin belts is critical in maintaining the barrier integrity of the RPE monolayer, which is essential not only for preventing the translocation of toxic substances but also for sustaining proper retinal homeostasis. TEER assays, which serve as quantitative measures of RPE barrier function, are expected to show significant improvements following spermidine treatment, as the reactivation of autophagic flux facilitates the removal of aberrant proteins and supports the reestablishment of tight junction configurations (Han et al., 2022; Rivera et al., 2024).

Additional support for the expected effects comes from studies that have demonstrated spermidine’s capability to reduce oxidative stress and dampen inflammatory responses in ocular cells. Its role as a calcium chelator in RPE cells helps to prevent calcium overload—a known trigger for apoptotic signaling cascades—which further contributes to cellular survival and barrier preservation under challenging conditions (Han et al., 2022). Although some studies have noted that high doses of spermidine may induce cytotoxic effects, the proposed application emphasizes the use of optimized, low-dose regimens that capitalize on its beneficial actions while avoiding adverse outcomes (Han et al., 2022). In summary, the expected outcome in the proposed lipofuscin/chloroquine-challenged culture model is a pronounced enhancement in autophagic activity, a robust clearance of deleterious junctional components, and a concomitant restoration of TEER, altogether contributing to the reestablishment of RPE barrier function (Han et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating spermidine as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths and weaknesses emerge from the current body of literature. Among the key strengths is its multifaceted mechanism of action that integrates autophagy induction, anti-oxidative stress effects, and anti-inflammatory properties. These features are highly relevant given the pathogenic complexity of dry AMD, which involves chronic oxidative damage, impaired autophagic clearance, and disruption of RPE cell integrity (Han et al., 2022). The proposed mechanism—specifically, the inhibition of EP300 leading to the deacetylation of autophagy proteins—is an attractive strategy because it directly targets the molecular processes implicated in the progression of dry AMD, namely the disruption of RPE barrier integrity and the accumulation of toxic lipofuscin derivatives (Luo et al., 2025; Han et al., 2022). In addition, the fact that spermidine is already available as a dietary supplement with an established safety profile in various contexts provides a translational advantage, potentially facilitating rapid progression into clinical testing and eventual therapeutic application once efficacy is further validated (Han et al., 2022; Hassani et al., 2022).

However, the candidate also presents significant challenges. One of the principal concerns is the narrow therapeutic window associated with its use. Multiple studies have reported that while low doses of spermidine are cytoprotective and enhance autophagic flux, higher concentrations can exert deleterious effects by inducing oxidative stress, necrosis, and impairing retinal function (Han et al., 2022). This dose-dependent toxicity necessitates rigorous pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies, alongside detailed dose-response assessments in preclinical models, to ensure that therapeutic levels can be achieved without triggering adverse outcomes. Moreover, although there is substantive evidence supporting spermidine’s beneficial effects in other ocular contexts, direct evidence from models of dry AMD remains sparse. The majority of the existing literature has focused on conditions such as glaucoma, optic nerve injury, or diabetic retinopathy, while studies specifically addressing the restoration of tight junction integrity (i.e., ZO-1/occludin belts) in RPE cells under conditions mimicking dry AMD are less prevalent (Han et al., 2022). Therefore, while the mechanistic rationale is sound, further experimentation is needed to rigorously evaluate its efficacy in restoring TEER and proper junctional architecture in models that accurately recapitulate the pathophysiology of dry AMD.

Another consideration is the complexity of EP300’s role in cellular physiology. EP300 is involved in a broad spectrum of processes beyond acetylation of autophagy-related proteins, including regulation of gene expression, cell cycle progression, and responses to DNA damage. As such, systemic or even localized inhibition of EP300 by spermidine could potentially lead to off-target effects or undesirable alterations in cellular homeostasis. Although the goal is to achieve selective inhibition that reactivates autophagic flux without broader disruption, the specificity of spermidine’s EP300 inhibition remains an area that requires deeper mechanistic study and possibly the development of more targeted delivery systems to the RPE (Han et al., 2022; Luo et al., 2025).

Furthermore, while the water solubility of spermidine is advantageous for pharmacological formulation and administration, ensuring that sufficient concentration reaches the target tissue in the retina poses its own set of challenges, especially given the anatomical barriers present in the eye. Formulation strategies that enhance ocular bioavailability while preventing rapid clearance will be critical in translating the promising in vitro effects to in vivo systems. Regulatory considerations also come into play: although spermidine is marketed as a dietary supplement, repurposing it for a new indication like dry AMD will require demonstration of efficacy and safety through well-designed clinical trials that address its dosing, pharmacokinetics, and long-term effects on ocular tissues (Han et al., 2022).

Despite these challenges, the hypothesis that spermidine-mediated EP300 inhibition could lead to the restoration of autophagic flux and consequently preserve RPE junctional integrity represents a novel and mechanistically grounded approach. Given that EP300 hyperacetylation has been implicated in the dysregulation of autophagy and the subsequent accumulation of oxidized and aggregate-prone proteins in the RPE, targeting this pathway is a strategic move designed to address a root cause of dry AMD pathology rather than merely alleviating downstream symptoms (Luo et al., 2025; Han et al., 2022). The dual action of spermidine—both as a promoter of autophagy and as a modulator of inflammatory and apoptotic pathways—further strengthens its candidacy for repurposing in this disease setting.

Ultimately, the overall evaluation suggests that while spermidine is a promising candidate with a mechanistically sound rationale for use in dry AMD, its further development will depend on comprehensive preclinical studies that validate its efficacy in restoring RPE barrier function and on the safe optimization of its dosing parameters. The ability of spermidine to re-establish TEER in lipofuscin/chloroquine-challenged RPE cultures would provide compelling proof-of-concept data that warrant progression to more advanced models. In parallel, studies that elucidate the precise molecular interactions between spermidine, EP300, and the autophagic machinery will be necessary to form the basis for future targeted therapies. Overall, the repurposing of spermidine for dry AMD appears to be a promising avenue that is supported by multiple lines of evidence, provided that its potential toxicities can be managed and its beneficial effects confirmed in disease-relevant models (Han et al., 2022).

In conclusion, spermidine’s established roles in autophagy induction, anti-oxidative stress, and inflammation modulation position it as a compelling candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its potential mechanism—mediated by the inhibition of EP300 leading to deacetylated autophagy proteins, enhanced clearance of damaging cellular constituents, and restoration of tight junction protein integrity—provides a targeted strategy that addresses key pathogenic mechanisms in the RPE. While the preclinical data supporting these actions are robust in related ocular contexts, the specific application to dry AMD remains in need of further rigorous investigation. Given its favorable safety profile as a dietary supplement and its water solubility, spermidine is an appealing candidate for rapid translational studies; however, careful attention must be paid to its dose-dependent toxicity, ensuring that effective yet nontoxic concentrations are identified for therapeutic use. Further research should also focus on targeted delivery strategies to the retina, validation of EP300 inhibition specificity, and demonstration of tangible restoration of RPE barrier function in clinically relevant models. If these challenges can be addressed through well-designed preclinical and subsequent clinical studies, spermidine may emerge as a viable repurposed therapeutic agent for dry AMD, potentially altering the treatment landscape for this currently unmet medical need (Han et al., 2022).

Beyond the molecular and cellular dimensions, the translational potential of spermidine in human clinical settings will depend on its pharmacokinetic profile, formulation stability, and the ability to achieve sufficient concentrations in the posterior segment of the eye. Preclinical models that mimic the chronic oxidative and inflammatory milieu of dry AMD will be invaluable in establishing the therapeutic index of spermidine. Moreover, advanced techniques such as high-resolution imaging of RPE layer integrity, along with electrophysiological assessments like TEER measurements, will provide critical endpoints for evaluating treatment efficacy. It is also imperative that the community addresses the potential off-target effects of prolonged EP300 inhibition, as EP300 plays diverse roles in cell regulation beyond autophagy, including transcriptional control of genes essential for cell survival. Focused studies on the long-term effects of spermidine in isolated RPE cultures and in animal models of dry AMD will help in delineating the balance between beneficial autophagic stimulation and possible detrimental effects associated with non-specific acetylation changes (Luo et al., 2025; Han et al., 2022).

Furthermore, the interplay between spermidine’s autophagy-inducing properties and the modulation of inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and TNF-α underscores its multi-targeted approach toward restoring RPE function. Such multi-modal action may prove particularly advantageous in a complex, multifactorial disease like dry AMD, where oxidative stress, impaired autophagy, and chronic inflammation converge to drive disease progression. Data from in vitro studies using RPE cells exposed to conditions that simulate the pathogenic environment of AMD, such as lipofuscin accumulation and lysosomal inhibitors, can yield critical insights into the dose-dependent effects of spermidine. These investigations will also clarify whether spermidine can indeed preserve, or even restore, intercellular junctions comprising proteins like ZO-1 and occludin, thereby re-establishing the functional barrier properties indispensable for retinal homeostasis (Han et al., 2022).

In addition, the implications of EP300-mediated acetylation extend to the regulation of diverse cellular processes, including chromatin remodeling and gene expression, which are pivotal in the context of age-related degenerative diseases. Spermidine’s ability to modulate these processes positions it not only as a potential therapeutic but also as a tool to further elucidate the molecular underpinnings of dry AMD pathogenesis. Emerging evidence suggesting that EP300 hyperacetylation may play a role in the deterioration of autophagic flux in the RPE provides a mechanistic rationale for targeting this pathway. Nonetheless, the challenge remains in ensuring that the inhibition of EP300 is sufficiently selective to avoid unintended disruption of its broader regulatory functions. Future work employing molecular techniques, such as chromatin immunoprecipitation and transcriptome profiling, may shed light on the extent of EP300 inhibition by spermidine and help refine its therapeutic application (Han et al., 2022; Rivera et al., 2024; Tenchov et al., 2024).

The current proposal, which centers on using spermidine to counteract the deleterious effects of lipofuscin buildup and chloroquine-induced autophagic blockade, is particularly innovative in light of the paucity of effective treatments available for dry AMD. Given that autophagy plays a decisive role in ensuring cellular quality control, approaches that can enhance autophagosome formation and clearance are likely to yield significant clinical benefits. Importantly, by preserving the integrity of the RPE’s tight junctions, spermidine may help mitigate the breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier—a key event in the progression of retinal degeneration. The anticipated improvement in TEER, a surrogate marker for barrier function, lends a quantifiable endpoint to gauge therapeutic efficacy in preclinical assays (Han et al., 2022).

From a translational perspective, the fact that spermidine is already utilized as a dietary supplement is a compelling argument for its potential repurposing. Its established safety in long-term human use, combined with its natural occurrence and ease of formulation due to its water solubility, reduces many of the regulatory barriers typically associated with novel pharmacological agents. However, this same advantage must be balanced against the need for precise dose control, as the dichotomy between beneficial autophagy induction and harmful cytotoxicity remains a critical parameter of interest. Robust preclinical studies that employ rigorous dose titration and long-term safety evaluations will be essential in laying the groundwork for eventual clinical trials in patients with dry AMD (Han et al., 2022).

In summary, the repurposing of spermidine for the treatment of dry AMD is supported by a convergence of experimental data that demonstrate its ability to modulate autophagic flux, reduce oxidative stress, and maintain cellular junctional integrity in RPE cells. The proposed mechanism—wherein spermidine exerts selective inhibition on EP300, leading to the deacetylation of autophagy proteins and subsequent restoration of autophagic and barrier functions—is firmly grounded in current understanding of both spermidine’s bioactivities and the pathogenic processes underlying dry AMD. Nevertheless, key challenges in terms of dose optimization, off-target effects, and the translation of in vitro findings to in vivo efficacy remain to be addressed. Comprehensive studies that focus on these aspects will determine whether spermidine can ultimately serve as a viable therapeutic option for dry AMD—a condition for which effective treatments are urgently needed (Han et al., 2022; Luo et al., 2025).

Given the multifactorial nature of dry AMD and the limited therapeutic options currently available, the exploration of spermidine in this context represents an exciting and innovative frontier in ocular drug development. The proposed experimental approach, which emphasizes the restoration of autophagic flux and tight junction integrity, is poised to yield critical insights into the molecular pathology of dry AMD and may pave the way for the development of more effective therapies. However, the ultimate success of this approach will be contingent upon rigorous preclinical validation, careful dose optimization, and the development of targeted delivery strategies to ensure that effective concentrations of spermidine reach the RPE without eliciting detrimental side effects (Han et al., 2022).

To conclude, spermidine, as exemplified by Sigma S3266, emerges as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its intrinsic properties—as a natural polyamine with well-documented autophagy-inducing, anti-inflammatory, and anti-oxidative activities—coupled with a plausible mechanism involving EP300 inhibition, support its potential utility in restoring cellular homeostasis in the RPE. While the therapeutic promise is underscored by a breadth of preclinical data from related ocular models, the specific application to dry AMD requires targeted confirmation through robust experimental paradigms. The strengths of spermidine, including its favorable safety profile as a dietary supplement and its multi-target action, must be balanced against the challenges of dose-dependent toxicity and the necessity for precise modulation of EP300 activity. With careful experimental design and comprehensive preclinical validation, spermidine may indeed progress as a viable strategy to slow or halt the progression of dry AMD, ultimately offering a new avenue of treatment for patients burdened by this degenerative disease (Han et al., 2022).

Proposal for Arimoclomol (MCE HY-18871)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Arimoclomol (also known as BRX-345) is a synthetic hydroxylamine/hydroxamic-acid–derived small molecule developed as a heat-shock response (HSR) co-inducer that amplifies stress-inducible transcription of heat shock genes under conditions of proteotoxic stress, principally through prolongation and potentiation of heat shock factor-1 (HSF1) activation on heat shock elements (HSEs) in target promoters (Penke et al., 2018; Parfitt et al., 2014; O’Leary, 2019). In the hydroximic-acid derivative family (bimoclomol, arimoclomol, NG-094, BGP-15), several members synergistically enhance heat-induced Hsp expression; arimoclomol and bimoclomol have been shown to increase HSF1 activity via hyperphosphorylation and to amplify heat-shock gene expression in eukaryotic cells while sparing basal Hsp expression in unstressed cells, thereby acting as bona fide co-inducers rather than primary HSF1 agonists (Penke et al., 2018). The compound was originally advanced from the bimoclomol chemotype as a more drug-like analogue with similar HSR-potentiating properties and improved pharmacology, and it falls within a broader class of pharmacologic HSP70/HSF1 modulators investigated for neurodegenerative protein-misfolding diseases (e.g., ALS, NPC, tauopathies), as well as select retinal degeneration models (rhodopsin retinitis pigmentosa) (Parfitt et al., 2014; Venediktov et al., 2023; Penke et al., 2018). At the biophysical level, hydroximic-acid derivatives can intercalate into cellular membranes, a property hypothesized to contribute to regulation of HSF1 activation/attenuation kinetics and restoration of a protective Hsp profile under stress (Penke et al., 2018). In neuronal cell systems, arimoclomol has also been used in combination with primary HSF1 activators (e.g., celastrol) to achieve robust induction of inducible Hsp70s (HSPA1A, HSPA6) and other stress response proteins at lower inducer doses, consistent with its role as a co-inducer that amplifies pre-existing HSF1 activation (Deane, 2019).

Within the retina, arimoclomol has been evaluated in rod photoreceptor models of misfolded rhodopsin (P23H transgenic rats), where it enhanced Hsp70/Hsp90 expression and improved proteostasis, photoreceptor structure, and visual function; however, there is no published evidence in dry AMD models or direct demonstrations of RPE barrier rescue by arimoclomol, and at least one PRPF31-mutant RPE (RP11) cell system screening showed no aggregate-reducing effect of arimoclomol while an mTOR inhibitor (rapamycin) reduced aggregate burden via autophagy induction (Parfitt et al., 2014; Georgiou, 2021). The broader Hsp70/Hsc70 system, chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA), and macroautophagy are mechanistically central to RPE proteostasis and AMD pathobiology, establishing a strong rationale for HSF1–HSP70–targeted therapy, but translation from photoreceptor models and exogenous Hsp70 delivery to endogenous induction in RPE remains to be validated for this agent (Kumar et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2015; Subrizi et al., 2015).

Therapeutic History  
Arimoclomol’s development history is anchored in neurodegeneration and protein-misfolding indications. In SOD1-mutant ALS mice, arimoclomol increased Hsp70 expression and improved motor neuron survival and function, extending lifespan; it progressed to human ALS trials (including a phase 3 program), with mixed outcomes across adult and pediatric indications (O’Leary, 2019; Venediktov et al., 2023). Mechanistically consistent with HSF1 co-induction, arimoclomol is positioned to upregulate a suite of inducible chaperones and components of the proteostasis network rather than single chaperone overexpression, a strategy considered preferable for matching the endogenous disaggregation/refolding machinery and preserving feedback attenuation (O’Leary, 2019).

In the retina, arimoclomol has been tested extensively in rhodopsin retinitis pigmentosa (RP) models driven by the P23H misfolding mutation. In P23H-GFP cell models, arimoclomol reduced inclusion incidence and insoluble rod opsin, decreased higher-molecular-weight rhodopsin species, and improved viability, with contemporaneous increases in Hsp70/Hsp90 implying potentiation of the HSR in stressed photoreceptors (Parfitt et al., 2014). In P23H transgenic rats, daily intraperitoneal dosing (10 mg/kg) improved scotopic ERG a- and b-waves, preserved outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness, increased outer segment (OS) length, and improved ultrastructure, consistent with disease modification through HSR and unfolded protein response (UPR) potentiation; Hsp70, Hsp90, and HSF1 were assayed directly in these studies (Parfitt et al., 2014). The authors further observed increased eIF2α phosphorylation and discussed enhanced IRE1/XBP1 activity, indicating crosstalk with ER stress responses (Parfitt et al., 2014). Of note, arimoclomol’s activity appeared contingent on the presence of misfolded-protein stress (i.e., stress-selective action), potentially limiting off-target effects in healthy tissue (Parfitt et al., 2014).

Beyond photoreceptors, the Hsp co-inducer class has retinal neuroprotective precedents: bimoclomol improved early electrophysiologic signs in diabetic rat retina, and the Hsp inducer geranylgeranylacetone protected retinal ganglion cells in a rat glaucoma model, underscoring that Hsp70 induction can be protective across retinal cell types and diseases of proteostasis and stress, although these are class exemplars rather than arimoclomol-specific RPE data (Hesselink, 2016). Separately, exogenous Hsp70 protein delivery to RPE has shown diffusion to the retina and RPE after intravitreal administration, intracellular uptake, lysosomal localization, and protection from oxidative stress and inflammation in ARPE-19 cells, supporting the concept that increasing Hsp70 activity in RPE can be beneficial, albeit via protein pharmacology rather than endogenous induction (Subrizi et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2020).

Crucially for dry AMD translation, the current literature set provides no in vivo animal or clinical study of arimoclomol in AMD/dry AMD, and no direct measurements of RPE barrier integrity (tight-junction protein preservation or transepithelial electrical resistance [TEER]) following arimoclomol in RPE or AMD models; an RPE disease model of PRPF31 mutation with progressive aggregate accumulation reported that arimoclomol failed to reduce aggregates, whereas rapamycin decreased aggregate load and induced LC3 processing consistent with autophagy activation (LAMP1 and p62 remained unchanged), highlighting context-dependent efficacy and suggesting autophagy induction may be more decisive than Hsp co-induction in some RPE aggregate pathologies (Georgiou, 2021). Thus, while arimoclomol has a positive retinal track record in photoreceptor proteotoxicity and a robust extraocular development history, there is no direct evidence yet of arimoclomol ameliorating dry AMD phenotypes or preserving RPE barrier function in disease-relevant systems (Parfitt et al., 2014; Georgiou, 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
Arimoclomol is an HSR co-inducer that amplifies HSF1-driven transcription of inducible heat shock proteins under pre-existing cellular stress. Mechanistically, arimoclomol prolongs HSF1 binding to HSEs, increases HSF1 activity (e.g., hyperphosphorylation), and thereby increases transcription of Hsp70/Hsp90 and related chaperones, with limited impact in unstressed cells (i.e., stressor-dependent co-induction) (Penke et al., 2018; O’Leary, 2019; Parfitt et al., 2014). In neuronal cells, arimoclomol enhanced celastrol-induced HSF1 activation to elevate HSPA6, HSPA1A, HSPB1, DNAJB1, and HO-1 at doses that preserved viability and differentiated morphology, supporting efficient co-induction when paired with a primary HSF1 activator (Deane, 2019). In P23H photoreceptor models, arimoclomol reduced insoluble rhodopsin and inclusion incidence, decreased high-molecular-weight species, increased retinal Hsp70/Hsp90, and improved ERG/ONL/OS outcomes; the study observed increased eIF2α phosphorylation and discussed potentiation of the UPR (BiP/IRE1/XBP1), consistent with arimoclomol acting at the intersection of cytosolic HSR and ER homeostasis (Parfitt et al., 2014).

Hsp70 Biology in RPE and AMD. Inducible Hsp70 (HSPA1A/Hsp70-1) is a central, evolutionarily conserved ATPase chaperone that assists folding of nascent chains, refolds damaged/misfolded proteins, buffers aggregation, facilitates “protein triage” toward degradation pathways, and protects cells from apoptosis and inflammatory signaling (e.g., NF-κB pathway), with expression controlled by HSF1 (Ryhänen, 2011; Kivinen, 2018). In the RPE, Hsp70/Hsc70 function intersects both the ubiquitin–proteasome system (UPS) and lysosome-dependent proteolysis. Hsp70 can present misfolded proteins to the UPS via CHIP E3 ligase, regulate disaggregation with co-chaperones HSP40/HSP90/HIP/HOP, and is required for aggregate handling; in proteasome failure, protein aggregates in ARPE-19 cells co-localize with Hsp70 and p62, with p62 undergoing autophagic clearance while Hsp70 binds reversibly and evades autophagic degradation (Kumar et al., 2020; Kivinen et al., 2014; Ryhänen, 2011). Hsp70 is also integral to chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA): cytosolic Hsc70/Hsp70 recognizes KFERQ-containing substrates, delivers them to LAMP-2A at the lysosomal membrane, and ATPase-driven “entropic pulling” and luminal chaperones enable translocation and degradation; oxidative stress reduces HSP70 expression in RPE, impairs CMA, and can dysregulate macroautophagy cross-talk, contributing to RPE death (Chang et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2020). Extracellular Hsp70 roles in RPE are complex: exogenous rhHsp70 injections protected against subretinal fibrosis via TLR2/TLR4 and IL-10 induction, while oxidized-lipid stress (4-HNE) can increase extracellular Hsp70 efflux and pro-inflammatory cytokines, indicating that compartmental localization of Hsp70 critically determines immunomodulatory outcomes (Kumar et al., 2020).

Evidence for arimoclomol in RPE cells. Direct mechanistic evidence for arimoclomol action in RPE is limited. A cell-culture report in ARPE-19 asserts that Hsp70 overexpression “with the help of a co-inducer like arimoclomol” suppressed IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α and increased IL-10 and TGF-β1, consistent with Hsp70-mediated IκK/NF-κB inhibition; however, the study details are summarized in low-quality review literature, and direct demonstration of arimoclomol-driven HSF1 activation in RPE is not provided (Kumar et al., 2020). Another ARPE-19-focused review excerpt states that arimoclomol acts on HSF1 to increase cytosolic Hsp70 without increasing extracellular Hsp70 and improved resistance to 4-HNE–induced oxidative stress (relative to paeoniflorin); again, the primary data are not provided here and the review is of limited quality, so these findings should be treated as provisional until replicated (Kumar et al., 2020). Importantly, in an isogenic patient-derived PRPF31-mutant RPE (RP11) model with progressive cytoplasmic aggregate accumulation, a 7-day treatment screen across HSR/UPR/autophagy modulators showed that rapamycin (mTORC1 inhibitor) reduced aggregate load and shifted LC3-I to LC3-II, whereas arimoclomol did not reduce aggregates under the conditions tested, arguing that in this RPE disease context autophagy activation via mTOR inhibition outperformed Hsp co-induction (Georgiou, 2021).

Non-pharmacological Hsp70 induction and autophagy in RPE inform plausibility. Subthreshold retinal thermal stimulation in pig and mouse RPE in vivo induced HSF1 and Hsp70, increased LC3B-II and decreased p62 (consistent with autophagy activation), and increased LAMP2, suggesting potential CMA upregulation, without apoptosis at ~44 °C, confirming that RPE supports coordinated HSR–autophagy programs with an exploitable therapeutic window (but autophagic flux was not directly quantified in vivo) (Amirkavei et al., 2022; Amirkavei et al., 2020). These data reinforce the therapeutic logic for HSF1–Hsp70 upregulation in RPE to restore proteostasis but do not directly validate arimoclomol’s efficacy in RPE (Amirkavei et al., 2022; Amirkavei et al., 2020). Exogenous rhHsp70 trafficking to lysosomes and protection against oxidative stress in ARPE-19 further supports the notion that increasing Hsp70 activity, whether by protein delivery or endogenous induction, can be beneficial to RPE survival under AMD-relevant stressors (Subrizi et al., 2015).

Autophagy and barrier integrity under AMD-relevant stressors. AMD-relevant toxicities (Aβ, lipofuscin/A2E, oxidants) perturb autophagy/lysosomes in RPE, with Aβ decreasing occludin and ZO-1 in ARPE-19 and activating autophagy markers in vitro and in vivo, and A2E promoting lysosomal membrane permeabilization and cell death; impaired UPS and autophagy with aging lead to aggregate accumulation (including p62-positive aggregates) in RPE and drusen, highlighting the importance of restoring both proteasomal and autophagic clearance to protect RPE function and barrier integrity (Wang et al., 2023; Viiri, 2019; Ryhänen, 2011). Hsp70/p62 roles in this axis are mechanistically established: Hsp70 prevents aggregation and participates in aggregate handling, while p62 is an autophagic receptor degraded by autophagy and accumulates when autophagy is impaired; pharmacologic AMPK activation can accelerate p62 clearance during proteasome inhibition and improve RPE survival (Viiri, 2019). To date, arimoclomol has not been shown to modulate CMA or macroautophagy in RPE, nor to preserve tight junctions or TEER in AMD-relevant models (Georgiou, 2021; Kumar et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
Assay hypothesis and rationale. The working hypothesis is that arimoclomol will potentiate stress-triggered HSF1 activity in RPE, elevating inducible Hsp70 and coordinated chaperone networks to stabilize junctional proteostasis, reduce misfolded protein burden, and normalize autophagy (including potentially CMA), thereby preventing degradation of occludin/claudin and restoring TEER under oxidative or drusen-like stress (e.g., H2O2/4-HNE, A2E/lipofuscin, Aβ) (Kumar et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2023). This mechanism is biologically plausible: Hsp70 is abundantly expressed in RPE under stress and supports folding and refolding, substrate triage to proteasome via CHIP, and delivery of specific substrates to CMA via Hsc70/LAMP-2A; its induction suppresses NF-κB–driven pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and can raise IL-10/TGF-β1, which together could indirectly protect junctional complexes from cytokine- and stress-mediated degradation (Kumar et al., 2020). Reducing intracellular aggregate load and restoring proteostasis would be expected to mitigate the downstream cascade of mTORC1 activation, p62/LC3-I accumulation, and tight-junction disruption observed in stressed RPE models (e.g., PRPF31-RPE), although in that system arimoclomol was ineffective while rapamycin reduced aggregates, underscoring that Hsp co-induction alone may be insufficient when autophagy is the principal bottleneck (Georgiou, 2021).

Evidence supporting expected effects in RPE assays:  
- Hsp70 induction in retinal tissues has been achieved via HSF1 activation by heat or pharmacologic inducers; in photoreceptor P23H models, arimoclomol increased Hsp70/Hsp90 and reduced aggregation/toxicity, consistent with the proximal arm of the proposed mechanism (HSF1→Hsp70→improved proteostasis) (Parfitt et al., 2014; Amirkavei et al., 2020).  
- In ARPE-19 summaries, arimoclomol increased intracellular (not extracellular) Hsp70 and improved resistance to 4-HNE oxidative stress, and Hsp70 overexpression with help of a co-inducer like arimoclomol suppressed pro-inflammatory cytokines, supporting cell-autonomous proteostasis and anti-inflammatory contributions that would be favorable for junctional stability (Kumar et al., 2020).  
- Exogenous rhHsp70 delivery to RPE localizes to lysosomes and reduces oxidative toxicity and inflammation, demonstrating that raising functional Hsp70 in RPE is sufficient to afford cytoprotection, a downstream functional goal of HSF1 co-induction (Subrizi et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2020).

Evidence arguing for tempered expectations and the need for combination strategies:  
- In PRPF31-mutant RPE, arimoclomol did not reduce aggregates in a 7-day screen, whereas rapamycin shifted LC3 processing and reduced aggregate markers, suggesting that when autophagy is the limiting axis, direct autophagy activation (e.g., mTORC1 inhibition) is required; Hsp co-induction alone may not clear established aggregates or repair autophagic flux (Georgiou, 2021).  
- In primary neuronal ALS models, arimoclomol often failed to induce measurable HSPA1A/HSPA8 and its protective actions occurred without detectable Hsp70 upregulation; HDAC inhibition enhanced Hsp induction by other inducers, arguing that Hsp co-induction efficacy is cell-type and chromatin-context dependent and may require combination therapy to overcome induction thresholds in some cells (potentially relevant to differentiated RPE) (Comaduran et al., 2024).  
- AMD-relevant stressors directly disrupt tight junctions (Aβ reduces occludin and ZO-1 in ARPE-19) and invoke autophagy/lysosomal dysfunction; because arimoclomol’s effects on CMA/macroautophagy in RPE are unproven, barrier rescue may not occur unless autophagic flux is also corrected (Wang et al., 2023).

Assay implementation guidance for decision-making:  
- In vitro human RPE models (primary/donor iPSC-RPE monolayers with high TEER) should be stressed with 4-HNE, H2O2, A2E, or Aβ to recapitulate AMD-relevant proteotoxic and inflammatory conditions, and arimoclomol tested across concentrations paralleling prior cell work (e.g., 10–100 µM) with and without a priming HSF1 activator (celastrol ≤0.3 µM) to evaluate requirement for co-induction, keeping in mind the neuronal data identifying 50 µM arimoclomol + 0.3 µM celastrol as an optimized low-toxicity combination (Deane, 2019).  
- Primary readouts: HSF1 activation (nuclear translocation, Ser phosphorylation), Hsp70/Hsp90 induction (immunoblot, qPCR), autophagic flux (LC3-II turnover with/without bafilomycin, p62 dynamics), CMA markers (LAMP-2A levels, lysosomal Hsc70/Hsp70 substrate colocalization), proteasome activity, aggregate load (FK1, ubiquitin, p62 bodies), and barrier integrity (TEER, ZO-1/occludin/claudin-19 immunostaining continuity) (Kivinen et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2015; Viiri, 2019; Wang et al., 2023).  
- Cytokine profiling (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-10, TGF-β1) to detect Hsp70-linked NF-κB effects reported in ARPE-19 (Kumar et al., 2020).  
- Positive comparators: rapamycin for autophagy induction; exogenous rhHsp70 as a proteostasis rescue control; heat-based Hsp70 induction within non-damaging windows to confirm pathway responsiveness (Georgiou, 2021; Subrizi et al., 2015; Amirkavei et al., 2020).

Given the aggregate of evidence, the most realistic expectation is that arimoclomol will increase inducible Hsp70 in stressed RPE if HSF1 can be productively co-induced, reduce misfolded protein accumulation and inflammatory signaling, and potentially improve barrier metrics indirectly by attenuating stressors that degrade junctional complexes; however, without concurrent normalization of autophagic flux and CMA, tight-junction rescue and TEER restoration are uncertain, particularly in models where autophagy is the primary deficit (Georgiou, 2021; Kumar et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2015).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths supporting arimoclomol for dry AMD RPE barrier rescue:  
- Mechanistic fit: Hsp70/Hsc70 are central “gatekeepers” of RPE proteostasis across the UPS and lysosomal systems, including CMA; restoring inducible Hsp70 via HSF1 co-induction directly targets key failure nodes in RPE aging and AMD pathogenesis (aggregation, impaired clearance, inflammation), aligning with known disease biology (Kumar et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2015; Kivinen, 2018).  
- Demonstrated retinal efficacy in proteostasis-driven degeneration: arimoclomol increased Hsp70/Hsp90, reduced mutant rhodopsin aggregation, and preserved photoreceptor structure/function in P23H rats, with evidence of concurrent UPR potentiation; this validates the platform concept that HSF1 co-induction plus ER stress modulation can modify retinal degeneration, albeit in photoreceptors rather than RPE (Parfitt et al., 2014).  
- RPE permissiveness to Hsp70-based cytoprotection: exogenous rhHsp70 diffuses to RPE, is internalized, localizes to endolysosomal compartments, reduces IL-6 and cytolysis, and improves viability in oxidative stress paradigms; thus, augmenting Hsp70 in RPE is sufficient to produce protective effects, supporting the feasibility of endogenous induction with a co-inducer if pharmacology is adequate (Subrizi et al., 2015).  
- Stress-selective amplification: arimoclomol preferentially acts in stressed cells, limiting risks of unwanted Hsp70 induction in healthy tissue; this attribute is advantageous for chronic ocular therapy where avoiding constitutive pathway activation is desirable (Parfitt et al., 2014).  
- Clinical development and safety experience: extensive non-ocular development in ALS/NPC provides informative safety and pharmacology context; while ocular distribution is not established in these sources, the systemic safety window is a favorable starting point for repurposing (Venediktov et al., 2023; O’Leary, 2019).

Key weaknesses and uncertainties:  
- Lack of direct evidence in dry AMD/RPE barrier endpoints: no published data demonstrate arimoclomol preserves RPE tight junctions (ZO-1/occludin/claudin), restores TEER, or improves drusen-like pathology in vivo; ARPE-19 reports of arimoclomol-induced Hsp70 and anti-inflammatory effects are secondary summaries in low-quality reviews without primary detail (Kumar et al., 2020). In contrast, direct AMD-relevant in vitro data show that Aβ disrupts tight junction proteins, and autophagy failure correlates with p62 accumulation and aggregate burden, but the ability of arimoclomol to reverse these specific defects in RPE is untested (Wang et al., 2023; Viiri, 2019).  
- Negative/neutral result in PRPF31-RPE aggregation screen: arimoclomol did not reduce cytoplasmic aggregates in a rigorous 7-day screen in RP11-RPE; rapamycin reduced aggregates and shifted LC3 processing, suggesting that in certain RPE aggregate pathologies, autophagy activators outperform Hsp co-induction; whether arimoclomol could complement autophagy induction to achieve barrier rescue remains to be determined (Georgiou, 2021).  
- Uncertain induction competence in differentiated RPE: Primary neurons display high thresholds for inducible Hsp70 (HSPA1A) induction, with arimoclomol often failing to raise Hsp70; Hsp induction can be enhanced by HDAC inhibition, implying that chromatin accessibility and cell state are important variables; differentiated RPE monolayers may similarly require co-induction strategies (e.g., low-dose celastrol or epigenetic modulators) to achieve robust Hsp70 upregulation (Comaduran et al., 2024; Deane, 2019). If arimoclomol cannot reliably induce Hsp70 in mature RPE under clinically relevant stress, the strategy will falter.  
- CMA/macroautophagy modulation by arimoclomol in RPE not established: despite Hsp70’s mechanistic role in CMA, no data show arimoclomol improves CMA or autophagic flux in RPE, which are crucial to clearing damaged proteins/lipids under AMD stress; relying on Hsp70 alone without restoring autophagic flux may be insufficient to protect tight junctions (Chang et al., 2015; Georgiou, 2021).  
- Translational pharmacology: Retinal/RPE exposure of arimoclomol following systemic dosing is not presented in this corpus; ocular delivery strategies and RPE pharmacokinetics for arimoclomol are undefined here, in contrast to exogenous Hsp70 delivery where diffusion and tissue uptake were measured (Subrizi et al., 2015). Without ocular PK/PD and RPE Hsp70 induction data, dosing strategies for barrier rescue remain speculative.

Recommendation and development path:  
- Proceed to targeted preclinical validation in human iPSC-RPE monolayers and AMD-relevant stress paradigms, with rigorous endpoint panels including HSF1–Hsp70 induction, autophagic flux/CMA markers, aggregate clearance, cytokine modulation, and barrier integrity (TEER, ZO-1/occludin continuity), using rapamycin and rhHsp70 as comparators and benchmarking against known disruptions by Aβ and A2E (Georgiou, 2021; Subrizi et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2023).  
- Explore co-induction strategies: combine arimoclomol with low-dose celastrol to lower the induction threshold, and/or with autophagy activators (rapalogs/AMPK agonists) to correct flux while elevating chaperone capacity; justify combinations by neuronal data demonstrating enhanced Hsp induction and by RPE data showing autophagy dependence of aggregate clearance (Deane, 2019; Viiri, 2019; Georgiou, 2021).  
- If cell data are positive (robust Hsp70 induction, reduced aggregate burden, TEER protection), advance to ex vivo retina or small-animal models of RPE oxidative/drusen-like stress, with ocular pharmacokinetic measurements to confirm RPE exposure and on-target Hsp70 induction; consider local ocular delivery if systemic exposure is inadequate (Subrizi et al., 2015).  
- Maintain a realistic risk view: if arimoclomol fails to induce Hsp70 adequately in differentiated RPE or fails to impact autophagic flux, pivot to alternative HSF1 activators or to exogenous Hsp70 delivery or autophagy-centric therapies, where evidence in RPE is stronger (Subrizi et al., 2015; Georgiou, 2021).

In sum, arimoclomol is a mechanistically coherent candidate for restoring RPE proteostasis via HSF1–Hsp70 co-induction, supported by strong photoreceptor data and broad neurodegeneration experience, but it lacks direct evidence in dry AMD models and has an RPE aggregation screen result that favors autophagy induction over Hsp co-induction; rigorous, well-controlled RPE studies with barrier readouts are required before committing to translational development for dry AMD (Parfitt et al., 2014; Georgiou, 2021).
