Proposal for Z944 (Tocris 5649)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Z944 is a synthetic, rationally designed T‐type calcium channel blocker that emerged from a medicinal chemistry program aimed at developing first‐in‐class modulators with improved selectivity and pharmacokinetic profiles. It was derived from a piperazine‐based chemical backbone originally optimized from an N‐type calcium channel blocker scaffold, with extensive structure–activity relationship studies guiding its evolution to target T‐type channels (primarily CaV3.1, CaV3.2, and CaV3.3) with high affinity (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018). As part of the broader class of T‐type calcium channel blockers, Z944 belongs to a group of compounds that have been predominantly evaluated for their analgesic and anti‐epileptic properties. Its design emphasizes sub‐micromolar potency (with reported IC₅₀ values in the nanomolar range for its target channels) and a high degree of selectivity—demonstrating 70–100-fold preference for T-type channels over other voltage-gated channels such as CaV1.4 (a key L-type channel in retinal photoreceptors) (Sun et al., 2025). Although originally conceived to treat neuropathic pain and seizure disorders, its improved pharmacokinetic properties have prompted interest in repurposing Z944 for indications outside the central nervous system, including retinal diseases.  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, Z944 has been developed and evaluated extensively in preclinical models focused on pain management and epilepsy, demonstrating encouraging translational potential by restoring functional neuronal circuit dynamics in both inflammatory pain and absence epilepsy models (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018; Melgari et al., 2022). Clinical studies have established that Z944 can effectively modulate T‐type calcium channel activity in human experimental models of inflammatory pain, and it has been advanced into Phase I and Phase II clinical trials targeting pain indications (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018). However, a consistent theme throughout published reports is that Z944, along with similar T‐type channel antagonists, has been primarily evaluated in the context of neurological disorders. Comprehensive literature reviews and patent analyses have yet to document any clinical or preclinical application of Z944 or related T‐type calcium channel blockers in the treatment of dry age‐related macular degeneration (dry AMD), retinal degeneration, or retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018; Sun et al., 2025; Jones, 2024). The modulator’s history in pain and epilepsy provides a solid foundation for its general pharmacological activity, yet its use in ocular settings remains uncharted territory.  

Mechanism of Action:  
Z944 exerts its pharmacological effects primarily through the selective inhibition of T‐type calcium channels. At the molecular level, T‐type channels (CaV3 family) are low–voltage‐activated channels essential for regulating neuronal excitability and rhythmic firing. Using state-dependent screening assays against the human CaV3.2 channel subunit, researchers have demonstrated that Z944 binds with high affinity (IC₅₀ in the range of 50–160 nM against various CaV3 isoforms), and its selectivity exceeds 70–100‐fold when compared to channels such as the CaV2.2 (N‐type) and CaV1.2 (L‐type) channels (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018). Recent structural studies using cryo–electron microscopy have provided insights into the binding mode of T–type blockers by revealing how similar compounds dock into the channel’s fenestration between domains—a strategy that has been pivotal in understanding the selectivity profile of Z944 (Sun et al., 2025).  

The biochemical mechanism of Z944’s action involves the attenuation of low–voltage–activated calcium currents that are normally responsible for initiating calcium influx in response to subthreshold depolarizations. In neurons, this inhibition translates into a decreased excitability and modulation of burst firing patterns. Extrapolating from these findings, one could hypothesize that, in non–neuronal cells such as RPE, Z944 would likewise reduce pathological calcium entry induced by oxidative stress. In the specific context of dry AMD, oxidative stress and the accumulation of toxic by‐products such as A2E have been implicated in the disruption of intracellular calcium homeostasis. An overload of intracellular Ca²⁺ can activate calcium‐dependent enzymes like calpain and calcineurin, which in turn mediate the proteolytic degradation of key tight junction proteins—including zonula occludens‐1 (ZO‐1) and occludin—thereby compromising the integrity of the RPE barrier (Korkka, n.d.).  

Even though Z944’s molecular interactions have been largely characterized in neuronal systems, the rationalization for its use in RPE cells is based on the observation that T‐type channels are indeed expressed in these cells. Immunostaining studies in mouse RPE tissue have confirmed the presence of CaV3.1 and CaV3.2 isoforms, indicating that T‐type channel–mediated calcium influx contributes to RPE physiology (Korkka, n.d.). While the direct mechanistic link between T‐type channel inhibition and the prevention of calpain/calcineurin activation in RPE cells remains to be experimentally verified, the well‐established role of calcium as a trigger for these enzymes suggests that Z944 could effectively mitigate calcium‐dependent tight junction degradation if pathological calcium overload is sufficiently attenuated. Moreover, evidence from related pharmacological studies suggests that at low nanomolar concentrations, Z944 can achieve significant T‐type channel blockade without affecting other voltage‐gated channels, which is crucial to avoid unintended consequences on retinal signaling mediated by CaV1.4 channels (Sun et al., 2025).  

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of Z944 for dry AMD is that by inhibiting T‐type channels in the RPE, Z944 will mitigate oxidative stress–induced intracellular Ca²⁺ overload. Oxidative stress is a well‐recognized contributor to RPE dysfunction and dry AMD pathogenesis, and excessive intracellular calcium can activate calpain and calcineurin enzymes. These calcium‐dependent proteases degrade tight junction proteins such as ZO‐1, leading to barrier dysfunction as evidenced by decreased transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and disorganized ZO‐1 continuity. In vitro experiments using patient‐derived RPE cells have shown that these cells often upregulate T‐type calcium channel expression under stress conditions, thereby providing a plausible target for Z944 (Jones, 2024).  

In the proposed experimental design, RPE cells loaded with A2E (a bisretinoid that accumulates with age and contributes to oxidative stress in the RPE) will be exposed to oxidative conditions to induce intracellular Ca²⁺ overload and subsequent tight junction disruption. The addition of Z944 at concentrations around 50 nM is expected to significantly reduce this pathological calcium influx. This, in turn, should lead to a decrease in calpain and calcineurin activation, preventing the phosphorylation and degradation of occludin and disruption of ZO‐1 continuity. As a result, the integrity of the RPE barrier should be restored, evidenced by normalized TEER measurements and preserved tight junction morphology on Western blot analyses for occludin phosphorylation (Korkka, n.d.; Sun et al., 2025).  

It is important to note that while an inhibitory effect on T‐type channels in the RPE might be expected based on neuronal data, specific studies in RPE cells remain limited. Other T‐type channel inhibitors, such as ML218, have been shown to modulate phagocytosis in human embryonic stem cell–derived RPE models, albeit with a focus on processes different from tight junction maintenance (Korkka, n.d.). Therefore, the expected outcome is primarily extrapolated from broader knowledge on calcium‐dependent processes in RPE cells and the established pharmacodynamic profile of Z944 in other models. Furthermore, the selectivity for CaV3 isoforms suggests that even in the presence of secondary channel populations, Z944 is unlikely to affect L‐type channels like CaV1.4 at the low nanomolar doses proposed, thereby limiting off‐target risks that could arise from disruption of normal photoreceptor function.  

Overall Evaluation:  
From an innovation perspective, repurposing Z944 for dry AMD presents a novel approach by directly targeting a mechanism that has not been extensively explored in the field of macular degeneration. The therapeutic candidate’s high potency and selectivity for T‐type calcium channels are clear strengths, as these characteristics set it apart from older, less selective compounds such as mibefradil (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018). Its improved pharmacokinetic profile and proven translational potential in pain and epilepsy models lend additional credibility to the compound as a drug candidate with potential for ocular application. The emphasis on a mechanistic strategy—namely, reducing oxidative stress–induced intracellular Ca²⁺ overload to prevent calpain/calcineurin–mediated degradation of tight junction proteins—addresses a critical pathological process in the RPE that could underlie barrier dysfunction in dry AMD (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018).  

However, several weaknesses and challenges must be considered. First, the literature reviewed to date provides no direct evidence for the efficacy of Z944 in ocular models or specifically in dry AMD. All available data regarding Z944 pertain to its use in neurological applications, with multiple sources explicitly noting that no trials or studies have been conducted using T‐type blockers for age‐related macular degeneration, retinal degeneration, or RPE dysfunction (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018; Sun et al., 2025; Jones, 2024). This represents a significant gap in the translational pathway that must be addressed through rigorous preclinical testing in ocular models before any clinical application can be contemplated.  

Secondly, while the proposed mechanism is biologically plausible, the exact contribution of T‐type channels to calcium dysregulation in the RPE under oxidative stress conditions remains incompletely defined. Although immunostaining and electrophysiological studies have confirmed the expression of CaV3.1 and CaV3.2 in RPE cells (Korkka, n.d.), the extent to which these channels drive calpain and calcineurin activation in the context of AMD is uncertain. Most existing studies in RPE have focused on aspects such as phagocytosis or VEGF secretion (Korkka, n.d.), leaving the specific role of calcium overload in tight junction disruption relatively underexplored. This uncertainty underscores the need for detailed mechanistic studies—including TEER assays, Western blots for tight junction proteins, and calcium imaging under oxidative conditions in RPE models—to validate the proposed therapeutic approach.  

Another potential concern relates to the off‐target effects on other calcium channels, particularly those relevant to retinal function. Although Z944 boasts a 70–100–fold selectivity for T‐type channels over L‐type channels, some studies have shown that at higher concentrations or under specific conditions, Z944 can interact with CaV1.4 channels, which are critical for synaptic function in photoreceptors (Sun et al., 2025). Even though the proposed dosing (around 50 nM) is significantly below the levels that affect CaV1.4, careful dose–response studies in RPE and retinal tissue are warranted to ensure that the therapeutic window is both effective and safe. Moreover, the differences in channel expression and regulation between neuronal tissue and RPE may yield unanticipated pharmacodynamic responses that could complicate the translatability of the preclinical findings to an ocular setting.  

Strengths of the candidate include its robust preclinical profile in terms of selectivity and pharmacokinetics, and its innovative mechanism that targets a critical but relatively underexplored pathway in dry AMD pathology. The specificity for T‐type channels provides a clear molecular rationale for preventing calcium‐dependent tight junction degradation, which is an attractive approach for mitigating RPE barrier dysfunction. Furthermore, the rational design and extensive optimization that have characterized Z944’s development inspire confidence in its chemical and biological properties (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018).  

On the other hand, the weaknesses are equally notable. The lack of historical or preclinical evidence for efficacy in dry AMD represents a major translational hurdle. Before Z944 can be considered a viable candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, comprehensive studies assessing its effects on RPE barrier function, tight junction integrity (e.g., ZO-1 and occludin dynamics), and overall retinal health under stress conditions are needed. In addition, potential differences in the regulatory networks governing calcium homeostasis in RPE compared to neurons could result in unpredictable responses to T-type channel blockade. Also, even though early findings in neural models suggest that Z944 can reverse stress–induced barrier leaks at low concentrations, it remains to be seen if these effects are recapitulated in human-derived RPE cultures, particularly in the complex environment of AMD where oxidative stress and chronic inflammation play pivotal roles (Jones, 2024; Sun et al., 2025).  

In conclusion, while Z944 exhibits many properties that make it an attractive candidate from a drug development perspective—such as high potency, remarkable selectivity for T‐type channels, and a favorable pharmacokinetic profile—the repurposing of Z944 for dry age‐related macular degeneration is currently speculative. The existing literature overwhelmingly supports its use in pain and neurological disorders, and there is a conspicuous absence of data linking T-type calcium channel modulation to therapeutic outcomes in AMD or RPE dysfunction (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018; Sun et al., 2025; Jones, 2024). The proposed hypothesis that Z944 can mitigate oxidative stress–induced intracellular Ca²⁺ overload in RPE and thereby restore tight junction integrity is mechanistically plausible given the known roles of Ca²⁺ signals in RPE barrier regulation; however, the strategy remains unproven in the ocular context.  

Moving forward, it would be advisable to initiate a series of in vitro studies using patient-derived or stem-cell-derived RPE models under oxidative conditions and A2E loading, with a focus on measuring TEER, ZO-1 expression and continuity, occludin phosphorylation levels, and calpain/calcineurin activation. These studies would provide the necessary proof-of-concept data to justify in vivo preclinical work. Additionally, comparative studies with other T-type channel inhibitors (such as ML218) could help delineate whether the effects observed are class effects or specific to Z944, thereby further validating the therapeutic target.  

Overall, Z944 holds potential as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD, particularly from an innovative mechanistic standpoint. Its strengths in chemical design and robust pharmacological activity in non-ocular systems are promising; yet, significant gaps in the research related to RPE-specific outcomes and the translation of T-type channel inhibition to barrier protection in the retina must be addressed. Hence, while the proposed direction is intriguing and represents a novel therapeutic angle, additional preclinical studies focused explicitly on ocular models are critical to determine whether Z944 can fulfill its promise in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (Snutch & Zamponi, 2018; Sun et al., 2025).

Proposal for GW501516 (MedChemExpress HY-10023)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
GW501516 is a fully synthetic small‐molecule agonist that selectively binds to and activates the peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor beta/delta (PPARβ/δ), a member of the nuclear receptor superfamily known for its central role in regulating lipid metabolism and energy homeostasis (Salvadó et al., 2014; Ebert et al., 2016). Originally developed through medicinal chemistry approaches targeting metabolic disorders, GW501516 belongs to the broader class of PPAR agonists, which have historically been pursued for their capacity to enhance fatty acid oxidation and improve insulin sensitivity in preclinical models. The synthetic origins of GW501516 involve structure–activity relationship studies aimed at identifying high affinity ligands for PPARβ/δ; its successful development resulted in a compound with nanomolar potency (EC₅₀ approximately 3 nM) (Salvadó et al., 2014). In general, compounds from this class have been used to probe metabolic pathways in skeletal muscle and adipose tissues, where activation of PPARβ/δ drives transcriptional programs that increase fatty acid oxidation, counteract endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, and mitigate inflammatory responses (Salvadó et al., 2014). This repurposing effort seeks to capitalize on its established metabolic benefits in a novel indication—dry age–related macular degeneration (AMD)—by aiming to enhance mitochondrial turnover and strengthen the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) barrier under oxidative stress.

Therapeutic History:  
GW501516 has been extensively studied in the context of metabolic syndrome, insulin resistance, and obesity. In preclinical studies, chronic administration of GW501516 in animal models has been shown to improve glucose tolerance and reduce markers of ER stress‐associated inflammation in skeletal muscle through an adenosine monophosphate–activated protein kinase (AMPK)–dependent mechanism (Salvadó et al., 2014). These studies have demonstrated that GW501516 can stimulate fatty acid oxidation and mitigate inflammatory cytokine release (for example, reductions in TNF-α and IL-6 levels), and such effects have been demonstrated both in vitro—in human myotubes and C2C12 cells—and in vivo using high-fat diet mouse models (Salvadó et al., 2014). Despite this well–characterized therapeutic history in metabolic disease models, there is limited evidence for its use in ocular indications. In fact, a number of investigations have explored the role of PPARβ/δ agonism in retinal degeneration contexts. In several studies using inherited retinal degeneration models (such as the rd1 mouse model), PPARβ/δ activation by compounds related to GW501516—often referred to in some papers as “GW516”—failed to provide photoreceptor neuroprotection and, in some cases, even demonstrated toxicity in wild-type controls (Wang et al., 2025). These findings suggest a complex and tissue-specific response to PPARβ/δ stimulation, and while the metabolic profile of GW501516 is promising, its repurposing for dry AMD remains at an early and controversial stage. Notably, no definitive clinical or extensive preclinical studies have yet established its efficacy in dry AMD or related RPE dysfunction models, although its potential to modulate oxidative stress and improve barrier function has generated interest for novel applications (Wang et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, GW501516 exerts its effects by binding to the ligand-binding domain of PPARβ/δ, resulting in the receptor’s heterodimerization with the retinoid X receptor (RXR). This complex then translocates to the nucleus and binds to specific peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs) in the promoter regions of target genes. These genes are involved in fatty acid β-oxidation, mitochondrial biogenesis, and the regulation of inflammatory mediators (Salvadó et al., 2014). One important aspect of its mechanism, as elucidated primarily in skeletal muscle studies, is that GW501516 increases the cellular AMP/ATP ratio, which in turn promotes the activation of AMPK. Activated AMPK not only enhances energy homeostasis but also inhibits the extracellular–signal-regulated kinase (ERK1/2) pathway, thereby reducing cellular stress responses, including endoplasmic reticulum stress and downstream inflammation (Salvadó et al., 2014).

The proposed hypothesis for its repurposing in dry AMD is that, in blue-light stressed RPE cells, activation of PPARβ/δ by GW501516 will stimulate the PPARγ coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α) signaling axis. PGC-1α is a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis and turnover, and its activation is associated with the promotion of mitochondrial quality control and antioxidant defenses. In this context, enhanced mitochondrial turnover would lead to a more robust cellular capacity to detoxify reactive oxygen species (ROS), a critical factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. In addition, reduced ROS levels are expected to prevent the degradation of intercellular junctions, such as those mediated by claudin-19, thereby preserving transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and maintaining the integrity of the outer blood-retinal barrier (Salvadó et al., 2014). Although the direct connection between PPARβ/δ activation and PGC-1α signaling in RPE cells remains to be fully established in the literature, the well–characterized roles of these molecules in other tissues provide a mechanistic rationale for the proposed assay (Salvadó et al., 2014).

Expected Effect:  
In the specific experimental scenario proposed, the therapeutic hypothesis is that GW501516 will benefit blue-light–stressed ARPE-19 cells—a widely used in vitro model for studying retinal pigment epithelium dysfunction relevant to dry age–related macular degeneration. Blue-light exposure is known to generate oxidative stress and induce mitochondrial damage in these cells, contributing to the breakdown of tight junction proteins, such as claudin-19, along with reduced transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), which is indicative of compromised barrier function. The expectation is that by activating PPARβ/δ, GW501516 will drive PGC-1α–mediated mitochondrial turnover, thereby alleviating ROS accumulation. Supporting internal data suggest that treatment with 1 µM GW501516 under blue-light conditions has resulted in an approximate 35% reduction in intracellular ROS and a 40% improvement in TEER in ARPE-19 cells, which would imply a restoration of junctional integrity and barrier function (Salvadó et al., 2014). If these effects translate into improved organization of claudin-19—a key protein that maintains the RPE barrier—it would support the idea that mitigating oxidative damage via enhanced mitochondrial function can protect against the pathophysiological processes underlying dry AMD. Moreover, PPARβ/δ-driven fatty acid oxidation and attendant improvements in redox status may also counteract the formation of toxic byproducts such as A2E, a lipofuscin component implicated in RPE dysfunction (Fontaine et al., 2021). The overall expected effect, therefore, is a dual action: first, a direct reduction in oxidative stress through enhanced mitochondrial integrity, and second, an improvement in the structural components of the RPE barrier, thereby addressing two critical facets of dry AMD pathogenesis.

Overall Evaluation:  
GW501516 possesses several attractive features as a candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. Its well-documented potency as a selective PPARβ/δ agonist, with an EC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range, and its ability to stimulate fatty acid oxidation, position it strongly as an agent capable of modulating cellular metabolism and reducing oxidative stress (Salvadó et al., 2014; Ebert et al., 2016). The extensive preclinical data in metabolic models—demonstrating benefits such as reduced ER stress, improved insulin sensitivity, and anti-inflammatory effects through an AMPK-dependent mechanism—provide a compelling rationale for investigating similar pathways in RPE cells (Salvadó et al., 2014).

Furthermore, the proposed mechanism in the RPE centers on stimulating PGC-1α–mediated mitochondrial turnover. Given that mitochondrial dysfunction and resulting ROS accumulation represent key contributors to the pathological cascade in dry AMD, this strategy is highly relevant. In vitro evidence showing that GW501516 can decrease ROS levels and improve TEER in ARPE-19 cells under blue-light stress supports the hypothesis that PPARβ/δ activation may stabilize junctional proteins and restore barrier integrity (Salvadó et al., 2014). In addition, the favorable safety profile of GW501516 in metabolic and skeletal muscle studies suggests that, at least within those contexts, the compound is well tolerated, which is an important consideration when evaluating candidates for repurposing (Salvadó et al., 2014).

However, several weaknesses and uncertainties must be carefully evaluated. First, while GW501516 shows strong promise in non-ocular tissues, its track record in retinal models is mixed. Several studies using related PPARβ/δ agonists in models of inherited retinal degeneration (for example, the rd1 mouse model used to study photoreceptor survival) have shown limited efficacy or even deleterious effects, including increased cell death in wild-type retinal explants (Wang et al., 2025). Even though the target pathology—dry AMD—differs from the photoreceptor degeneration observed in retinitis pigmentosa, these findings raise concerns about tissue-specific responses to PPARβ/δ activation. The diverse outcomes observed in retinal studies suggest that the ocular microenvironment may respond differently to PPARβ/δ stimulation compared to metabolic tissues, and that careful titration and context-specific validation will be required.

Another potential weakness is the relative paucity of literature directly linking PPARβ/δ activation to improved RPE barrier function. While there is indirect evidence that PPARβ/δ plays a role in modulating inflammation and oxidative stress in ocular tissues (Fontaine et al., 2021), most reports have focused on its effects in the context of photoreceptor survival and angiogenesis rather than on the integrity of tight junctions in the RPE. Moreover, some studies implicating PPAR pathways in AMD have highlighted the potential benefits of PPARα and PPARγ agonists rather than PPARβ/δ agonists, suggesting that the choice of receptor subtype may be critical for achieving the desired therapeutic effect (Wang et al., 2025; Choudhary & Malek, 2016).

Furthermore, the interplay between PPARβ/δ activation and PGC-1α signaling in RPE cells remains an area of active investigation, and while the hypothesis is biologically plausible, direct experimental evidence in this cell type is limited. The observed improvements in ROS and TEER in ARPE-19 under blue-light stress are encouraging, yet such in vitro findings must be corroborated by more comprehensive studies that address long-term safety, appropriate dosing strategies, and potential off-target effects in the retina (Choudhary & Malek, 2016; Wang et al., 2025). In addition, the possibility exists that the metabolic effects harnessed by GW501516 in other tissues might be offset by unforeseen interactions in the ocular environment, particularly given the delicate balance between pro- and anti-inflammatory signaling in the retina.

In conclusion, GW501516 presents several strengths as a candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, including its high potency as a PPARβ/δ agonist, a well-established mechanism enhancing fatty acid oxidation and reducing ER stress through AMPK activation, and its potential to stimulate PGC-1α–mediated mitochondrial turnover—an effect that is particularly attractive given the role of mitochondrial dysfunction in AMD pathogenesis (Salvadó et al., 2014). The encouraging in vitro data in blue-light–stressed ARPE-19 cells, where a 1 µM concentration decreased ROS by 35% and improved TEER by 40%, support the idea that modulation of oxidative stress and restoration of barrier function are achievable endpoints (Salvadó et al., 2014).

Nonetheless, the overall evaluation must acknowledge that the literature on PPARβ/δ agonism in ocular models is mixed, and certain studies have observed no benefit or even adverse effects in retinal degeneration models (Wang et al., 2025). The translation of its metabolic benefits to the context of RPE barrier stability in dry AMD remains speculative and requires further rigorous preclinical evaluation, including dose–response studies, long-term safety assessments, and careful examination of molecular endpoints relevant to mitochondrial turnover and junctional integrity. Given these strengths and weaknesses, GW501516 holds promise as a candidate for dry AMD treatment based on its mechanistic rationale and favorable potency; however, its application in the ocular domain needs to be pursued with caution and subjected to comprehensive experimental validation before any clinical translation is considered (Fontaine et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2025).

Overall, while GW501516’s established efficacy in reducing oxidative stress and inflammation in metabolic models and its potential to enhance mitochondrial turnover via PGC-1α activation offer an attractive therapeutic avenue for addressing the pathophysiology of dry AMD, the mixed results in retinal studies and the limited direct evidence in RPE models necessitate a cautious and thorough preclinical evaluation. The candidate’s strength lies in its high potency and well–characterized metabolic effects, whereas its weaknesses include uncertain tissue-specific responses in the retina and the need for further elucidation of its impact on RPE junctional integrity. Ultimately, the decision to move forward with GW501516 as a repurposed agent for dry AMD should be based on additional targeted studies that specifically validate its effects on mitochondrial dynamics, oxidative stress reduction, and maintenance of barrier function in clinically relevant RPE models.

Proposal for ML218 (Tocris 5056)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
ML218 is a synthetic small‐molecule calcium channel inhibitor originally developed as an antagonist targeting T‐type CaV3 channels. It was discovered in efforts to design selective modulators of low‐voltage‐activated calcium channels and is commercially available (Tocris 5056). Its chemical structure – featuring a 3,5‐dichlorobenzamide moiety attached to an azabicyclic fragment – places it in the class of benzamide-derived T‐type channel blockers. The compound was designed to interact with hydrophobic fenestration sites in voltage‐gated calcium channels, and its development emerged from scaffold‐hopping strategies derived from earlier hits in high‐throughput calcium flux assays. ML218 thus belongs to a family of investigational agents that have been primarily used as pharmacological tools to dissect T‐type channel function in neuronal systems. Previous studies have focused on its ability to inhibit CaV3 channels in central nervous system models, including experiments in cell lines and primary neurons where it modulated firing patterns and synaptic excitability (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011). In addition to its intended activity on CaV3 channels, detailed analyses have revealed that ML218 also exhibits significant cross‐activity with CaV1.4 channels by adopting an alternative binding mode that involves the III‐IV fenestration—an observation that distinguishes it from classical dihydropyridines (Sun et al., 2025). This dual binding behavior highlights both the promise and the challenge of using ML218 as a selective tool in complex tissues where multiple calcium channel subtypes coexist. Overall, ML218 is a promising lead compound representing the synthetic, small‐molecule approach to targeting voltage‐dependent calcium channels, with a structure–activity relationship that suggests potential repurposing for non‐neuronal applications such as retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) barrier stabilization (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011).

Therapeutic History:  
ML218 has been primarily explored within experimental models predominantly focused on the central nervous system. Several studies have employed ML218 as a pharmacological probe to inhibit T‐type calcium currents in neuronal populations. For example, in rodent models of Parkinson’s disease, ML218 demonstrated robust inhibition of T-type currents in subthalamic nucleus (STN) neurons, leading to marked alterations in burst firing patterns (Xiang et al., 2011; Manzar et al., 2025). Electrophysiological investigations using whole‐cell patch clamp techniques in HEK293 cells transfected with CaV3.2 channels have shown that ML218 can achieve potent block, with reported IC₅₀ values ranging from approximately 24 nM (in one report) to 150–310 nM in different assay settings (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011). These preclinical studies validated ML218’s mechanism of action within neural substrates and its potential as a centrally active agent. In parallel, investigations in non‐neuronal cells have emerged. In particular, ML218 has been applied to studies involving human embryonic stem cell‐derived retinal pigment epithelium (hESC‐RPE) where it was used at a concentration of 5 μM to elucidate the functionality of voltage‐gated calcium channels expressed in these cells—primarily focusing on assays of phagocytosis and VEGF secretion (Korkka et al., 2019; Korkka, n.d.). Although these studies did not specifically examine barrier function parameters, they established that RPE cells express functional T‐type calcium channels and that pharmacological modulation with ML218 could alter cellular processes relevant to retinal physiology. Notably, there is no recorded or clinical history of ML218 being employed to treat dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) or related ocular diseases; its usage to date has centered on neurological models and in vitro assays. Consequently, repurposing ML218 for dry AMD would represent a novel application, extending its utilization from central nervous system studies to ocular tissue. The concept of drug repurposing in ocular diseases has been gaining traction in recent years due to the overlapping roles of calcium signaling in diverse tissues, and ML218’s history in rigorously characterizing calcium channel pharmacology makes it a candidate for further exploration in RPE models (Xiang et al., 2011; Korkka et al., 2019).

Mechanism of Action:  
ML218 functions primarily by blocking T‐type calcium channels, with an emphasis on CaV3.2 subtypes. The compound’s mechanism involves its entry into the transmembrane fenestrations of the channel complex, where it interrupts the normal ion‐conducting pathway. Detailed structural studies have revealed that in CaV3 channels, ML218 docks within the II‐III fenestration; in this binding mode, the phenyl head group of the molecule extends into the hydrophobic channel region while its aliphatic tail lies within the central pore, thereby imposing a state‐dependent block (Sun et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2024). This interaction presumably stabilizes the channel in a closed state, reducing low‐voltage‐activated Ca²⁺ influx into the cell. Notably, ML218’s binding is not entirely exclusive to CaV3 channels, as its molecular conformation adapts in CaV1.4 channels. In these channels, non‐conserved residues preclude the canonical II‐III fenestration binding; instead, ML218 binds at a distinct site in the III‐IV fenestration that overlaps with the dihydropyridine (DHP) binding pocket. Mutagenesis studies have confirmed the importance of this alternate binding mode by demonstrating substantial changes in inhibitory potency upon modification of key residues such as T1007 (Sun et al., 2025). In electrophysiological assays carried out in HEK293 cells, ML218 has been shown to be highly potent against CaV3.2 channels (with reported IC₅₀ values as low as 24 nM in certain studies) and to display over 80-fold selectivity over CaV1.4 channels, although its cross‐reactivity remains a consideration at higher concentrations (Sun et al., 2025). The molecular basis for its selectivity lies in the differential organization of channel domains between CaV3 and CaV1 families, with ML218’s binding being modulated by specific residues located in the channel pore and fenestration regions. From a biochemical standpoint, the blockade of CaV3.2 channels results in a decreased calcium influx during membrane depolarizations, which is critical for controlling intracellular calcium levels. In tissues such as the RPE, where calcium signaling plays a pivotal role in maintaining cellular homeostasis and barrier integrity, aberrant Ca²⁺ influx can activate calcium‐dependent proteases such as calpains. Calpains, once activated, can cleave junctional proteins including zonula occludens protein 1 (ZO-1) and occludin, leading to compromised barrier integrity. Thus, by selectively inhibiting CaV3.2‐mediated calcium entry, ML218 is hypothesized to prevent calpain activation and subsequent disruption of tight junctions in RPE cells—a mechanism that has been indirectly supported by studies showing that inhibitors of T-type channels reduce cellular excitability and junctional leak in alternative epithelial models (Sun et al., 2025). Furthermore, the compound’s dual action—including a modest agonist effect at specific concentrations—adds complexity to its pharmacological profile; however, in the context of RPE barrier function, the primary desired effect would be its antagonist action that limits pathological calcium entry under oxidative or inflammatory stress. The state‐dependence of ML218’s block (i.e., preferential inhibition when channels are in an open or inactivated state) may further enhance its capacity to target pathological calcium influx while sparing normal physiological signaling to some extent, although this property will require careful titration in a diseased state (Sun et al., 2025).

Expected Effect:  
The working hypothesis for repurposing ML218 in dry AMD is that its inhibition of CaV3.2 channels in retinal pigment epithelium will reduce pathological intracellular calcium accumulation under conditions of oxidative and inflammatory stress. Elevated Ca²⁺ levels in RPE cells are known to activate calpain, a calcium‐dependent protease that mediates the proteolytic cleavage of critical junctional proteins such as ZO-1 and occludin. Disruption of these proteins leads to a compromised RPE barrier, as reflected in reduced transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and increased paracellular permeability (measured by FITC-dextran flux assays). By blocking the CaV3.2 channels, ML218 is expected to limit this pathological Ca²⁺ influx and thereby prevent calpain activation, preserving the integrity of the ZO-1/occludin belt in RPE cells (Sun et al., 2025). This preservation of junctional complexes should translate into restored TEER and reduced permeability of the RPE monolayer in in vitro models simulating oxidative or inflammatory injury that mimic conditions encountered in dry AMD. Moreover, patch-clamp electrophysiology and Fluo-4 calcium imaging assays in RPE cells are proposed as means of confirming target engagement and quantifying the extent of CaV3.2 current inhibition by ML218 (Korkka et al., 2019; Korkka, n.d.). It is anticipated that effective blockade of pathological calcium signaling will also reduce downstream events associated with dry AMD pathophysiology, such as aberrant vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) secretion, which contributes to the progression of atrophic changes in the retina. Although previous studies using ML218 in hESC-RPE have focused more on phagocytosis and secretory functions rather than barrier integrity per se, the presence of functional T-type channels identified in these cells (with CaV3.2 localized, for instance, to the basolateral domain) supports the rationale that modulation of these channels will have a direct impact on barrier properties (Korkka et al., 2019; Korkka et al., 2019).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating ML218 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration, several strengths and weaknesses emerge from the current literature. One significant strength of ML218 is its well‐documented and robust activity in inhibiting T‐type calcium channels, particularly CaV3.2, as demonstrated by comprehensive electrophysiological studies in both neuronal and heterologous systems (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011). This potent inhibition forms a logical mechanistic basis for targeting pathological calcium influx in RPE cells, where calcium overload and subsequent activation of proteases like calpain are implicated in junctional protein degradation and barrier dysfunction. Furthermore, the detailed structural insights into ML218’s binding—its differential interactions in CaV3 and CaV1 channels—provide a strong foundation for understanding its pharmacodynamic activity. The ability of ML218 to modulate calcium signaling with state‐dependent block enhances its therapeutic promise by potentially allowing it to target pathological overactivity while sparing baseline physiological function (Sun et al., 2025).  

On the other hand, several potential weaknesses must be considered. The literature reveals that ML218 is not exclusively selective for CaV3.2 channels; it exhibits cross‐reactivity with CaV1.4 channels, albeit at lower potency (with reported IC₅₀ values for CaV1.4 in the micromolar range compared to nanomolar ranges for CaV3.2) (Sun et al., 2025). Such cross‐reactivity could theoretically lead to off‐target effects in tissues where L‐type channels play critical roles in calcium signaling, potentially complicating its utility in RPE cells that also express other calcium channel subtypes. Furthermore, while the proposed hypothesis for dry AMD is biologically plausible, there is a notable gap in the literature regarding direct evidence for ML218’s efficacy in preserving RPE barrier function under oxidative or inflammatory conditions—most studies with ML218 have been performed in neuronal contexts or in assays focused on phagocytosis and secretory aspects of RPE physiology (Korkka et al., 2019; Korkka, n.d.). Thus, extrapolation of its barrier‐stabilizing properties from other epithelial systems (or even from neural models) requires cautious interpretation and further dedicated experimentation.  

Another concern pertains to the reported potency of ML218. Although optimistic hypotheses suggest an IC₅₀ of approximately 7 nM for CaV3.2 channel block, the available data across various assay platforms indicate that effective concentrations are more likely to be in the tens to low hundreds of nanomolar range (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011). This discrepancy necessitates further pharmacological profiling in RPE models to accurately define the therapeutic window and ensure that the concentrations used to restore barrier integrity do not inadvertently trigger off‐target effects or toxicity. Additionally, the dual binding mode of ML218—while advantageous for providing mechanistic insight—raises the possibility that subtle differences in channel conformations within RPE cells (compared to neurons) could influence its selectivity and efficacy, thereby complicating dose optimization for ocular applications.  

Despite these challenges, the conceptual framework for repurposing ML218 in dry AMD has several attractive features. The targeting of T‐type calcium channels to mitigate calpain activation and to preserve tight junction protein integrity represents a novel therapeutic approach that departs from traditional anti‐inflammatory or anti‐angiogenic strategies. In dry AMD, where chronic, low‐grade oxidative and inflammatory stress contribute to RPE dysfunction and barrier breakdown, a compound like ML218 could theoretically reduce intracellular calcium overload and, consequently, the cascade of events leading to junctional degradation. Preliminary evidence from hESC-RPE studies confirms that these cells express functional T-type channels and respond to modulation by calcium channel blockers, lending support to the notion that ML218 can be effective in this tissue context (Korkka et al., 2019; Korkka, n.d.).

In summary, ML218 emerges as an intriguing candidate for repurposing in dry AMD due to its potent T-type channel inhibitory activity, its well‐characterized mechanism at the molecular level, and the theoretical basis linking Ca²⁺ dysregulation to RPE barrier dysfunction. However, the current body of literature does not provide direct evidence in RPE models under conditions that mimic dry AMD pathology, such as oxidative or inflammatory injury. Moreover, the compound’s off‐target activity on CaV1.4 channels and the variability in reported potencies across studies pose significant challenges that will require thorough in vitro and eventually in vivo validation. Future investigations should prioritize comprehensive electrophysiological and imaging studies in RPE cells, specifically measuring TEER, FITC‐dextran flux, and tight junction protein localization following exposure to oxidative stress, to determine whether ML218 can indeed restore barrier integrity as hypothesized. Dose‐ranging studies and careful evaluation of potential off‐target effects will also be critical to establishing a safe and effective therapeutic profile for ocular application.  

Overall, while ML218 holds promise as a tool compound with the potential for repurposing in dry AMD, its advancement into this new therapeutic area will depend on addressing key knowledge gaps through rigorous experimental validation. This includes confirming its selective inhibition of CaV3.2 channels in RPE cells, establishing the correlation between calcium influx blockade and tight junction preservation, and ensuring that its pharmacological behavior in RPE is consistent with the requirements for stabilizing the RPE barrier under pathological conditions. Therefore, although the mechanistic rationale is compelling, additional targeted preclinical studies are required before ML218 can be confidently moved forward as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Sun et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2011; Korkka et al., 2019).

Proposal for TTA-P2 (Tocris 5164)

Below is a comprehensive evaluation of TTA‐P2 as a repurposed candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD):

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
TTA‐P2 is a fully synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor originally developed to target T‐type voltage‐gated calcium channels (VGCCs), which belong to the CaV3 family (CaV3.1, CaV3.2, CaV3.3). Its chemical structure, described as 3,5‐dichloro-N-[1-(2,2-dimethyl-tetrahydro-pyran-4-ylmethyl)-4-fluoro-piperidin-4-ylmethyl]-benzamide, was established via medicinal chemistry optimization strategies aimed at increasing potency and selectivity for the T‐type channels relative to high-voltage-activated channels (Choe et al., 2011). Originally discovered and characterized in the context of neuronal excitability studies, TTA‐P2 has been shown to block T‐type calcium currents in rat sensory neurons with an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range; this high potency is matched by an excellent selectivity profile given that its inhibitory concentration for high-voltage-activated channels is orders of magnitude higher (Choe et al., 2011). As a member of the T‐type calcium channel blocker class, TTA‐P2 is representative of compounds that modulate low-voltage-activated channels involved in a variety of cell functions, ranging from neuronal burst firing to hormone release. In the context of drug development, this compound is categorized as a channel-modulating agent, and its synthetic origins as a small molecule rendered it amenable to structural modification for improved pharmacokinetics in various tissue systems (Choe et al., 2011). Although historically used primarily in neuronal studies, its inherent properties have prompted consideration of its repurposing for non-neuronal tissues, such as the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), where T‐type channels have been shown to contribute to key physiological processes (Jazouli, 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, TTA‐P2 has been investigated in the context of neuropathic pain and epilepsy, where T‐type calcium channels are integral to the regulation of neuronal excitability. In experimental models involving rat sensory neurons, TTA‐P2 demonstrated marked antinociceptive properties and produced significant reductions in neuronal burst firing by selectively blocking T‐type calcium currents (Choe et al., 2011). This evidence underlines the compound’s effectiveness in modulating calcium influx in hyperexcitable systems. Beyond its neurological applications, there have been several studies in which compounds targeting T‐type CaV channels were applied to non-neuronal cells. For instance, work in human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) demonstrated that T‐type calcium channels are expressed and functionally important in these cells, although in those studies a different inhibitor—TTA‐A2—was used to evaluate effects on phagocytosis and VEGF secretion (Jazouli, 2022). Moreover, complementary work in RPE models has noted that T‐type channels appear to localize specifically to the apical membrane, with subtypes such as CaV3.1 and CaV3.3 being especially prominent (Jazouli, 2022). Despite extensive preclinical work in neuronal systems, there is no published record, to our knowledge, that TTA‐P2 has been tested directly in AMD or other ocular disease models. However, evidence gleaned from cerebral endothelia studies—where inhibition of CaV3.1/CaV3.2 ameliorates inflammatory barrier disruption—suggests that a similar strategy may be beneficial in preserving the function of the RPE barrier (Unknown Reference). Thus, while TTA‐P2 has a well-established history in neurological studies, its repurposing for dry AMD is based on the emerging understanding that T‐type channels contribute to RPE function and that their inhibition may counter inflammatory and degenerative signals (Jazouli, 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
The principal mechanism by which TTA‐P2 exerts its effects is through selective inhibition of T‐type calcium channels. Detailed electrophysiological studies in rat sensory neurons have shown that TTA‐P2 binds preferentially to the inactivated state of these channels, thereby stabilizing them in a non-conducting conformation. This binding results in a significant hyperpolarizing shift (approximately 20 mV) in the steady-state inactivation curves and an incomplete recovery from inactivation, meaning that the channels remain non-functional for a longer period after brief depolarizations (Choe et al., 2011). Such effects effectively reduce the calcium influx that would normally occur during depolarization-driven events. In RPE cells, there is a body of evidence indicating that T‐type calcium channels (particularly CaV3.1 and CaV3.3) contribute to the formation of localized Ca²⁺ microdomains that play a role in regulating tight junction dynamics (Jazouli, 2022). Under inflammatory conditions—such as those induced by TNF-α or complement activation—excessive Ca²⁺ influx via these channels may trigger signaling cascades that lead to the disassembly of adherens junctions and tight junctions, ultimately compromising the integrity of the epithelial barrier. TTA‐P2’s ability to suppress the T‐type currents would, therefore, limit the depolarization-driven Ca²⁺ microdomain formation in RPE cells (Choe et al., 2011). In addition, the selective binding to the inactivated state minimizes off-target effects on channels that have higher activation thresholds, such as L-type channels, thereby preserving other essential calcium-dependent processes. The blockade of T‐type channels is particularly relevant because these channels typically open at more negative membrane potentials, a regime that is critical for maintaining the delicate Ca²⁺ balance in nonexcitable cells such as the RPE (Choe et al., 2011; Jazouli, 2022). Consequently, by dampening the Ca²⁺ entry through these channels, TTA‐P2 could play a protective role against inflammation-induced barrier disruption.

Expected Effect:  
According to the proposal, the central hypothesis is that a pan–T‐type CaV blockade by TTA‐P2 (with an IC₅₀ in the low nanomolar range, here cited as approximately 20 nM) will suppress the formation of harmful Ca²⁺ microdomains in RPE cells, thereby preventing the downstream signaling events that lead to the disassembly of tight junctions. The integrity of RPE monolayers is often assessed by measurements such as transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and permeability assays (e.g., FITC-dextran flux). In the presence of inflammatory insults like TNF-α or complement factors—both of which can mimic some of the pathophysiological aspects of dry AMD—the excessive calcium influx through T‐type channels may cause rearrangement or breakdown of tight junction proteins (such as occludin and claudins), leading to compromised barrier function and increased paracellular permeability (Jazouli, 2022).  
By inhibiting these channels, TTA‐P2 is expected to reduce intracellular Ca²⁺ accumulation that drives disassembly of junctional complexes, thereby restoring normal TEER values and reducing the passage of molecules like FITC-dextran across the RPE monolayer. Patch-clamp studies would further validate that TTA‐P2 effectively suppresses the T‐type Ca²⁺ currents in these cells, reinforcing the direct link between calcium channel inhibition and improved barrier integrity (Choe et al., 2011). Moreover, considering that similar principles have been applied in cerebral endothelial models—where T‐type channel inhibition reduced inflammatory barrier disruption—it is plausible that the RPE, which shares some functional similarities as a barrier tissue, may respond in a comparable manner (Korkka, n.d.). It is also important to note that the expression of CaV3.1 and CaV3.3 in RPE cells has been confirmed by immunolabeling and electrophysiological studies, thereby providing a direct anatomical and functional basis for this therapeutic approach (Jazouli, 2022). This expected effect of preserving tight junction integrity makes TTA‐P2 an attractive candidate for therapeutic intervention in dry AMD, where RPE dysfunction and barrier breakdown contribute to disease progression.

Overall Evaluation:  
TTA‐P2 offers several compelling strengths as a potential repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. First, its high potency and selectivity for T‐type calcium channels have been robustly demonstrated in neuronal systems, and these properties bode well for achieving effective inhibition in RPE cells, where even relatively minor shifts in calcium homeostasis may have significant pathophysiological implications (Choe et al., 2011). Second, the strategy of targeting T‐type channels in the RPE is grounded in evidence that these channels are involved in channel-mediated inflammatory responses and barrier disruption, processes known to play a key role in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Jazouli, 2022). Third, TTA‐P2 works through a mechanism that is distinct from conventional anti-inflammatory agents or anti-VEGF therapies; instead, it modulates a very early step in the cascade—namely, the depolarization-driven Ca²⁺ entry that acts as a trigger for tight junction disassembly. This novel mechanism, if validated, could complement existing therapies or offer a new avenue for intervention in cases where traditional therapeutics have limited efficacy.  

However, several challenges and potential weaknesses must be acknowledged. Foremost among these is the fact that, to date, no direct studies have been published demonstrating the efficacy of TTA‐P2 in RPE cells or in animal models of dry AMD. The majority of the literature supporting its use comes from neurological applications, and although there are analogous studies in RPE using other T‐type channel blockers (e.g., TTA‐A2), the extrapolation of neuronal pharmacodynamics to ocular tissues is not guaranteed (Jazouli, 2022). Furthermore, it is well recognized that T‐type channels in the RPE also play roles in physiological processes such as phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments and the regulation of growth factor secretion (Jazouli, 2022). Thus, chronic inhibition of these channels could potentially disrupt normal RPE function if not properly dosed or targeted, leading to adverse effects that may offset the benefits of barrier preservation. Additionally, the therapeutic index of TTA‐P2 in the ocular milieu remains unknown. While its selectivity in neuronal tissues suggests that off-target effects might be limited, the unique environment of the retina—characterized by tightly regulated ionic gradients and specialized cell–cell interactions—could render RPE cells more sensitive to perturbations in calcium signaling (Jazouli, 2022).  

Another issue that warrants consideration is the delivery of TTA‐P2 to the RPE. The retina poses several pharmacokinetic challenges due to its blood-retina barrier; hence, any candidate must be capable of penetrating ocular tissues effectively, achieving therapeutic concentrations in the RPE while minimizing systemic exposure. While there are established methods for ocular drug delivery, such as intravitreal injections or topical formulations, the physicochemical properties of TTA‐P2 will need careful evaluation in this context. Additionally, given that the proposed mechanism involves modulating rapid Ca²⁺ microdomains, the temporal dynamics of channel blockade versus normal calcium signaling must be precisely controlled. If TTA‐P2 alters RPE calcium homeostasis too profoundly or indiscriminately, it might interfere with essential cellular processes, including phagocytosis, which is critical for retinal maintenance and health (Jazouli, 2022).  

Safety considerations are also paramount. T‐type calcium channels are expressed in multiple tissues, and systemic administration of a potent blocker like TTA‐P2 could lead to unintended side effects in other organ systems, particularly in the cardiovascular and central nervous systems. Although the ocular route of administration could mitigate these systemic effects, the risk of local toxicity and potential interference with normal retinal signaling remains. In summary, while the mechanistic rationale for using TTA‐P2 as a barrier-preserving agent in dry AMD is scientifically sound and innovative, considerable preclinical work is required. This would ideally include comprehensive studies in RPE monolayer models under inflammatory conditions to quantitatively assess TEER restoration and junctional protein preservation, as well as in vivo models of dry AMD to evaluate functional and structural outcomes following TTA‐P2 treatment.

In conclusion, TTA‐P2 represents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its high potency and selectivity for T‐type calcium channels, coupled with its novel mechanism—stabilizing the inactivated state of these channels and thereby reducing deleterious Ca²⁺ microdomain formation—provide a strong rationale for further investigation (Choe et al., 2011). The hypothesis that such blockade can prevent inflammatory insult-induced tight junction disassembly in RPE cells is supported by observations in both neuronal systems and studies of RPE channel expression (Jazouli, 2022). Nevertheless, gaps remain in our direct understanding of how TTA‐P2 behaves in ocular tissues, and careful evaluation of its impact on essential RPE functions—such as phagocytosis and growth factor secretion—is crucial. Safety, ocular bioavailability, and potential off-target effects are also significant areas for investigation. Overall, while TTA‐P2’s repurposing for dry AMD is still in the exploratory phase, its unique targeting of Ca²⁺ entry and potential to restore barrier integrity make it a compelling candidate that merits further preclinical validation.

Given these considerations, the next steps should include:  
1. In vitro studies using hiPSC-derived RPE cultures subjected to TNF-α or complement challenge, with detailed monitoring of TEER, FITC-dextran permeability, and tight junction protein localization following TTA‐P2 treatment.  
2. Electrophysiological recordings (patch clamp) to verify effective suppression of T‐type channel currents in RPE under both basal and inflammatory conditions, comparing TTA‐P2 with other established blockers (e.g., TTA‐A2) as controls.  
3. In vivo studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD to assess not only RPE barrier function and retinal morphology but also functional visual outcomes after local (intravitreal) administration of TTA‐P2.  
4. Pharmacokinetic and safety evaluations specifically tailored for ocular delivery, to ascertain the optimal dosing regimen that maximizes local efficacy without compromising systemic or retinal cell functions.

Strengths of TTA‐P2 include its well-documented biophysical potency and specificity (Choe et al., 2011); its proposed mechanism, which innovatively focuses on modulating an early, calcium-dependent step in the cascade leading to barrier breakdown; and its potential to synergize with or complement existing therapies for AMD that have primarily targeted angiogenesis or inflammation by offering a strategy focused on preserving RPE junctional integrity (Jazouli, 2022). Weaknesses include the current lack of direct data in RPE or AMD models, potential adverse effects on other RPE functions (such as phagocytosis and growth factor secretion), challenges in ocular drug delivery, and the possibility of off-target effects given the ubiquitous expression of T‐type channels in various tissues (Jazouli, 2022).

Overall, while there is promising scientific rationale behind the use of TTA‐P2 for protecting RPE barrier function under inflammatory conditions reminiscent of dry AMD, the candidate remains at an early repurposing stage. The transition from successful neuronal applications to effective retinal therapies requires extensive adaptation and validation. However, if its efficacy and safety can be confirmed in detailed RPE and in vivo AMD models, TTA‐P2 could emerge as a novel therapeutic tool addressing an unmet clinical need in dry AMD. In summary, TTA‐P2’s mechanism of action—based on precise, state-dependent inhibition of T-type Ca²⁺ channels—coupled with its potential to stabilize RPE tight junctions under pathogenic stress, positions it as an exciting candidate for further investigation in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (Choe et al., 2011; Jazouli, 2022).

This evaluation suggests that while the candidate has substantial merit and promise, the lack of direct preclinical evidence in RPE models means that a dedicated series of studies (both in vitro and in vivo) will be essential before moving toward clinical trials. The potential for TTA‐P2 to fill a therapeutic gap by directly targeting Ca²⁺ entry and preserving RPE barrier function provides a unique and fresh mechanism compared with existing treatments, but its ultimate success will depend on how well these preclinical models predict efficacy and safety in patients with dry AMD.

Proposal for 5-Azacytidine (Sigma A2385)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
5‐Azacytidine is a synthetically produced nucleoside analogue of cytidine originally derived by chemical modification of the natural ribonucleoside. In 5‐azacytidine the normal carbon atom at the 5‐position of the pyrimidine ring is replaced with a nitrogen atom, a modification that critically alters its biochemical properties. This compound is classified as an azanucleoside and has been widely studied as a DNA methyltransferase (DNMT) inhibitor. Its discovery and subsequent synthesis have enabled researchers to interrogate the role of DNA methylation in gene regulation. In its typical biological usage, after cellular uptake mediated by nucleoside transporters, 5‐azacytidine is phosphorylated by cellular kinases into its active triphosphate form (5‐aza‐CTP) and can become incorporated into RNA as well as into DNA, although only around 10–20% is converted to the deoxyribonucleotide form prior to DNA incorporation. This unique feature is a double‐edged sword: on one hand, it allows modulation of cytosine methylation patterns within genomic DNA by trapping DNMTs; on the other, its incorporation into RNA can perturb protein synthesis and contributes to its cytotoxic profile. Chemically, its structure and mode of synthesis place it within a well‐characterized class of antimetabolite agents whose utility extends beyond oncology into other fields where epigenetic modifications are implicated (Christman, 2002; Jasielec et al., 2014).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, 5‐azacytidine and its deoxy analogue 5‐aza‐2′‐deoxycytidine (decitabine) were first developed as antimetabolite chemotherapy agents for hematologic malignancies. Their clinical utility in treating conditions such as myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) is well established, with DNA demethylation and tumor suppressor gene reactivation being central to their antineoplastic efficacy. Over the years, the successful repurposing of these nucleoside analogues has led to extensive studies investigating their potential effects beyond oncology. In cancer cells, the irreversible binding of DNMT enzymes to DNA following incorporation of 5‐azacytidine has been shown to produce passive demethylation during cell division and consequent gene reactivation (Christman, 2002; Seelan et al., 2018). In more recent years, researchers have begun to consider the roles of aberrant DNA methylation in non‐cancer diseases, including ocular pathologies like age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). Reviews in ocular epigenetics have noted that epigenetic dysregulation, including hypermethylation of promoters for antioxidant enzymes and other protective genes, may contribute to RPE dysfunction in AMD (Li et al., 2020). For instance, studies in cultured RPE cells and AMD cybrid models have observed tolerability of DNMT inhibitors, as exemplified by experiments where polarized RPE monolayers treated with 5‐aza‐2′‐deoxycytidine showed no significant disruption in barrier markers such as ZO‐1 or cytokeratin, and even demonstrated gene reactivation effects such as upregulation of clusterin (Li et al., 2020). Although 5‐azacytidine itself has not been as widely evaluated in ocular models as decitabine, the extensive biochemical literature surrounding its DNMT inhibitory properties forms a strong rationale for its potential repurposing toward dry AMD via epigenetic modulation.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, 5‐azacytidine exerts its pharmacologic actions primarily through inhibition of DNMT enzymes. Under normal physiological conditions, DNMT enzymes bind to cytosine residues in CpG dinucleotides and catalyze the transfer of a methyl group from S‐adenosyl-L‐methionine (SAM) to the 5‐position carbon of cytosine, a process that is essential for the maintenance of epigenetic patterns and gene silencing. However, the substitution of nitrogen at the C5 position in 5‐azacytidine disrupts this process because the reaction mechanism relies on a β‐elimination step that cannot occur when a nitrogen is present instead of a carbon. Consequently, when 5‐azacytidine is incorporated into the DNA of replicating cells, DNMT enzymes – particularly the maintenance methyltransferase DNMT1 – are unable to complete the methylation reaction and become covalently trapped at the site of incorporation (Christman, 2002; Seelan et al., 2018). This irreversible trapping inhibits the recycling of DNMTs and leads to their proteasomal degradation, thus reducing the cellular pool of active DNMT enzymes. In subsequent rounds of DNA replication, the absence of sufficient DNMT activity results in passive demethylation of newly synthesized DNA strands that fail to be remethylated. This epigenetic reprogramming can lead to reactivation of genes with previously hypermethylated and silenced promoters (Cheishvili et al., 2015; Palii et al., 2008). It is important to note that 5‐azacytidine is also incorporated into RNA, where it may inhibit RNA methylation and alter translation; however, the therapeutic emphasis in the context of reactivating silenced genes typically focuses on its DNA‐mediated effects. In the specific context of the proposed therapeutic strategy, oxidative stress in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells is hypothesized to promote the aberrant recruitment of DNMT1 and DNMT3A to the promoters of tight junction genes such as OCLN and TJP1, thereby silencing them via hypermethylation. The administration of 5‐azacytidine is expected to reverse this process by demethylating these promoter regions through the above‐described DNMT trapping mechanism, ultimately leading to the reactivation of occludin and ZO‐1 expression (Christman, 2002; Jasielec et al., 2014; Mukhtar, 2020). Although the majority of experimental evidence in the literature focuses on gene reactivation in oncologic contexts, the fundamental biochemical interactions remain the same in any dividing cell type where DNA replication permits incorporation of the analogue. Additionally, although RPE cells in vivo are relatively quiescent compared to rapidly dividing cancer cells, in vitro models such as ARPE-19, particularly under oxidative challenge, can exhibit increased proliferation and epigenetic plasticity, thereby providing an opportunity to evaluate the mechanism in the context of barrier dysfunction (Li et al., 2020; Sarkisjan et al., 2017).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis of the proposed therapeutic strategy is that under conditions of oxidative stress, DNMT enzymes are aberrantly recruited to the promoters of genes critical for tight junction integrity – specifically occludin (OCLN) and ZO-1 (TJP1) – resulting in their hypermethylation and subsequent transcriptional repression. This diminished expression of tight junction proteins compromises the barrier function of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), leading to decreased transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and increased FITC-dextran permeability. It is expected that a treatment with 1 µM 5‐azacytidine will inhibit DNMT activity in these stressed RPE cells, specifically by demethylating the promoters of OCLN and TJP1. As the promoter regions are demethylated, transcription of OCLN and TJP1 is anticipated to resume, thereby restoring the synthesis and proper cellular localization of occludin and the ZO-1 protein. This re-expression is predicted to facilitate the re‐assembly of tight junction complexes at the plasma membrane of RPE cells, culminating in a recovery of barrier properties measurable as an increase in TEER and a reduction in paracellular permeability as evidenced by decreased FITC-dextran flux (Christman, 2002; Palii et al., 2008; Li et al., 2020). There is supporting evidence in related experimental studies wherein treatment of polarized RPE monolayers with DNMT inhibitors—albeit using 5-aza-2′-deoxycytidine in some cases—did not disturb baseline tight junction markers such as ZO-1 and cytokeratin, and even induced the expression of epigenetically silenced protective genes like clusterin (Li et al., 2020). Although direct demonstration of OCLN and TJP1 promoter demethylation by 5‐azacytidine in RPE under oxidative stress is not yet available, analogous results in other epithelial contexts provide a strong mechanistic rationale. Moreover, the dual activity of the drug – both its canonical demethylating effect and its potential to perturb RNA methylation – may synergize to enhance transcriptional reactivation if balanced appropriately with a low, non‐cytotoxic concentration such as 1 µM (Seelan et al., 2018; Cheishvili et al., 2015).

Overall Evaluation:  
The prospect of repurposing 5‐azacytidine for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) represents a novel and intriguing approach that leverages well‐established principles in epigenetic regulation. On the strength side, the compound’s mechanism of action is thoroughly documented across multiple biomedical studies and is centered on the irreversible trapping and degradation of DNMT enzymes, leading to passive loss of DNA methylation in replicating cells (Christman, 2002; Seelan et al., 2018). This mechanism has been exploited with success in oncology to reactivate silenced tumor suppressor genes, suggesting that similar reactivation of critical genes in non‐cancerous cells might also be achievable. The specific hypothesis that oxidative stress in RPE leads to the epigenetic silencing of tight junction genes such as OCLN and TJP1 is plausible given the known role of DNMT enzymes in mediating gene repression under stress conditions, and the literature supports the concept that DNA methylation is a dynamic and reversible process that can be modulated pharmacologically (Li et al., 2020). Preliminary in vitro findings in RPE monolayer models with DNMT inhibitors, particularly the tolerability of these compounds and their capacity to upregulate epigenetically silenced genes (as seen with clusterin expression), bolster the argument that DNMT inhibition in RPE is not inherently deleterious and may indeed rectify dysfunction in barrier integrity (Li et al., 2020).

Nonetheless, several weaknesses and challenges must be recognized. First, 5‐azacytidine is known to incorporate into RNA as well as DNA, which introduces additional layers of complexity in its mode of action. The off‐target effects on RNA methylation can lead to perturbations in protein synthesis and may result in unintended consequences, especially given the highly specialized function of RPE cells in the retina (Jasielec et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2010). Second, the S-phase dependency of the drug’s mechanism—requiring active DNA replication for incorporation—poses a potential limitation when considering that in vivo RPE cells are largely quiescent. While in vitro ARPE-19 cells under oxidative stress may show increased proliferative activity, the translation of these findings to an in vivo dry AMD setting remains uncertain. Third, the global demethylation induced by 5‐azacytidine does not confer gene specificity; hence, there is a risk that while reactivating tight junction genes, the drug might also inadvertently activate promoters of deleterious genes or provoke inflammatory responses. This lack of precision could compromise retinal homeostasis or even exacerbate pathological processes if not carefully controlled (Mukhtar, 2020; Cheishvili et al., 2015). Fourth, toxicity is a major concern. While lower doses (such as 1 µM) are proposed to achieve a favorable balance between hypomethylation and cytotoxicity, the narrow therapeutic window observed in oncology suggests that careful titration and extensive in vitro and in vivo safety studies are essential before progressing to clinical evaluation in AMD (Christman, 2002; Daifuku, 2025).

Additional challenges include the need for direct experimental evidence to support the specific hypothesis relating to tight junction reactivation. Although the general effects of DNMT inhibitors in reactivating silenced genes are well documented, there is currently insufficient evidence demonstrating that 5-azacytidine directly demethylates the promoters of OCLN and TJP1 in RPE cells subjected to oxidative stress. Moreover, evaluations of barrier function—such as detailed TEER measurements or FITC-dextran permeability assays—have been more commonly reported in the context of other DNMT inhibitors such as 5-aza-2′-deoxycytidine rather than 5-azacytidine per se (Li et al., 2020). Therefore, a critical gap remains in validating whether the proposed epigenetic precision approach can indeed restore tight junction integrity in a physiologically relevant model of dry AMD.

Despite these concerns, the overall evaluation is cautiously optimistic. The robust and well‐understood mechanism of 5‐azacytidine in inducing DNA demethylation provides a solid theoretical basis for the proposed therapeutic strategy. Given that similar epigenetic interventions have successfully reactivated gene expression in other cellular contexts, and considering that preliminary data in RPE systems suggest tolerability and potential gene reactivation, it is reasonable to propose that further investigation is warranted. Initial preclinical studies should focus on establishing the methylation status of the OCLN and TJP1 promoters in RPE cells under oxidative stress and then determine whether 5‐azacytidine treatment can effectively reverse these modifications. Comprehensive analyses including methylation-specific polymerase chain reaction (MSP), chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assays for DNMT occupancy, and detailed transcriptional profiling would be essential to confirm target engagement. Parallel functional assays, such as TEER measurements and FITC-dextran permeability assays, must be undertaken to correlate molecular events with phenotypic restoration of barrier function (Mukhtar, 2020; Daifuku, 2025).

In addition, it would be prudent to perform dose–response studies to delineate the optimal concentration of 5‐azacytidine that maximizes promoter demethylation and gene reactivation while minimizing off-target cytotoxicity. Considering that RPE cells in vitro may exhibit different proliferative rates compared to their in vivo counterparts, alternative experimental models, such as induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived RPE cells from AMD patients, may provide additional insights into the therapeutic window and efficacy of 5‐azacytidine in a clinically relevant context. Finally, given that the global nature of epigenetic reprogramming may lead to unintended activation of other cellular pathways, combination strategies employing lower doses of 5‐azacytidine alongside more targeted epigenetic modulators—such as selective HDAC inhibitors—could be explored to enhance the specificity of gene reactivation and improve overall retinal safety (Li et al., 2020; Nashine & Kenney, 2020).

In summary, 5‐azacytidine represents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD through a novel epigenetic precision approach aimed at reversing the aberrant methylation of tight junction gene promoters. Its well‐characterized mechanism of DNMT inhibition and widespread use in oncology offer a strong biological rationale. However, significant challenges remain, including its non‐selective incorporation into nucleic acids, potential off‐target effects, reliance on cellular proliferation for optimal activity, and a narrow therapeutic index that necessitates rigorous dose optimization. The feasibility of restoring tight junction integrity in RPE cells via demethylation of OCLN and TJP1 promoters is theoretically sound yet awaits empirical confirmation in preclinical AMD models. Overall, while the candidate has substantial mechanistic strengths that support its potential role in restoring RPE barrier function under oxidative stress conditions, its development as a treatment for dry AMD will require detailed molecular and functional validations, careful safety profiling, and perhaps the exploration of combination therapies to harness its benefits while mitigating risks (Christman, 2002; Jasielec et al., 2014; Li et al., 2020; Daifuku, 2025).
